div.p: na d a Sir Andrew Clarke,
For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated.

it is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Aadrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here Is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital "Tea Is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there Is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind Is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions bore and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the house will say to me : ' Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup ot tea.' I say • thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, • I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew.' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and tills thecup up with water. Now I call it positlyecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has beoome so powerful in its effects upon the nervmis system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, BO disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produces alarm of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not Injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the oiti fashioned teaspooaful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within Ave minutes you mast pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what Cals.:W.4 fashioned eels like. The colour of the tea after it is °rowed will be found tote mush paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be iseceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its user is persisted in, It will very soon be found to be much moresuitabie for the system, and if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. "PAPA, why do we wish people a good appetite,' and not good thirst?" "Because that isn't necessary." "WHATEVER you do, my boy, begin at the bot- tom and work up." "But, father, suppose I was going to dig a well?" CHICAGO MAN (to stranger) : "Row are you? ice day to-day. Where do you hail from?' Stranger (German prince) : "Sir, I do not hail; _ .

reign." FIRST IRISHMAN: "Pore Flanagan has jist been drowned." Second Irishman : "flea a lucky bhoy. Oi always thought he'd be hanged." CUSTOMER. (to baker's boy) : "Is your bread nice and light?" " Baker's boy (confidentially) : "Yes, ma'am; it only weighs ten ounces to the pound." WOMAN" (t 0 tramp): "You seem to have an appetite ? " Tramp : " Yes, madam, that is all 1 have left in the world which I can rightly call my own." Gamekeeper to sportsman who has just missed another easy shot :—" I think you wos a bit nigher him thot time sorr." A GENTLEMAN, whose watch had been stolen by a pickpocket, declated that he could not imagine how it could have been taken, as it was continually OD its guard." "OH, Clara, that cloak you are wearing is a perfect fright! You ought to get a new one. Have you seen my new muff?" "Yes, Kate, I saw you at church with him Sunday night." "No," said George Henry, I didn't go there to court the girl, only called occasionally to pass the time, you know; but first thing I knew they had me up for breach of promise, and so, you see, I went to court at last." FRIEND of Ptaywright : "Tell me, now, what do you consider your gleatt.st wukl" wright : "Getting my plays accepted after they are written." "WHAT is your objection to Charles, papa ?" asked Maud. "He plays poker,". said papa. " But so do you. You played with him last night." "I know it—but he won."—American Paper. O'KELLY : "is it breaking yer long neck yez afther in the dark ?" Dolan: "Sere an' Oi can't foind the matches." O'Kelly : "Then strike a bight and Ink for thim like a sensible person." " TnEtz is more pleasure in giving than re. ceiving," was the proverb that a mother was trying to instil into a youthful mind. "That's true about castor oil, mother," was the answer she

got. " JOHN," said Maud, when she caught her fiance throwing a kiss to her former rival, "I am afraid you are fickle." "Indeed, I am not," replied John innocently. "I've always loved that girl." " HELL°, old man, have any luck shooting?" "I should say I did ! Shot 17 ducks in one day." "Were they wild ?" " Well—no—not exactly; but the farmer who owned them was." OLD FOGEY (reading paper) : "It says they weighed anchor; but confound them, they don't say how much it weighed. What I want is facts, but these netvspapers never tell what a man wants to know." THE day before a duel. "I assure you, sir, that I mean business, air." "And I too, sir." "There will be at least one corpse, sir." "I quite agree with you, sir." "And it won't be mine, sir." "Nor mine either, sir." AN excellent story is told of a British soldier in Egypt. His colonel, observing bins one morning wending his way to camp with a fine Egyptian rooster in his arms, halted him to know if he had been stealing chickens. GENTLEMAN (at an evening party) : "Madam, will you tell me why low dresses are called full dress' ?" Lady: "For the same reason, I sup- pose, that a picked chicken is called a dressed chicken.'" "ANYONE can see with half an eye," remarked the potato to the plum pudding, "that you have got an awfully swelled head." "On, rot !" rejoined the Autocrat of the Christmas Table, "you're the unfortunate fellow who's always get- ting famines up; but I bring only joy to mankind." A FRENCH newspaper defines a fugitive to be "a coward who has the courage to manifest his fear." The same journal tells of a lady who was buying a jersey at one of the fashionable shops. "It it really well made?" she asks. "Oh, Signora; is is made with a conscience. Don't you see how elastio

WHEN GIRLS OUGHT TO MARRY.—" No," said a fond mother, speaking proudly of her twenty- five-year-old daughter, "no, Mary isn't old enough to marry yet. She cries whenever any •, one scolds her; and until she becomes hardened ' enough to reply vigorously she isn't fit for a wife." "Timex we shall have an eirly spring, Farmer Robinson?" inquired a visitor. " Wa-all, can't I say much 'bout that, but there's soroe indicashuns • of it." " What are they?" "I had seven letters from city folks Saying they'd be up to see me 'fors " WHY don't you go to work?" said Yorick to his eldest born. "Don't you know that a rolling atone gathers no moss ? " "Well, father," replied I I the lad, "not to evade your question at all, but 11 merely to obtain information, may I ask of what earthly use all the moss in the world would be to 1 me? I don't want to build any blooming bird's I nest." s4l—" Sweet, what a lovely ball we are having ' this evening." She—" Ye-es I Delicious." He-- I " Trfave you ever attended a military ball?" No, have you?" He—" Not exactly, but I saw one once taken out of a man's arm." She—" Oh, did you?" And then she thought a few moments, 1 but nothing occurred to her that would enkble her to get even. A certain doctor who was noted for a keen eye to business was driving along the street of a coun- try town, when his horse took fright and ran away. I He was thrown violently oat of his trap, and ren- dered senseless. Presently he recovered a little from his. unconsciousness, and, noticing the crowd 1 which had gathered about him, asked, "What's the matter, gentlemen? Anybody hurt? I am Dr. B---. Can Ibe of any service ?" The most experienced judge of human nature -may at times find himself mistaken. Dr. X is one of the kindest of schoolmasters, but incessant vigilance has made him ocoasionally over-sus- picious. At Latin class, the other day, his eye fell on a boy, to whom the order was given, "Jones, go out of the room, and take that sweet out of your mouth." Jones, a shy, timid boy, attempted to speak, but was quite inaudible. A titter ran round the room, as the boy next to Jones replied, "Please sir, he can't. It's a gumboil !" ASTONISHED PATIENT.—A well-known physician once seat his man with a box of pills to a patient, I and a hamper containing six live pullets to be left at the house of a friend. Unluckily the messenger ' bunglqj over his errand, and took the hamper to the •eht and the pills to his master's friend. Imagine the consternation of the patient on re- ceiving along with the fowls the following pre- scription: "Two of these to be swallowed every half-hour." A Berlin scientist proves conclusively that the generous use of salt is condu- cive to longevity." Cowboy: "Well, there, no denyin' that fellers as is too fresh don't live long out our way." "I AM an Agnostic," remarked a young man, In swelling accents. "And an Agnostic is what? inquired an elderly gentleman. "An Agnostic.', replied the fresh youth, in a manner expressive of his pity for his interlocutor's ignorance —" an Agnostic is a fellow, you know, who isn't sure of anything." "I see,' replied the old gentleman. "But how does it happen, then, that you are sure you are an Agnostic 1" JOITNTY bad been to the house of a neighbour to play with the children. "Well, Johnny," asked his mother, on his return, "did you enjoy your- self ?" "Oh, yes, ma; and they are going to have Irish stew for dinner 1" "Haven't I told you times out of number that you must never repeat people's -nses ?” "But, what you have beard at ma, I didn't hear any thing about the stew; I ..-znelled it with my nose."
"CAPITAL" CHAT.
-- The Duchess of Su theriand,w ho is already known as an authoress, is, the "Bookman" says, engaged on a novel dealing with English social life. She hopes to found a literary salon in London. •

Mr. Cecil Rhodes has altered his plans since he arrived. He will not return to S.,uth Africa before the end of November according to present arrange- ments. After this week he intends to give himself up almost entirely to company business.

Lord Cromer had more than one interview with Lord Rosebery before he left for Egypt, and is said to have received satisfactory assurances as to our future policy in that country. He has not yet de- cided to retain his present post after the end of the winter. Sir Auckland Colvin and Sir Gerald Portal are expected to visit him before Janurry. Both are spoken of as likely successors if he resigns.

To Bonnerjee a Bannerjee succeeds. This, per- haps, is the best way of notifying the change—it is but a slight one—in the secretaryship of the Indian National Congress. The secretary who spells him- self with an" o"is on his way to Bombay. His successor, a learned pundit from Ripon College, Calcutta, has started for England, and is to have a reception at which Mr. Dadabhai Naoroji will pro- bably preside, early in December.

Leicester has lost its lady doctor by the death, at the age of 46, of Miss Mary Royce, L.S.A. The deceased lady took up the study of medicines as an adjunct to the charitable and philanthropic work she had conducted for nearly a quarter of a century in one of the poorest districts of the town, and it was amongst her own people,as she loved to regard them, that she chiefly practised. For more than a score of years she conducted, almost single-handed, a class for youths and men which numbered nearly 100 members.

A change is to take place immediately in the conduct of the " Art Journal," the oldest of the -- an." ntmia. 'rho otlitvrahip Ir.oe boon con- ferred on Mr. David Coral Thomson, the well- known director of the Goupil Gallery in Bond- street, and the author of an excellent critical biography of the chief masters of "the Barbizon School. ' Mr. Thompson was connected with the " Art Journal "from 1881 to 1885, so that he will bring to his editorial duties a good deal of previous knowledge of the work, as well as wide experience of artistic matters gained in other ways.

They seem to have no difficulty in Australia in getting their public men to write on all manner of topics. In the " Antipodean," the new Australasian annual which is to appear at Christmas, Sir Henry Parkes will not only have a couple of poems, but also an imaginary conversation between a couple of worthies. Sir Samuel Griffith, the Premier of Queensland, is to contribute an article on the Kanaka question, and the Hon. W. 0. Hodgkinson, Minister for Education in Queensland, will have a contribution entitled " Ah Kim ; or, Is Marriage a Fraud ?" Sir Henry Parkes's two volumes of re- miniscences ought to be ready very soon now.

Archbishop Vaughan is now engaged in making his visitation to every Catholic mission or church in his diocese. His Grace, on these occasions, cxamines the financial condition of the mission and schools, and goes minutely into everything con- nected with the due administration of religion. Moreover, he publicly invites any members of the congregation, who may wish to see him privately, to do so, to make complaint of any shortcomings on the part of their pastors. It is some time since such visitations were made, and quite a stir has been caused in Catholic circles. The Archbishop will not receive any.addresses, having stated that the one be received on his elevation to the archbishopric will suffice for the entire diocese.

Mr. Matthews, the late Home Secretary, is now I touring the colonies in company with Mr. and Lady Hilda Brodrick. Up to date no Antipodean Press- man seems to have succeeded in getting an inter- view with the most unpopular member of the Salis- bury Government, but there are some anecdotes about him circulating in the colonial papers. One of them alleges that when a young barrister Mr. Matthews was characterised by a phenomenal and practical piety. He joined a Roman Catholic con- fraternity whose chief object was to labour for the spiritual benefit of the poor. It is said that long before " slumming" became a fashionable pursuit. Mr. Matthews was wont to spend much spare time in the courts and alleys around St. Giles's and Drury-lane. We never heard that over here.

Mr. Sleath, who has just been sentenced to two years' imprisonment for his leadership of the Broken Hill Silver Mine strikers, has proved himself a splendid organiser of labour at the Antipodes, and the savagery of the sentence just pronounced upon him is the best indication of the unpleasant sensation his abilities have inspired. Long before his two years are up he will be repre- senting his fellow-miners in the New South Wales Parliament. One of the present labour members of that Parliament was also sentenced to two years for his connection with the shearers' strike, but he was out in less than a month, and defeated at the polls the wealthy squatter who had previously em- ployed him. Mr. Sleath, as secretary of the Broken Hill branch of the Miners' Association, was the life and soul of the strike against the contract system.

Miss Ada Rehm:, the well-known actress, has' according to the latest American mail, been paid a remarkable compliment. She has accepted the in- vitation of the promoters of the World's Fair at Chicago to stand as the model for a magnificent statue of Justice, which is about to be cast for the great exhibition. She has been chosen for this honour as being, physically, "one of the most per- fect types of American womanhood." Now, as it happens, Miss Behan is not an American. She was born in Limerick, spent her girlhood days in that historic city, and rejoices in the good old Irish name of Crehan. She was ten years of age when her parents emigrated to the United States. All the same, Miss Rehan is a worthy model for the figure of Justice. The statue is to be in solid silver, Bft. high, and will stand on a gold pedestal. Sixty thousand pounds is the estimated cost.

The Grand Duchess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, who has just arrived in London, fs an English princess She is, in fact, the Princess Augusta of Cambridge, the sister of the Duke of Cambridge and the Duchess of Teck, aunt of Princess May, and the Fitz Georges, and daughter of the Dowager Duchess of Cambridge, who for so many years occupied the house in St. James's Palace which will shortly be the bridal residence of th., Duke of York. The Grand Dueness herself in the Duchess's lifetime had a certain por- tion of this house set aside for her, which had staircases of its own and could be shut off from the other part by a door when the twe ladies were not" friendly." The Queen, however, never con- firmed this arrtingement, and so it lapsed when the Duchess died. Since then the Grand Duke and Grand Duchess have taken a house in James-street, Buckingham-gate, which is known as Mecklenburg House. Here they generally spend a portion of the season ; but as the Duchess has only come over for a flying visit she is now staying at the Savoy Hotel.

div.head: CLOSING A COLLIERY.
div.p: CLOSING A COLLIERY.

The Whitehaven Colliery Company have decided, owing to the sharp competition in the coal trade and the cost of output, to close their Wellington Pit. Nearly 500 men will be thrown out of employment. MR. JOHN MORLEY AND EVICTIONS.

Mr. John Morley, replying to Sir Frederick Milner, who thinks the inquiry by the Evicted Tenant's Com- mission will not serve much good purpose unless it deals with the causes that led to eviction, says he has no in• tention of opening a court to try either Irish members or Irish landlords. Parliament. press, and platform furnish ample room for these recriminating scuffles and barren skirmishes. He seeks a way out of a practical difficulty, and he hopes and believes that the Commission will be both received and conducted in the sensible and conci- liatory spirit that marked the discussion on the subject in the House of Commons in June, 1891. He designs the Commission to be an agent of healing and of peace ; not an occasion for reviving old irritations. Ilk other words, he means business, and not a mere movoAn an angry game.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1892.
DOWN BY THE SEA.

, IrWITROETT—THE—BASSINETTEI Y.JOHN PEERS. tv 4,.. ; -‘-:-. 4. '(concluded.) Thursday was to have been devoted to a re- visiting of Penarth. But man proposes ---" and has sometimes the misfortune to be accepted" growled the much married cynic. But, as one swallow does not make a summer, so one dissatisfied Benedict need not stop the marriage bells. My citrator, my guide, philosopher, and friend, found that his duties called him to a place happy in the name of Ty derwen deg—the house of the fair oak—where some Corporation work had laid bare a section of the Silurian rocks. So I gladly availed myself of this opportunity of making the acquaintance of an old friend—the trilobite—at home. We here disin- terred from its old time resting place the remains of a shell-backed creature, like an exaggerated wood- louse. Now this simile may not add dignity to this find, but in a country which pays respect to a man because his ancestor "came over with the con- queror," even this lowly creature should hold high rank. For it lived and flourished, and found its grave here millions of years before the earth in the fulfilment of its mission, had achieved the latest—if not the last—of its animated triumphs in the shape of man. The time this little thing tells of makes the hoar antiquity of Egypt or Chaldcea fall into mere matters of yesterday. In these old world Silurians we have evidence of the lapse of time which, to ephemeral man, is a veritable eternity. Vainly does the mind attempt to comprehend the magni- tude of the period elapsed between then and now; a period so vast that the whole of the known his- tory of the world is too small to be used as a gauge to measure its immensity! And yet some of us take a pride in the fact that an ancestor" came over with the Conqueror !" How does this little pride look when viewed in the light of the fact that the common ancestry of mankind is to be traced even further back than the Silurians ? These are in leed topsy-turvey times, when a living shellfish, the Tinzula. can boast a longer line and bluer blood than all the Howards ! After a very pleasant afternoon spent in thus resurrecting this ancient nobility we returned to Cardiff, bear- ing a few characteristic representatives of the period. Friday, being the laA working day of my stay here, was to be spent in a visit to the beech beyond Lavernock Point. In pursuit of this plan I took train for Barry, and walked on past Barry Castle the very existence of which the porters denied, so low are the mighty fallen—a pictur- esque old ruin built of the local flaggy Lies lime- stone. A quarry of this on the left hand, some half a mile further, was probably the source from whence the stvie was got to build this old-time strong place. A hasty overlook failed to detect any fossils in this disused delph. Here the road began to descend one side of a steep, thickly-wooded glen, with a brawling brook making appropriate music below. Very pleasant the leafy shade afforded by the interlacing branshes over-head, through which in occasional glimpses could be seen the white- flecked blue of a lovely day near high noun. Soon this pleasing umbrageousness gave place to an open park-like glade through which the white road wound in serpentine curves until again lost in the embrace of the opposite tree-clothed slope. But here I left the beaten track, and followed the lead of the brook to the sea. The afore-mentioned glade gradually opened out into a marshy shore, across which an embankment kept out the sea. But here the rising tide and a projecting cliff ren- dered furthei advance inadvisable, if not impossible. This made a detour necesssary. So my old friend the dusty road was sought, along which 1 plodded in search of Mr. Storrie's six-feet-long specimen of plesiosaurus—the swan-neck lizard of the Lies, lying at the cliff's foot somewhere—but where ? Inquiry of the natives led to no result. They had heard of such an occurrence, but could not answer the more important question, where? An old man whom I found mending his ways—the highway—was par- ticularly inqusitive as to the when, the how, and the why of the matter? "Came out of the cliff did it, how had it got there ?"got there when that part of the cliff was the sea bottom ! How then had the sea bottom become the cliff? &c. &c. ; I might have been there now expounding the elements of geology to this brother of the stone- hammer. But, " Ars—including science—/onga " —how does it go? But the long and the short of it is, that life—especially that part of it I can spend here, seeking the Lies lizard—is all too short to satisfy the intellectual cravings of this ancient Welshman.

By subsequent direction I found my way down to the cliff head, along which I walked to find a practical descent to the beach. This walk along the breezy cliff head I shall never forget. The salt- laden wind swept quickly up the cliff face, fresh and bracing. The wide though land-locked Bristol Channel lay rolling at my feet, its further shores just dimly blue in the distance, its surface enliv- ened by here and there a sail. And here on the very edge of the precipitous cliff itself dense masses of blackberry bushes grew, crowded with fruit, ripe, and ready to the hand. The fruit to me seemed firmer than our own, and not 80 delici- ously juicy. After a while, I came upon a sort ef ravine of the depression in the cliff, down which I could climb to the beach. And what a beach to walk along, or to be cast upon from the sea I Here the great has edges stood like giant stony-ripples but sharp edged, and some five or six feet thick, tilted to an angle of some 25 or 30 degrees. To walk along such a beach was not an easy task, but the novelty of the task made I.ID for the difficulty of its achievement. The usual Has fossils were again m evidence. In a softer band bet ween the thicker lime stone strata gryphera ineurea of rather large size. This is a pecudar-looking shell which Paddy has named " The Devil's toe-nail." Surely his black- ness must have had a frequent change of toe nail ; he must have sloughed it pretty often to have left so many behind him. The walk back was very pleasant when it became less heroic, and the fast-falling tide enabled me to pass the before impassible—Bull Cliff I think was its name and on to the before-mentioned embankment. Here I found a lot of people assembled to enjoy themselves. One section had been amusing themselves by kicking a football, which had resented the indignity, and avoided further maltreatment by a flight over the bank and far into the water, upon which it sat com- placently, rising and falling with the waves, as though mockingly curtsey ing to its late tormentors. As the wind was off shore, all the gamesters could do was to throw vengeful pebbles at the jeering spheroid. And of such ammunition there was no stint, for tons upon tons were piled upon the sea- ward face of this embankment—the debris of the cliffs on either hand. And indeed a strange sound did the waves make among these loose has pebbles, as I got to a more exposed part of the shore. The incoming wave would bring up a great quantity of these rounded stones with a noise chiefly its own, but the retreat was accompanied by a rush and a rattle quite strange to one used to the less noisy behaviour of our sandy surges. But now black clouds gathered over the tumbling water and above the cliff along which I had come, looking threaten- ingly for rain, so I hastened towards Barry. Only a threat after all, but I had left without a sight of the saurian. The boards by which this treasure had been covered, and which were to have been my in- dication of its locality, had been washed away. 60 I lost my chance of seeing this old world swimming lizard in gilts. But my compensation for this loss was ample if the pleasure of the trip was alone to be counted; though the bag was not empty for I had secured a few more of the fossil labels of this forma- tion, including the said satanic toe-tips. Saturday morning was devoted to packing my treasures for despatch by rail, and in bidding good- bye to places and to folk, in which, and with whom, I had thoroughly enjoyed myself. The return train was timed to start from Cardiff at 1.45, which promise it fulfilled by leaving the station before the next hour was up. The return journey, taken as a whole, was a very pleasant one. To watch the varying changefulness of the flying scenery, and when this palls to note the almost in- finite variety in the persons and individual charac- teristics of one's fellow-passengers, is in itself a diversion, and often more than that—highly in- structive. Upon first entering the compartment in which I travelled, it presented the appearance of a nursery—or an asylum for foundlings. One young- ster—in the earlier stage of that period—was repos- ing at full length on the seat, in sole charge of which two elder ones presided. To our great re- lief, however, a more responsible nurse turned up, and exercised maternal jurisdiction over the lot. My vis-a-vis w!is a young lady, evidently of a lite- rary tut ti of mind, if one might judge by the assi- duity with which she alternately took notes of external phenomena, nibbled biscuits, and pored over her novelette. I was the victim of a curious longing to see the inside of this lady's head, if it could be done without inconvenience to her, curious to find if the threads of old plots were not even still threading the mazes of her cerebellum I

In maiked contrast to this one was the lady in black—dark, dour,and dolorous—possibly not with- out cause. There was the old grandmother with the picnic basket, and the sulky child made much of by its mother, which became the sulkier the more there was made of it. There was the statue.que young lady in the far corner, whose face—sphynx- like in its tixitude—never changed from first to last. So much so, that one almost longed for a collision or some minor catastrophe—to test its stony steadiness. However,eventually, the journal she was perusing ceased to attract, and the stately head, with its toppling superstructure of bonnet, gradually reclined more heavily upon the five- button gloved hand—and Nature had her revenge— she had conquered Art. Past the little roadside statiens we flew contemptuously, and after a some- what prolonged stay and a change at Chester, the train discharged me at —so far as my railway journey was concerned—
THE TEILAIINTJS.

div.head: SELECTED READINGS.
div.p: SELECTED READINGS.
HOW A CONJURER WAS "HAD."

The Chevalier Hermann contributes some inter- esting stories of his life to the "North American I Review." He says: It is certain that every presti- digitator since the world first knew of necromancy I has met with accidents, and although I have been singularly lucky in this direction, I was fooled once,' and in a very peculiar way. I paid a visit to the Paris Bourse before the asphaltum pavement bad been put down around the square upon which that great monetary institution stands. The square was then paved with regular block pavement, which, owing to the great traffic, was frequently out of repair. While inside the edifice, I had seen the stockbrokers and heard them howl in their frenzy of speculation, and my mind had wandered off in altogether a different direction after I got out and stood on the broad granite stairs of the temple of Mammon with a few of the stockbrokers, friends of mine, who had gathered around me and asked me to do something." A gang of workmen stood directly before us, and one of the stockbrokers said "Why don't you play a trick on them?' I thought I would. I walked down the broad stairs among the pavers and extracted from under one of the cobble stones a 100-franc gold coin, which is about the size of one of our double eagles. Instead of being amazed, the paver looked at me and said, "Mollie," meaning half. There was a law, at least at that time, in France that the finder shall have half of anything found. I, naturally, did not want to give up half, and I thought it would be a good thing to find another coin, so as at least to show the fellow that it was a trick, and straightway I put my hand down again and brought out a five-franc piece. The paver looked at me again, his face wreathed in smiles this time, and once more said, "Half," which would be 52i francs, rather a good day's earnings. Well, as I did not seem willing to give up half, as he wanted, he began to talk loud. I then changed my tactics, explaining to him that it was a trick ; and to illustrate it I picked up a five-centime coin of the reign of Louis Philippe (an old pocket piece I happened to have with me), but even this failed to satisfy the workman, and his wild gesticulations and loud talk having collected more than 500 or 600 people around us, I thought it best to compromise with him. But no, he would listen to no compro- mise; he clung to his rights tenaciously, and I was compelled to give half, not alone of the 100-franc piece, but of the five franc piece as well, and then he insisted upon having even half of the 10-sou piece.

div.head: AN HEROIC DEED.
div.p: AN HEROIC DEED.

" A ship ashore A ship ashore ! " was the cry which ran through the streets of St. Andrews, Scotland, one fearful winter day more than three- score years ago. The thiilling cry aroused every inhabitant. Citizens, students from the University, and sailors rushed with pale faces and rapid steps along the streets towards a bay to the east-ward of the town. Standing on the shore the crowd was terror-stricken and paralysed through beholding a vessel stranded on a sandbank, but a few rods from the beach. She was shrouded in sully mist. The waves dashed furiously against her, and broke over her decks with irresistible fury. Yet, through the thick air and the driving sleet, the people on the shore could now and then catch glimpses of the doomed crew clinging with the clntch of despair to the rigging of the wrecked vessel. There were many bold, brave men in that sympathising erowd of spectators, but none who dared to venture through the mighty surges to save those ill-tated sailors. It seemed, indeed, to the stoutest

heart, too mighty a task for7mortal Man to attempt All could sympathie with the wrecked ones; none but God, they thought, could save them. But there was one heroic soul in that eager, wistful crowd who thought that man, with God's help, might snatch those perishing men from a watery grave. He was a young man, a University student, strong in body, but still stronger in spirit. "Bring me a rope !" he cried ; " 1 will try to save them." A strong rope was brought and fastened about his waist. Followed by the prayers of many and the good wishes of all, this chivalric youth struggled with desperate courage through the terrific surf into the deep water beyond. Then with the strength of a young giant, guided by the skill of the experienced swimmer, he slowly worked his way towards the vessel's side, lie had nearly reached it, when his friends, alarmed by the length of time and slowness of his progress, bogan pulling him back. Then his courage rose to the sublimest height of self-sacrifice. He forgot himself. He would save the men clinging in desperation to yon vessel's shrouds, or perish in the attempt. Grasping the knife that he carried between his teeth, he cut the rope by which his kind-hearted friends were drawing him to shore and safety. He buffeted the big waves successfully. Ho reached the breaker- swept deck of the stranded sloop. After a word of cheer to the crew, he took a fresh rope, plunged anew into the surging waters, and swam back to the beach. But four days of starvation, unrest, and exposure had robbed these poor creatures on board the wreck of both courage and strength. Not one of them dared attempt to escape by means of the rope. What then? Must they perish P Nay, not yet. The brave student will risk his life again in their behalf. Many speak harshly of their lack of pluck. He pities their weakness. He rushes into the surf once more, struggles through the crested waves, boards the sloop, and brings off a man to the shore. Six times he makes the perilous trip, and saves a human life each time. The seventh time his charge is a boy, so weak and so helpless that he loses his hold upon him twice,and twice he dives for him into the seething depths and brings him up. Finally he reaches the beach with the limp corpse-like lad,the last of the rescued crew. The crowd which had hitherto watched the gallant young hero's movements with breathless stillness, now break forth into a loud, triumphant cheer, which neither the roar of the wind nor the thunder of the waves can drown ; they recognise the presence of a genuine hero. The name of this noble young scion of true chivalry was John Honey, one of the college friends of the celebrated Dr. Chalmers. His effort on that memorable day cost him his life; not directly, how- ever, for he lived a few years; but the seeds of a mortal malady were sown by his humane exertions on the grandest day of his life. Ile died at Ben- doehy in 1814, and Chalmers preached such a grand and thrilling sermon Neside his open grave as led one who heard it to say: "I have seen many scenes, I have heard many eloquent men, but this I have never seen equalled or even imitated." The man was worthy of such a sermon. No deed of war, no act of knightly chivalry, ever rose to a loftier height of moral nobleness than young Honey's rescue of those Scottish sailors. It Was bold, brave, cool, perilous, persistent, and, above all, humane. It was in deed and in truth heroism of the highest type.

div.head: IONIE,
div.p: IONIE,
PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY
CHAPTER XXI7I.

"YOU ARE BETROTHED TO ANOTHER, BUT YOUR HEART IS STILL MINE." It SO happened that lonie and Elaine had both been invited to a yachting party which was to take place the following week, and each—not expecting the other—had accepted the invitation. There was criite a party assembled on board the Hespera, when lonie and Miss Carriscourt made their appearance; and among the first they beheld was Arthur Rochester and Miss Granger. _ _

"They are here 1" murmured lonie-, turning pale. "Oh, Miss Carriscourt, let us turn around and go back. Believe me, I wish it most earnestly." "It is too late now," responded that lady. "Every one has seen us. Never fly from trials, my dear," she counselled wisely. "It is better far to meet them." - And with a smile on her face, though her little trembling hands were as cold as ice, lonie moved forward with wonderful self-possession. She was a general favourite, and very popular among her companions, and was soon surrounded by a bevy of young gentlemen and ladies. Arthur Rochester had bowed coldly, and turned haughtily away. lonie never knew what she was saying to those about her; her heart was beating so, and her head was throbbing. The objective point was a villa far up the Hud- son, where the party were to dine. Then, when the moon was up, gilding the water with thou- sands of arrowy sparkles, they were to set sail for home.

lonie was the gayest a the gay. No one, to have seen her, would have guessed those bewitching smiles covered an aching heart. No one could have believed that those bright eyes were heavy with unshed tears.

They reached the villa at length, and, after lun- cheon, there was an hour or more in the garden, a veritable fairy's bower of roses, gleaming statues, and rippling fountains. Arthur Rochester studiously avoided that portion of the grounds in which lonie was, being devotion itself to Elaine; so much so that even her jealous heart was satisfied.

But strange fate had decreed that they should be brons,ht together. As Arthur was standing in the midst of a group of young ladies his hostess came up to him, lightly touching his arm with her pearl and gold fan.

"If our friends will excuse you one moment, Mr. Rochester, there is a slight commission I have for you," she said. Excusing himself from Elaine and her friends, he turned to Miss Desmond, his hostess, with the charming smile that characterised him. "I am at your service, my dear lady," he said, gallantly. "Pray, command me." "Do you see that young lady standing over there across the grounds, near the fountain I" she asked.

Following her glance, Arthur bowed assent. "It is Miss Deering. Kindly say to her for me that we should be delighted to have her come to the parlour and sing for us. If I asked her she would refuse. She could not find it in her heart to refuse a similar request from you." "If you have failed to persuade Miss Deering, it Is quite useless for me to attempt to argue the ques- tion with her," he declared. . .

"I did not know but what you might suggest that you would assist her," replied the lady, archly. "I will do so," he replied, smilingly, "but I really imagine that will cause her to decline al- together."
With a courteous bow he left her, walking swiftly In the direction of the lady standing so silent and motionless in the dusky twilight by the fountain.

Overhead the golden-hearted stars had come out one by one and fixed themselves in the purple night sky, where a young moon hung like a cres- cent jewel, throwing its pale, dim light on the scene below.

The sighing wind trembling among the roses and amid the green foliage, where the fairy lamps gleamed and glowed, did not warn the girl who stood by the fountain of approaching foot- steps. She stretched out her white arms to the night sky with a bitter sob : "I cannot hear it " she cried out. "Heaven forgive me I I wish I were dead I " A step sounded on the green grass beside her, but she did hot hear; she did not heed it. . .

"Life is too bitter 1" she cried, piteously. "How long will it be, I wonder, before it ends I" Arthur Rochester had approached so near that he could have reached out his hands and touched her from where he stood. He saw, to his dismay, that It was not Miss Deering, but lonic. He forgot his errand— -forgot everything save that be stood once more in the presence of the girl he loved.
"lonic, he murmured, softly. She turned, with a startled, stifling cry, exclaim- ing, falteringly:
- • " Arthur —Mr. Rochester!"
"Yes, it is I, lonic," he said, adding, earnestly: "Why do I find you in tears? I am a strong man, but the sight of them weakens me, Are you ill—or —or—unhappy, dear?" _

The tender: 'Word slipped from his tongue quite before he was aware of it. He saw her shiver and turn away. Better that there should be coldness and anger between them than kindness. "I am neither ill nor unhappy. Thank you for your interest in inquiring," she said, icily. " lonie, you cannot deceive me like that," he cried. "You are unhappy; I can see it. Tell me why V' "You have no right to ask," she responded, proudly. "I have a right," he retorted, flushing, then "Do you think one who loved you as I have loved, can see you in grief without being deeply toucht d The words she tried to utter died away on her

lips. "You are soon to be wedded," he went On huskily, " and I find you in tears. Oh, lonie, try to deoeive the world as you may, you cannot deceive me. You are not marrying for love, and without love life will be one long torture. Now I pray to you, plead to you to look well before you take the final step." Suddenly he stopped short. Was he not walking blindly in the same path himself "Your supposition in this case is entirely un- founded," she said, coldly. "I am the best judge of my own heart."
"You are right," he said, bitterly. "Pardon me for interfering." . _

A sudden impulse came to her to kneel at his feet and tell him all; tell him bow she loved him—that parting from him was more bitter than death,—to cry out to him to save her from the fate that awaited her. But no—it ninqt not be.

He held out his hand to her, with wistful, yearn- ing eyes. Good-bye," he said, huskily : "from this hour I shall not cross your path, if it be in my power to avoid you." She bowed her head with haughty, careless grace and turned away, but the great, intense efforts at self-control were too much for her; as she took the firsestep forward she swayed suddenly to and fro, and would have fallen, if be had not sprung forward just in time to catch her in his arms. But she had not swooned; she struggled out of his embrace with a death-white face, and just in time to be observed by Elaine, who had come through the grounds in search of him. Elaine stood quite still as though rooted to the spot, and neither of them saw the gleaming white face throutrh the lilac branches. She should have made her presence known to them, but she did not; instead, she looked and listened with breathless interest, while the breath that passed her lips seemed like scorching fire. "You dre ill, Tonle," cried Arthur, anxiously. "In Heaven's name, bear me.' Do not turn from me._ Let me take you to the house, dear 7" . _ _
"Leave me, Arthur," she sobbed. "In pity's name, leave me:" :
She tried to draw her little hand from his clasp, but he held it firmly.

"lonie," he cried, huskily, "a terrible thought is burnimg its way to my brain—ft Is this: though betrothed to another, your heart is din mine. Do not, in this critical moment, seek to deceive me; for other lives than yours and mine rest on your answer." -

"Arthur," she answerid, piteously, "do not utter another word. I cannot bear it. Leave me. My heart is breaking. Do not make my cross harder to bear than it is." "Tell me this," be persisted, hoarse with emotion: "Have you learned to forget me, or is there some- tbackofal this .that has tkrtt been made clear

to me. You must speak, lonie." " Fate, whico I could not control, parted us," she whispered; "parted us just as surely as though one of us lay in the grave." Then, without another word, she left him—left him standing there looking after her, half blind with pain and 'egret. It was not of her own free will, then, that she had sent him away.
The thought was like new life-giving elixir to him.

"I should have probed the reason to its very foundation," he cried, excitedly, pacing up and down. "It is not too late yet. I will find out who and what it is that has parted me from the only woman whom I have ever loved, or could ever love."

In that moment of intense emotion he forgot Elaine, forgot the whole world, all save bole, aad the maddening thought though betrothed to another—she loved him still. . He had no desire to return to the merry throng he had left. It would be only torture for him to smile, to talk calmly, while his heart and his head were in such a mad whirl. He lit a cigar, and gave himself up to conflicting thoughts. As he paced up and down under the trees, clench- ing his strong hands together, and calling huskily upon lonie's name he never knew that, not ten feet distant, stood Elaine, with her heart on fire with jealousy as bitter as ever wounded a girl's heart.

CHAPT ER XXVII THE TRAGEDY. The longer Arthur Rochester pondered over lonie's words, the more convinced he became that there was something terribly wrong some- where. And while he was trying to solve the difficulty his hostess came to him. "As I live I—actually pa cing up and down l—day- dreamOng!" she cried, advancing, with a merry peal of laughter. "Do you know we have been looking everywhere for you, Mr. Rochester. You are very near being left behind. The party is just about returning to the yacht." These were the words that recalled his scattered senses. He walked quickly back to the house with his hostess, finding his friends already assembled on the porch. "T must apologise for my seeming carelessness, Elaine," he said, crossing over to where she stood. "I hope you will pardon my seeming neglect." "Where were you, and what detained you 7" she asked.

"I must plead guilty to smoking a cigar, pacing up and down under the trees," he answered, with a flush on his face, the meaning of which she well understood. He tried to talk to Elaine as he accompanied her back to the yacht; but it was a dire failure. His voice was husky and his sentences abrupt. Even had she not known all, she must have understood he was under a stress of great mental excitement. Not once did he glance towards lonie. He felt if he should do so he would lose his self-control. There was laughter, mirth and merriment as the white-winged yacht shot throught the waves on the homeward trip; but three hearts among them I were heavy enough. ' At length one of Arthur's friends called him aside to settle a question that had been brought up by one of the gentlemen present, and which a num- ber of young ladies were laughingly disputing. "I will remain here," said Elaine. ' He had scarcely left her ere she beheld lonic standing quite alone, a little way from her—an im- pulse which she could not control. Rising quickly, she crossed over to where lonie stood and laid her hand on her arm. "Arthur !" exclaimed lonie, faintly, turning fear- fully around. A bitter, sneering laugh fell from Elaine's lips. "It is not Arthur," she said, with bitter sarcasm. "It is Arthur's betrothed." lonic uttered a little startled cry as she saw the expression of the beautiful face looking into her own in the moonlight. "Miss Granger !" she faltered, more frightened than she would have cared to own. "Let me speak I" cried Elaine, in a tone of con- centrated fury. "I want a plain answer to my question. In the past what was Arthur Rochester to your "That is a question you should ask him," re- turned lonic. "As for me, I have nothing to say." "You loved him once!" cried Elaine. "And you love him now, even though you know that he is betrothed to me." "MISS Granger !" exclaimed lonic, in dismay. "Do not attempt to deny it 1" hissed Elaine. "Now listen to what I have to say to you. Do not come between my love and me. I will not brook it. There are thing women can forgive each other, but never that." "I have not sought to do so, Miss Granger," re- turned lonic, "nor would I." "I presume you think because he loved you once, a word or look would bring him to your side again; but I warn you to leave him alone. If you do nnt heed my words, beware my vengeance," cried Wane, in a low, sibilant whisper; "for it would fall upon you as surely as the sun rises and sets." She spoke with such fishing eyes—with such a threatening face—with such power and passion— that lonic shrank back, pale and trembling, from the terrible avalanche of words. "Let me pass l" she cried, haughtily. "I will hear no more." "You shall hear!" cried Elaine, clutching her arm more fiercely. "I am not done with you yet." "I shall not be detained against my will," replied joule, indignantly. In struggling to free herself from the other's hold lonic took a sten backward, and then— ,Cl4. -Wht) h&U pkture ill There was a dull, heavy 'thud as of a body striking the water; and } Elaine, standing there, fairly paralysed with horror, heard a faint org, then all was still. Her lisst Impulse was to cry aloud, " Helpl help! there has Ibsen s terrible accident. Miss Lawrence has fallen Into the water.. To her rescue, quick, for the lore of Heaven 1" Itried in-atter the words but they died away on her 'lips, leaving no sound. tragical the moon never shone upon a more relent tu all her rounds. The silver beams fell en the dark water—on the white-winged yacht, H with its groups el handsome maidens and brave , men, and a the figure of the horrified girl standing apart from the rest like a marble statue. It was terrible to see how she (wept to the brink and looked over it. It was scarcely a moment since Tonle had fallen in, but to Elaine it seemed endless interval Should she cry out for help to save the girl whom Arthur Rochester loved? Her heart almost ceased to beat at the thought. Her first terrible folly commenced in not putting the thought from her; there was danger in rumi- nating over it, a peril so horrible that she should base shrunk from it. The tempting voice of con- science whispered more boldly because she had listened to It : "Why should you save the girl who stands be- tween you and happiness? Arthur Rochester's heart will never turn to you while she lives. You would but have to stand motionless while the
yacht cleaved through the waters, leaving her far behind.

" Decide your own future. Will you save her whom your lover loves, when to save her means endless misery, fiery jealousy and innumerable heart pangs from you?" She did not cry out for help again. She did not see the waters cleave and the lovely white face rise above it for an instant, then as quickly dis- appear again. It was a weird, horrible scene to see Elaine crouch there, her face all wild with horror, gazing down into the waves where lonie had fallen. She had listened to the tempter's voice too long. She knew that she could have raised her voice, and with one word, one cry, have saved lonie ; but she did not utter it. The terrible force of the mightiest temptation that ever sued for the mastery of a human heart had overcome her. The moment was gone. She sank coweringly back in her chair ; the yacht sped on through the moonlit waters; and lonie was left by her rival to her terrible fate. As she sat there she heard some one break out Into a happy song in a rich, trolling masculine voice. A moment later three or four of the gentle- men joined in. "They would not sing if they but knew," mut- tered Elaine, with a gasping, terrible shudder. She listened to the words that fell from Arthur Rochester's lips, and her heart grew bitter, , cold and hard, for she knew he was singing for lonic 's benefit, thinking she must be listening to him. The words seemed to have a double meaning to her now, invested with all the yearning pathos of Arthur's fine voice. "She cannot hear him," she murmured,with a wild laugh, creeping to the railing and gazing fearfully down into the curling waves. Word for word, Elaine repeated the words after him, as he sung them. , Of coarse, they were meant for lonic not for her.

"What have I done that one face holds me so, And follows me in fancy through the day ? Why do I seek your love? I only know That fate is resolute, and points the way To where you stand, bathed in an amber light; Since first you looked on me I've seen no eight. What have I done? "What can he done? As yet no touch—no kiss, Only a gaze across your eyes blue lake ; Better it were, sweetheart, to dream like this, Then afterward to shudder and awake. Love is so very bitter, and his ways Tortured with thorns—with wild weeds overgrown. Must I endure—unloved—these loveless days? What can be done?" Miss Carriscourt, who had been talking to a party of ladies, looked about carelessly for lonic. "We are almost home," she said to the young lady nearest her. " lonie will be sorry. Young people are never satisfied with their fill ot pleasure, I often think." As she spoke she arose, and with a smile on her lips, started in search of her charge, among the throng of laughing, merry, chattering girls. Where was lonic? She did not see her. A moment later, the yacht touched the dock, and the nimble-footed lassits and their escorts were not slow, midst the laughter and mirth, in reaching terra firma. Miss Carriscourt looked around blankly. " lonic I" she called, "come this way, my dear. I do not see you." Even as she spoke her heart sank with a strange misgiving. No lovely face turned toward her. "lonic," she called again, raising her voice, "where are you ?" Arthur Rochester was making his way swiftly toward her. "What is the matter, Miss Carriscourt 7" he asked anxiously. She raised her terrified eyes to him, whispering in a fright; "Oh, Mr. Rochester ! I cannot find lonia. Where can she be? What can it mean?" (To be continued.)

div.head: NO SUMMER IS BIUGHT TO
div.p: NO SUMMER IS BIUGHT TO
EVERYBODY.

'WM does not remember the summer of 1887, Jubilee summer It was indeed .1 the Queens 3 weather*" for weeks and weeks. Only an occasional shower felt to moisten the earth and freshen vegetation. For the rest it was warm, brilliant sunshine all over the coun- try ; such a season as England does does not get nearly as often as we should like. People sat out of doors in the evenings—a thing not common. Saving a breeza once in a while the seas that girth Britain sparkled in the sun like jewels under a lamp. Yes, it was a summer that most of us marked with a white stone. And how the multitudes enjoyed it ! Yet not all, for when the heaven's rain quails somebody's dish is sure to be upside down. The following story tells us where one woman was and what was said to her whilst others were having holiday. _ _

div.head: [COPY.]
div.p: [COPY.]
I Charlotte Austed, of Church Street, Minster, near Ramsgate, Kent, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows :

In August, 1872, after a premature confinement, I fell into a low weak state, and did not gain strength. I bad a tired, heavy, weary feeling. At first I had a bad taste in the mouth, dry and parched lips, and thick phlegm covered my mouth and teeth. Sc bad was this that I was often forced to rinse and scrape my tongue and mouth to get the slime away. I had a poor appe- tite, and what I ate, however simple, gave ma pain at the chest, and I would retch and vomit until all food was rejected. Iliad great pain and tightness at the chest and both sides, as if I was bound, or held in a vice also pain between the shoulders and back. My heart would thump and throb so much that I trembled and shook from head to foot, and I was mazy, and feared that I should fall down in a fit. Later on a watery fluid or gas rose up into my threat and seemed as if it would choke me.

One night after a bad attack, 1 found that I had com- pletely I,)st my voice, and I could only speak in a whis- per. From that time, December 1372, I date 11137 serious trouble. I was attended by our doctor for over six months, and he gave me all kinds of medicines, but I got no relief, and became weaker and weaker. The doctor at last said he could do no more for me, and gave me a recommendation to the Canterbury Hospital (1 was living at Broadoak, Kent, at the time.) . _

I went to the hospital and whilst there was seen by several doctors, but from the first they held out rove hopes of my recovery. The, all said that I was suffer- ing from inflammation and weakness of the stomach. Whilst in the hospital I had frequent fainting Ats and would lie prostrate and lifeless for hours together and was so weak that I had to be lifted in and out of bed. After being under treatment seven months I was dig- charged as incurable and my husband was sent for, 11'13° took me home in a closed carriage. Upon reaching home! was placed in bed and our doctor sent for. After a time I got a little better, but was not long before I had a relapse and was again sent to the hospital. I continued in this half dead, half alive state for nineteen years, during which time I had to go as indoor patient to the Canterbury Hospital seven times. The hospital and other doctors all said "that my case was hopeless and incurable." When last in tke hospital (in 1887) one of the doctors who took a great interest in my case said to me. "Mrs. Austen, there is no hope for you. WA3 have tried everything that is possible, and nothing more can be done." I now gave up an hope of ever getting better in this world and kept on suffering until December of last year (1890 Just before Christmas), when I was at death's door. I had my bed in the sitting-room and was attended by a mefli- cal gentleman, but I got worse and worse and felt that my end was near. I had suffered so much that I prayed that God in his mercy would be pleased to take me, for I was tired of life. These pains became worse than ever and I had grown so weak tlaat all my friends thought I could not last much longer. My voice now was so faint that the doctor had to place his ear near my mouth to catch my words. Just at this time my daughter Annte, who was attending me, had a book given to her, and in it she read of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Cara- tive Syrup having cured a case similar to mine. Annie xclaimed, afte r reading the book," On mother, do try Seigel's Syrup." I said, "My dear, I have not the the money (for owing to my husband's death my MeaDs were very small), or I would." Hov,-ever, a ImlY friend who came to see me gave me a shilling and I put three half-pence to this and at once got a bottle from Minster. After taking the Syrup three days! found a little benefit my voice was stronger any my food gave me strength, and for the first time for years it digested. By the time I had taken half a bottle I could rest at night (for before I did not know what it was to have a good night'! rest ) I gained strength every day and ri,,vcr 10,l(e,1 behind after this, and soon all pain lett in and I went about my house well and strong. By talciii4 an °CO- sional dose of the syrup I keep well and am better at the present time than I was twenty years ago, that is before my trouble began. I consider that Seigel's SrruP has saved my life, and I thank God for making it known me, and have since my recovery thanked Aim daily for giving me the means to get the medicine. I tell every one I know of what Seigel's Syrup has done for me, and I wish others to know what saved my life after all other means failed. I hereby give my full permission to tbe proprietors of the medicine to make any use they think proper of this statement, in the hope that other poor sufferers may be benefitted. And I make this solemn declaration conicirmtiously believing the same to be true, by virtue of the provisions of the Statutory Declaration Act, 1835 (5 & 6 William IV., c, 62).

_ Declared at Minster, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County I of Kent, this 24th day of (Signed) June, 1891, the deponent 12LOTTE A tiSTEN. having affixed her Signature I Her X Wadi. in my presence, Before me,

(Signed) EDWARD PARRY, j A Commissioner to administer Oaths in the Supreme Court of Judicature. It was the old, old story. Alas ! how many times it is told when it wouldn't be, if men and women were some degrees wiser than they are. The story of indigestion and dyspepsia not recognised, or mistaken for sometking else, until the chance to cure had nearly slipped away. Well, thank Providence, fortune favoured Mrs. Austen at last, and the summer of 1891 (when we chanced to see her) was, better than that of 1887, even with weather incomparably worse.

div.head: BEWSEY FORGES.
div.p: THE BEWSEY FORGES.
AN UNSCIENTIFIC DESCRIPTION.

Together with the Englishman's friend, an um- brella, the writer set out the other evening towards Bewsey Forges. A thin drizzling rain was falling, the darkness was deep, thick, and supreme, and the gas lamps shed no lights stronger than could be derived from a candle in a scooped out turnip. Possibly the fault was not so much on the side of the gas, as on the side of the weather, or the Cor- poration. The town appeared to be forming itself into an English Venice—or a city of waterways. But as an averageWarrington pedestrian doesn't appreci- ate stalking into a puddle of water every other stride, this must be passed as an uninteresting item. The purpose of the visit was to view the various depart- ments in the forge and to write a description thereof. To an unsophisticated mind, this seemed a pleasant enough .duty ; but it eventually evolved itself into an almighty and unsiarmountable task. Attached to the manufacture of some of the most unimpor- tant looking beer barrel bands, the writer saw there was .an appalling cord'oination of the deep efforts of scientific minds, of clever engineering skill, and of ddft manual workmanship. He saw sufficient in the construction of ,one machine alone to render his stlescriptive pen cress-legged in the nib with petri- fication. So he ,concluded to give his readers a description of whet came under his simple observa- tion, unhampered with the customary garb of •scientific statistical pants, or technical jacket, or ltnalytically deducted and conclusified hat.

OUT OF "*.I'HE NIGHT INTO THE MILL. "Step carefully over the rails," said the guide *"and follow me." We had passed through 'the large gate at the Bewsey entrance, plunged into the 'dark damp night, and were crossing the yard. .Awat ahead sounded the clink, clink.; the bang, 'bang, the cog, clink, bang, of hammers hitting the sheets and plates of iron; and of engines puffing, like some overworked monsters, out of breath with their task. Ever and anon a lurid glare light up portions of the yard, and ascended skyward, reveal- ing the tall chimneys which towered their heads into the dark night, and the cloud of creamy look- ing steam which rises, as a little boy remarked, "to make more rain." Presently the guide said '"now step up here." With limited and gingerly agility, the writer mounted three steps. But as suddenly as though there had been at work some pantomime fairy's wand, 'the scene had changed." We were out of the night now, and were in the steel wire mill. The floor was constructed of thick plate iron and declined towards the ground from the point where we stood. But we were occupying

AN EXCITING r. OSITION. The visitor is usually started through the maze of many wonders from this point and gets a vivid impros- 'scion of that mill stamped upon his mind if he 'doesn't get any other impression. Sometimes a plate of sheet iron leaves an impression on his toes; but that's his own fault. When he comes from the darkness of the night and finds hims( If standing in the said position on the iron floor his impressions are startling and varied. At first his eyes are dazzled by the sudden glare of light, and the next moment his nerves twitch with fear, like overstrained fiddle strings. Coming swiftly towards him, hissing and twisting like some dreadful reptile- monster there is a red hot length of steel wire. On. on it comes, twisting here and twisting there with dreadful litheness., It hisses by your feet 1 Its endless body wriggles on and on in a rapid, unceasing length of shimmering heat. New it bounds from the ground as though it would encircle your leg. Your opening mouth betrays the coming- cry; but the guide suavely turns the frightful animal off with his urnbr elle, and kindly pretending not to uotice your alarm, observes " Its rather dangerous to get too near this wire some- times, because it would take your foot off if it caught it." Then he invites you to step over the wire and follow him, which you do ; and then wonder why the

WORKMEN WINE THE OTHER EYE at each other, and make weak attempts not to smile. But having gained more courage, you endeavour to gain more information. So the guide explains to you that in this department they make a kind of steel wire to any thickness. It is generally made-for wire mills in town and one often sees lurry loads of it being con- veyed to yeti ous places. You are taken round to a

STACY OF LONG STEEL BARS some inches thick. ihis you are told is bought by the company and reduced to any thickness of wire neces- sary. Then the process is pointed out. There is a large combustion furnace consisting of gas and coal heat. There are two men who look after this. They place the bars of steel in the furnace and get them into a condi- tion of" white heat." Branching off a few feet above the furnace you see the reducing and elongating patent. Nor being a mechanic you don't understand the con- struction of this ; but it seems simple enough. There are four square shaped mysterious machines. They look like large iron boxes to you, with holes in them. At the front of each affair, and on the iron-plated floor before mentioned, there are some yards of space just protected by an iron border a few inches high. Well now we get to the process. The men at the furnace have lifted the large door. The fierce heat shoots out and gives the surrounding stacks of iron a ruddy, shadowy aspect. The men have placed their large iron " tongs" in the furnace; and out they pull the white-hot bar of steel. It is carried to one of those box like apparatus, and the end placed in one of the holes. The whole of it disappears and in going through that little hole it comes out the other side

div.head: CONSIDERABLY LONGER AND THINNER.
div.p: CONSIDERABLY LONGER AND THINNER.

The man at the other side seizes it with tongs and turns it back into another hole. It goes through. The man wipes the perspiration from his face with his bare arm and probably whistles softly" We knocked 'em in the old, Kent-road." Then there is a splash'! rarr ! rarr !ra ! The I bar has come again. It darts out of the hole at aterrific rate, all red and seething hot. The end that comes out is seized by the man who whistles. He is wonderfully cool. With his iron tongs he quickly takes up that end of the substance, lifts it from the ground, circles it above his head, and thrusts the end into another hole in the apparatus. And all the tignelle is doing that the re- mainder of the hot rod is running, spinning, and bound- ing along the iron bed until its length is run, by which time the first end is coming out of another hole. This system goes on through the four elongating boxes until, when it reaches the last, that steel bar—probably two yards long and four inches square—has been elongated without loss of actual substance to a long length of Finch wire. It was the last part of the process we saw on first entering the mill. That snake-like creature was the elongated bar, and as it skipped along by us it was running into a wheel and wrapping itself into a bundle to be sent away. About 500 tons of those steel bars are made into wire weekly.

IN THE SMELTING MILL. " The men very seldom get hurt there" said my friend, as we marched along the dark yard again. After shinning it a little—that is, placing your shins with some force against unseen obstacles—We came to a big cloud of steam. The guide uttered three brief words. He said," Follow me straight," and disappeared into the cloud. I shipped a good cargo of wind, plunged into the steam and murmured 'suppose I'm going to walk into one of those wells I've heard of." But my anticipation was groundless for the next moment! stood by the side of my friend gazing upon one of the most impressive sights I have ever seen. This was where all the iron ore was smelted and made into solid blocks of iron. I tried to collect myself and seem scientific, and make criticis- ing inspections of the process. But I couldn't ever settle my thoughts, for they fizzed around like a newly mixed seidlitz powder. I felt I had arrived at the biblical capital renowned for its tropical heat and sometimes called Flades. Everything about was fire. All around were furnaces throwing out a combined heat and glare which blinded the eves, and scorched the face, and caused the flesh and Clothes to fraternize so much that they couldn't be parted. Before you, behind you, and all around you there darted an incessant army of men and youths each conveying on a small iron truck large, ponderous balls of red hot iron, which looked like con- solidated lumps of heat. Right in the centre of the department stood a tall man, to whom all these fire balls were taken. He stands there a mysterious looking being, and if he was labelled " Old Harry—the King" you would draw your breath and whistle gently in surprise.

- - THIS IRON KING'SSFACE is concealed by a wire mask,his legs are encased in plate iron leggings, and most of his other limbs are similarly protected. He is tall and sinewy. As we see him now he stands upright holding in his hands a long pair of grippers. In a moment one of his legends is here with a fire ball. It is quickly lifted on to an iron block, and then the next moment there is a loud crunching bang. The steam hammer has struck the fire ball and the tall man stands there in the centre of a thick heavy shower Of sparks looking like a centre piece in a large November firework. The sparks are gone. The tall man applies his grippers and turns the fire ball round. Then the sudden crunching bang of the steam hammer comes again, the blinding shower of sparks again appear, and die away. And so this noes on day 3nd night—of course with differ- ent men. The red hot fire ball is the heated iron ore. It is called pig-iron, because, one of the men said, it is so dirty. Whilst going through the heating process this pig iron is cleansed of all its native filth, and by the time it reaches the steam hammer it is pure iron. The steam hammer beats the fire ball until it becomes a shapely square or block of iron which we shall see used hereafter. About 2,000 tons of this goes through those furnaces and under the steam hammer weekly. (To be continued.)
