ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

The victory which Warrington achieved iltAltvie League Competition on Saturday, gives one an itchiv:g to figura- tively slap the whole team on the back, as& in resonant tones of joy and exultation, shout out the discrepit, much-used and bald expression "good old wire- pullers I" But it would be better to do the shoulder slapping figuratively. Somehow, if you hit a Warring- ton footballer on the back, he genera:Ay wants to smack you back again. "'Smack,' you back again ?" Why the phrase echoes itself back just into the very question which lots of people were going to put to 'Smack' Bate when be made his appearance on the field again on Saturday. Therwere even shaating : "Smack me bo- yah, so tha's getten back lad." He said he had, and to all intents and furposes they believed him.

at although " Smack " Bate had got back, many people were of the opinion that Broughton hadn't got backs—or had got very weak backs at any rate. Their half-backs and full-back were exceedingly poor, and were undotibtedly muck responsible for Broughton's failure, whir.th, by the way now places Warrington at the head of the list. Tomlinson, the full-back, appears to be an artist or a poet, for several times he stood still -and allowed the leather to pass him, whilst "Ili, eye, In a fine frenzy rolling. Doth glance From heaven to earth, and from earth to heaven." But Warrington likes those kind of players amongst hcr opponents

Whilst in this pleasant allusion to backs of a weak character,we might mention that Broughton Rangers are suffering from the loss of two backs who are accused of weakness, but who withal, were men who did lusty and commendable service for Broughton manipulators of the leather. These men were known as the Brothers Jams, and as rumour portrays them there they were a kind of modern Siamese twins. They came from Swan- sea some time ago and jainedthe Rangers. Then the charge of weakness was brought against them. But it wasn't the weakness which emaciates the face, and leaves in tlipant freedom flowing to the breeze the 76. 61. tweeds which hide away in darkness two teitfrafining legs! No, the Bros. James were accused of a weakness for Mammon. It was said they were bribed to leave a Swansea team, and to become professionals. But the football authorities after an investigation, found no evidence to show this, and for the present will not allow the James's to offer their brotherly help to any but a Welsh team.

But to revert to the victory on Saturday. It must of course have been ostensibly one of the plums which it is ordained Warrington shall receive. But it was a plum which had its dry, parched, exterior and large stone. Warrington won by three tries to nothing. Yet they did not play as they ought. In the first ,part of the game the forwards—such hard working men withal—were overcome by an ineffable imagining 'of their superior prowess. They walked about the field with the non- chalance of so many Borough surveyors. Thereupon Broughton forwards went for them right and left, and in the words o f ancient history, "did much good and hard service, and did thereby bang 'em that they clut- tered." And they only" cluttered "in time ! Brough- ton were quite their equals in forward flesh. When Warrington did get properly under weight, then they , displayed their strength. The passing of Bate was brilliant, and 'twas he, aided by nimble Evans, who brought about the best of the victory just before the interval, when Heesom and Webster did their duty with the tries.

Then there is the coming—or perhaps it would be better to say the "come"—back, Boscow. Well, the "Athletic News," and other papers say of him, "he played a brilliant game at full back, never making a mistake, and if a guarantee of Saturday's form could be given he would be just the very man for the county." We reiterate this remark, and we add "give them the guarantee Boscow. Go into the county, and shed some more glory on your native team." Of the three-quarters very little can be said, except that Plumpton was play- ing under the distress of a sore and painful throat. Turning to the forwards we feel called upon to offer G. Hampson some commendation. lie is a recruit from the "A" team. He is well built, active, very plucky, and will one day come out as one of our leading players. Fair Turner, Jolley, and Ashton were all also in good "trim."

Since Saturday the results of the Lancashire Rugby Cup Competition stand thus : For. Agst. Pid. Won.. Lest. Pro. G.T. G.T. Pts. Warrington Swinton 3 2 . 0 . 1 ... 2 1 ... 0 0 ... 5 Salford Rochdale Hornets St. Helens Recreation 2 ... 2 ... 0 ... 0 ... 1 3 ... 0 0 ... 4 Wigan Tyldesley Broughton 4 . 0 2 2 ... 0 1 ... 1 4 ... 2 Oldham Broughton Rangers The prospect is fine for Warrington. They are almost the pronounced winners. But there is one chance of thorn losing. They have got to keep down an iron heel on Swinton. They are only two games behind. Stand firm Warrington!

By the way is there anything in the rumour that Warrington first team is going to pay its officials ? Some of them certainly have a little more work to do. than can be modestly brought within the focus of pleasure.

Next Saturday Warrington meetthe St. Helens "Rees." at St. Helens. If they are to retain their position at the head of the list they will have to give the "Recs," no quarter. The latter have only lost one match this sea- son, and their friends the " Sainte " on Saturday piled four goals and a try against Sale, the second boating this season. Their aggregate score is 12 goals 23 tries against 2 goals 2 tries. Their real form will be severely tested during the next few weeks., when they meet such strong teams as Tyldesley, Runcorn, Morecambe &c., and if they pass through this ordeal successfully, they will be certain of a fine record att the end of the season. But speaking of the " Recs." A Manchester contempor- ary says: They will " during the next few weeks decide their future position in the Lancashire Cup Competition." Lucky " Recs!" The only team so privileged in the whole competition. How Rice to be able to decide I whether they will take the cup or not. But wont the other teams help them in this responsible undertaking? Maybe Warrington will sympathise with them on Satur- day and do something towards deciding the" Recs." position.

Mr. Percy Davies, the presidentef the Football Club, has offered a beautiful cup for the winner of the War- rington junior clubs competition. The cup is displayed in imposingly in a shop window, in Bridge-street. Alongside it there also stand two other cups. But the Quarters in which these two cups will be bestowed is a secret. Mr. Davies has locked it in his bosom, and there he says it will remain until the end of the season, when he will suddenly make two unexpected parties happy hv rewarding each with a cup. Those cups will then be "cups of happiness," but Mr. Davies does not say they will be " full."

_MISCELLANEOUS. With the death of sunny summer there comes the de- mise of the wheelman's season. For a few months this knicker-bockered spectre will cease from making rapid incursions to far-away houses of refreshment, lie will he missed chiefly by policemen and barmaids. War- rington cyclists, together with their friends from the district, had a kind of wake on the "dead season" on Monday night. They held a ball at the "Gym." They all kept awake all night, and had a pleasant, happy, union. Subsequently they had a bitter parting. There were few of them who did not shiver when they entered the bitter atmosphere of early Tuesday morning, when they " slid " quietly home in the growing dawn and evening dresses.

Speaking of the " Gyna." reminds us that no one has yet offered a public welcome to the new conductor of that institution, Mr. John Kinsley. He.arrived here a few weeks ago as the successor to Mr. Alexander. Mr. Kinsley was a pupil under Professor Renshaw at the Manchester Y.M.C.A. Gym. for seven years. Out of those seven years he was a'• leader " for six years, and is considered to be one of the Professor's most creditable pupils. He took several medals there for all round athletic abilities. But he debarred himself for amateur honours early. Whilst still a pupil, Profess,•r Renshaw used to take Mr. Kinslev to the various big sports in the country, and the two gave gmnastic displays. Mr. Kingsley would only do this for a salary, and thus became a professional. For some time he was a teacher at the Salford "Gym."

In 1888 Mr. Kinsley was appointed as conductor to the Douglas Gymnasium. In 1892 he left there and took control of the Swansea' Gym." He left that place a few weeks ago to come to Warrington. Mr. Kinsley's system is slightly different to Mr. Alexanders. But that naturally follows as the Manchester and Liverpool athletes work by two different systems. The Com- mittee of the " Gym." has not yet decided whether to enter the annual National Challenge Cup Competi- tion.

In a few weeks Mr. Kinsley expects to have under control some hundred boys from the People's College schoots, Heath-side schools, Wycliffe schools, and the Roman Catholic schools. The masters of these schools, we, believe, are considering the matter. There is no doubt they will give their boys the advantages of a littls athletic recreation, for there is certainly, amongst most schoolmasters, a growing regard for the import- ance of boys obtaining as much manly exercise as pos- sible.

CONVICTION OF ANOTHER WAR RINGTON PUBLICAN. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Mon- day, before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Aldermen Harrison, Sutton, and Francomb, and Mr. E. J. Guest, Patrick Flannaghan of 7 general-st., was charged with being found drank on the 25th of October at the Old Crow Inn, Fennell-st., kept by John Woodward Powell. Powell was also charged with permitting drunkenness on his premises on the occasion. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared for the prosecution of both defendants, and Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, for their defence, and it was decided to take Flannaghan's case ' first. —lnspector Spinks said at a quarter past one p.m., on the previous Tuesday, he visited the Old Crow Inn, and saw Flannaghan drunk, pouring out 'beer from a jug into a tot glass. He offered him the glass to drink, but he refused. Some distur- bance subsequently took place in the house, and he complained to the landlord, and Flannaghan was put out. He staggered across the street several times, and a man who was in his company was taken into custody., and he tried to take him away. The man gave the I name of Patrick Johnson, and Flannaghan met Sergeant Taylor next morning outside the Police Station, and gave him his correct name. He said to Sergeant Tay- lor, " What do you want me for ?" and the Sergeant asked him why he had given him his name as Johnson the previous day at the Old Crow Inn. He replied, ." never saw you, but [was there early that morning, and had a lot of drink." When witness saw him at the inn he had his arm round the neck of a young woman named Sarah: Ann Hansbury, and was kissing her. —On the landlord saying that the men had better go out, witness put Flannaghan out by the shoulder, and he staggered and fell.—By the Town Clerk : He was assisted by the woman Hansbury up Dial-court.-By Mr. Knowles : He could have walked home staggering, without assistance.—By the Bench: He would have locked him up if the woman had not taken him away.—Alderman Sutton : He was in a position to go without assistance; that is what I Wen—Alderman Harrison : If a man staggers he is not able to go without assistance.—Wit- ness, in reply to the Town Clerk, said Flannaghan, did not fall in consequence of the push he gave him.— Surgeant Taylor said on the evening of the 25th of October he went to the inn for the purpose of executing a warrant against a man who was there. P.C. Lewis also went in. They found ten persons in the tap room, among them the defendant, who was drunk. On the table was a jug containing about a pint of beer, and glasses. The defendant offered witness and Inspector Spinks a glass but they refused, and he drank it him- self. He said he was Patrick Johnson, gentleman, School Brow. Witness afterwards found he had given the wrong name and address, and went to the defend- ant's address, and next morning saw him, when he said he did not remember what had taken place. He said that what drink he had on the Tuesday was at the Old Crow.—By Mr. Knowles: Neither he nor the woman could stand very straight when they went out of the Inn. He might have got home without assistance.— Mr. Knowles A policeman's might means a peat deal.— Wm. John Lowe, engine driver on the ship canal, said Ire was in the inn at the time. The appearance of Plannaghan was consistent with his being drunk.—This , concluded the case against Flannaghan.—Mr. Knowles said if that was Mr. Whittle's case he was very much surprised, and denied that there was evidence to prove that he was drunk. He remarked that Alderman Harri- son had some time ago quoted Mr. Justice Lopes's defini- tion of drunkenness : Not drunk is he who from the floor, Can rise and touchy call for more; But drunk is he who prostrate lies Without tke power to speak or rise— and lie felt sure that as far as Alderman Harrison was cencerned the deferdant would not be convicted after that quotation on the part of the Alderman. A man looking a little flushed or a little fishy about the eyes could not on that account be said to be drunk.—The Chairman Mr. Harrison assures me your quotation is not correct.—Mr. Knowles: Justice Lopes's I—Alderman Harrison: It is not incorrect as far as its meaning is cohcerned.—The Chairman: We have a new definition this morning.—Mr. Knswles related an anecdote about an Irishman who got drunk on St. Patrick's Day who got amongst some trees, and said as he ran against them " I will sit down till this St. Patrick's Day procession gets past. (Loud laughter.) That man he said was drunk: (Laughter.) As to the defendant being found drunk, to be found drunk a man must have lost himself through drink and been picked up somewhere, which was last the case with his client.—Patrick Foy, labourer, 18 Platt-st., deposer' that he had some beer with the defendant on the date in question at the Old Crow, and that he was perfectly sober.—Jobn Finnerty,forge labourer,6B,Gockbedge-lane, also testified that Flannaghan was sober.—The defendant also asserted that he was sober on the occasion, stating that he only had a share of two half gallons divided among ten or twelve.—By the Town Clerk ; He gave Sergeant Taylor the name of Patrick Johnson and told him he lived in School Brow. He and a constable came next morning to witness's house for his real name, and he told them to find out. When he saw Sergeant Taylor on the 26th, he told him he was somewhat forgetful when he was drunk and could not remember anything that took place. Now he remembered everything.— Ihe magistrates, after ten minutes' private consultation, con- victed the defendant, and fined him ss. Mr. Knowles expressed astonishment at the decision. The charge against John Woodward Powell was then proceeded with. The defendant pleaded not guilty.— The Town Clerk cited a case to show that it was no de- fence to a charge of serving a drunken man with liquor to say that the publican did not know the man was drunk.—Mr.Knowles : We are not charged with serv- ing but permitting.—Alderman Sutton: Do you mean that the publican is responsible in either case P—The Town Clerk: That is the clear meaning of the decision. —Alderman Harrison thought such an absurd interpre- tation of the law, that if a publican served a drunken man, believing him to be sober, he was liable, was monstrous,and ought not to be tolerated.—ldr. Knowles said a man could not be convicted tinder such circum- stances accordingto common law.—The Town Clerk said the decision he had cited, was that if the high court and was binding on the courts below.—Mr. Knowles: That applies in cases where a publican is absolutely careless as to his duty.—The Chairman: I take it that the Bench can always take the circumstances into account.—Mr. Knowles assented to this.—The Town Clerk said ignor- ance by the publican was no excuse.—Alderman Sutton:

Club, a match between Mr. Thomas Hatton's Steel Grey Kate, oc the Seven Stars Inn, Warrington, and Mr. Dainteth's Spring Tit•el Jack, of the Dog and Dart Inn, Warrington, was decided. The 'cenditions were to trot two miles level, in saddle, for a*take of £5O. Odds of 30 to 20 were betted en Spring Heel Jack, but Mr. Dainteth's horse suffered an easy defeat. After going a lap Steel Grey Kate led by SRIC lengths, and Spring Heel Jack breaking twice, the leader increased her advantage to a dozen lengths at the half-distance. She maim ained her lead to the finish, winning by twelve lengths. Result :—Mr. T. Hatton's g m Steel Grey Kate, 16-0, W a rri n gton Bassnett 1; Mr. Dainteth's b h Spring Heel Jack, 14-3, Warrington Houlton 2. Won by twelve lengths. Time, 6inin. 43isec.

But surelv we sit for the purpose of ad ininisteri ng justice. —inspector Spinks repeated his evidence as to Fianna ghan being drunk, and said .ke pointed out to the landlord that the man was drunk, and he replied that he had had no drink for the last livair. Witness asked him why he allowed hira to remain there an hour drunk, and Powell replied ‘• Well we are in a curious neighbour- hood." Flannaghan and a Iran named Walsh, were also drunk, became noisy, and 'were put out. Walsh was I charged at that court with being drunk in Dial-street, , and convicted, and sent to jail in default of payment of I the fine. Powell was in court at the time, and said none 0 the men were incapable. In the course of Inspector Spinks's cross-examination, Mr. Knowles took exception to the way he answered his questions, and said if he answered him like that in other courts, he should tell him not to be so clever. He ought to be ashamed as a police inspector to answer like that.—ln- spector Spinks : Thatis all right.—ln reply to Afr. Knowles, he said the Old Crow Inn had had a bad reputation in certain respects before Powell came to it, but there had been no complaints as to these matters, since he took it. The locality was a rough one.—The Chair- man: We know f*r 30 years the house has had a bad character.—Mr. Knowles: And he is the man that has improved it.—P.C. Lewis having corroborated the inspector's evidence, Mr. Knowles addressed the court in defence. He remarked that Mr. Spinks looked like a teetotaller,and had, no doubt, a sen- sitive nose for smelling drink on a man.—Alderman Harrison : Ile is not a teetotaller.—Mr. Knowles said he thought he was. (Laughter.) Be denied that Flannag- hall was drunk, and pointed out that this was the first charge Powell had had against him, and urged the Bench not to ruin him by convicting him for what at most was an act of carelessness, supposing the man was drunk, Powell beings man 35 years of age, and having a wife and four children.—The Bench, after a quarter-of-an- hour's private conversation, convicted the defendant, fining him 20s. and costs, the license not to be endorsed, but the Chairman said they considered it was not a case in which the owners ought to expel him from the house, considering his character' simply because of this one case, in which, perhaps, he might have exercised a little more discretion.—Mr. Knowles thanked their Wor- ships, remarking that he was sure the owners would take their expressions into consideration.—The Town Clerk said he entirely endorsed the remarks of the Chairman.

div.p: " BAUR CLUB, AN-SETRA."

By Gyow, lads! Patricrott's the shop Fer deawnreet fun an' glee; So wheer yo go, yo count go wrung, Yore beaun' to hey a epree. In oatber North, Sewn, East, or West, l' every nook an' place, Tole puzzle lung befoor yo find A seaur er freawnin' face. Theer, yo may jine a fost-rate club, Wheer yo con play at Bows, Or Cards, or Billiards, or owt else, An' never hear o' rows. Theer welly ev'ry neet eth' wick Eaur Garden Angels caw; An' tho' ther's noan on urn we wings, They're genooin' to aw. Theer, three o'th' cronies allus ring Fer Irish whisky cowd ; Wile t'other three wud rayther hey " Glenlivet," if its owd I Theer, too, ther's one—but aw'll not breathe His name fer fear o' war— Duz like the smook an' flavour o' Another mon's cigar ! But if one, gettin' warm, shud ax A mate to stond him treat; Eaur good owd Cheertnon stops him we— " Nowe, thee be th' fee toneet Suppose yo wantet t' hey a" do" Fer th' wives' and childer's sake, To hey not very far to go, To buy yore Eccles Cake. Dear Eccles ! welly cover't o'er Wi' chapel an' we church, Built up by pious foke, to keep The Divil in the lurch ! I' one o'th' grandest chapels theer, Sum pleasant heawrs aw've spent; For tie congregation look'd so nice— So thoroly content. An th' Parson Bed, if we shud hey A trubblet-soul complaint, Eaur heart's desire shud be, to cum l' contract wi' a saint But ow wur not so ta'en we him, 14' heart wur we the choir, Wheer th' orgin plays a greyt part, an' St. "Frances"" Strikes the lyre l" Wheer—but, howd on !—yole noan want me Yore yeds wi' church to crom ; To mebbe know, i' church affairs Aw'm noan so mitch a-worn. Beside, like th' Pilgrim wi' his peyse. liw'm tired, an' sore we segs ; So, wishin' luck—good luck—to ow, Aw'll wind up— TUM 0' PEGS. Nyowton God bless o'. Nov. 4th, 1892.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES
AT WARRINGTON.
FIRST OF THE COURSE.

On Monday evening, the first of a course of lec- tures in connection with Victoria University, was given in the Museum Lecture Hall, by Mr. P. S. Wortington, ALA., of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, on 'Architecture as a record of history." The lectures were profusely illustrated with lantern slides, which were thrown upon the screen by Mr. Councillor Monks. There was a pretty large attendance. Mr. R. Davies presided, and said as president for the year. of the Literary and Philo- sophical Society, he had been asked to introduce the Lecturer. He had very great pleasure indeed in showing his sympathy with the movement by attending the lecture. It astonished him that a number of people were quite content to carry about with them a lot of happy ig- norance. They would live amongst vegetation and in the country, and would not know an oak from an elm or a beech,and walk out under the starry skies,yet if they were asked where the constellation of the Great Bear, the belt of Orion, and the Pleiades were to be found, they could not tell you. In fact, he doubted very much whether a great naany people in Warrington had ever seen them to know them. So it was with architecture. People went abroad and through their own country—and they need not go out of their own country to and admirable examples of architecture— I and saw a building, and unless they knew something about it no associations were called out, they saw it just as they would see a picture or the side of a moun- tain, and went away knowing nothing more about it. He took it that the object of the lectures was to deal with that part of their education which had been called liberal, and he was quite sure that everyone in that room, especially those who made a practice of attending the course, would derive not only pleasure but a great deal of information from what they beard. Mr. Wortington then delivered his lecture. In the course of it he said one often heard of the architecture of Greece or Rome or France or England, as if each was stparated from the other by a gulf as distinct as that which divided Dives from Lazarus. That was net the case, the story of architecture was one continuous whole. One style had grown out of the other, and there had been one continuous development up to the middle ages. • The building of Cologne Cathedral had been going on for 500 years. It was one of the finest things ever planned, and if it had been carried out in the spirit in which it was commenced might have been the finest building in the world. But it got beyond its time, and the spirit went off the workmen. Fine as it , was and beautiful, you got a feeling of cast- iron in looking at it. It was merely a working to drawings, and they were not worked out in the spirit in which they would have been had the work been exe- cuted at the time when such work was being done in larchitecture. It was not an original building ; archi- tecture was an imported art in Germany, and that was why the architecture of Germany was inferior, as a rule, to that of France. In France, however, he pointed out —and England had never got so low as that country in this respect—there had been a decline from true art, the , spirit of which had gone off the workmen and the more massive and masterly conception had been lost in the mere desire for clever work. In a perfect building, perfect work and perfect conception were combined, and he thought, there was really not one building in the world that combined these two except the Parthenon at Athens. The lecturer complained that the churches in England were too low, whereas in those of France and Germany their great height was one of their leading characteristics. He spoke of the low roofed churches of England having been commended as homely by one who bad travelled abroad; but, said the lecturer, he did not know whether one would not dispense with the homeliness if one could get grandeur. Repose, it was pointed out, was an essential characteristic of true architecture, and Milan Cathedral was shown on the screen as an example of the absence of this; there was no repose about it, remarked the lecturer: it was like a wedding cake, like gingerbread. That was not true art. All decoration, he impressed upon his audience, must be conventional. You could not put on a building an exactly natural flower or animal with anything like appropolatmess, to hemn its place. It would not satisfy the eve. So the Greeks thought: they found there was a certain amount of unrest in it. The lecturer in concluding bhowed that there was history in architecture, as you would see in it the ideals of a nation, and trace out national character. At the close the lecturer proceeded to examine the class formed in connection with the course of lectures.

div.head: LANCA.SIIIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: LANCA.SIIIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
PRESENTATION TO THE CHAIRMAN.

On Thursday afternoon, at a meeting of the Lanca- shire County Council, Sir William Flouldsworth, Bart., vice-chairman, presented to the Right Hon. Hibbert,first chairman of the Council, on behalf of his colleagues, an admirable life-size portrait of himself in recognition of his eminent services to the county. Mr. Hibbert suit- ably acknowledged the presentation. The portrait, which has been painted by Mr. Sydney fledge, RA., is an excellent likeness and a beautiful work of art. It will be hung in the County-hall at Preston.

div.head: STRIKE AT A BURTON BREWERY.
div.p: STRIKE AT A BURTON BREWERY.
SEVERAL HUNDRED MEN OUT.

A large number of the employes of Messrs. Bass and Co., of Burton, went out on strike on Wednesday night declining to accede to a new code of regulations issued by the head of the engineering department. It was hoped that a settlement would be effected, but to-day the str,ke has assumed serious dimensions, and several hundred more of the men in different departments have I come out. A mass meeting was held on Thursday after- noon, and a resolution unanimously carried that they should not go in under the new rules. The men formed in procession, and marched through the streets, but maintained such order as to render it unnecessary for the police to interfere. The firm's workmen number about 5.000.

HE LIFE-BOAT SATURDAY MOVEMENT IN WARRINGTON.

In connection with the Life-boat Saturday Movement, a special service was held in the Cairo- St., Chapel, Warrington, on Sunday evening, when an address was delivered by the Rev. F. K. Freeston. During the service the choir sang" The Life-boat " in a very effective manner. The hymns " Let the lower lights be burning," " Star of peace," and " Launch thy bark," were also sung. The rev. gentleman preaching on the text Psalm evii. 23, 24, said those of them who lived only on the Lind knew very little, and much too little,about those who went to sea in ships. The words of that old English song came to them with a sort of a re- buke in the refrain— - • • - -

Ye gentlemen of England, who ,it at home at ease, How little do you think upon the danger of the seas Ploy heard of shipwrecks and read of rescues. They perhaps sympathised with the one, and they certainly admired the other •, but yet, how little did they realise the risk, the hardship, the courage of those who did business in great waters ! This consideration would have been brought home to many of them by the an- nouncement that in Warrington this week would be inaugurated a Lifeboat Saturday. He confessed for one that he hailed that announcement with joy. Be thought that in following the lead of Manchester and Salford, and other Lancashire towns, they in Warrington had done the right thing. Surely there could hardly be,next to hospitals, a more deserving institution than the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. Just as they had a Hospital Saturday, was it not meet that they should have a Lifeboat Saturday? And just as they had a Hospital Sunday, would it not be meet that they should have a Lifeboat Sunday ? There were more than 4,000 wrecks during a year along the British coast. Some years there were more and some years less. And there were only 300 lifeboats. These figures suggested a very startling conclusion. Mr. Freeston went on to describe three of the most disas- trous shipwrecks which had taken place in recent times, in which remarkable daring'and bravery were exhibited. These were achievements, he said, which made them proud of English seamen. He would not depreciate the bravery exhibited on the battle-field. But here was truer bravery ; more deliberate, more long sustained, not under the stimulus of mad excitement, not bravery to save their own life, but bravery to save the life of others who had no claim upon them, except that of a brother in distress. Would it not be a great shame if they allowed such an institution to decline ? It had been said" Why not help the Lifeboat Institution from the State ? Why not make it a State agency ?" That was very plausible, and sooner than life should be lost let the State help. How much better if that institution should not have to go to the State, but if it should live and be supported by the willing offerings of the English people! He appealed to his congregation to give to the movement according to their means.

div.head: STABLE IN TILE HOUSE.
div.p: STABLE IN TILE HOUSE.

The CLERIC read a letter from Mr. Henry Daniel, of nearCheadley, who had been appointed on his applica- tion lunatic attendant for the House. His communica- tion stated that he had re-considered the matter in all its bearings, and had decided not to enter upon the duties. —MI. DAVIES : Frightened.—Mr. SHAW : It would frighten any man.—lt was stated that Daniel had been informed he would have to be at work every night for a fortnight, and so on.—The CLERK suggested that the Board should appoint a constable, a man who would be in every way a policeman, but constantly to take duty in the House, and give his services at night when occa- sion required. They could get such a man, who would actually be a police officer and he could be sworn before the boroagh magistrates and given all the authority of a constable. There were frequently duties to perform in connection with the Board's prosecutions in which he might be useful; and he would have charge of the lunatics and take them to the asylum, and also act as a peace officer in all matters in relation to the House.—Mr. Mule: Would that be a new departure?— The CLERK said if they made such an appointment, the Board, instead of baying a man living on thair premises, a great portion of his time doing nothing, could have an efficient policeman living near to them, and patrolling about, and at their service when required for night duty. —Mr. Muse: Do you know any other place where there is such a functionary ?—The CLERK said it would be rather unique, but the expense would be no greater.— Mr. RATCLIFFE : My idea was to have a man employed inside.—The CLERK, in reply to an observation, said if the Board could find a suitable gardener who could look after lunatics he would be a most useful person. He also mentioned that a policeman was employed at Dallam and Bewsey Forges; and asked if it would be well to write to Daniel to remove his erroneous impres- sions.—A Guardian objected to this course.—On the motion of Mr. RATCLIFFE, the matter of the appointment was referred back to the House Committee.
SCARLET FEVER AND SMALLPDX. The doctor's report stated that there were no fresh cases of scarlet fever in the House.—The workhouse master reported that most of the smallpox CELS6S were better.

div.head: DEATH OF THE WOMAN BUSH.
div.p: THE DEATH OF THE WOMAN BUSH.

The CLER;s7ated that in reply to the Local Govern- ment Board who had desired to be informed of the result of the inquest on the woman Bush, in case of one being held, he had informed them that an inquest had been held, and a post =rim examination having disclosed congestion of the lungs, a verdict of death from natural causes had been returned.

div.head: VACCINATION.
div.p: VACCINATION.

The CLERIC read a letter from Dr. Gornall, stating that he thought it would be a great advantage to the general public, if the Board would give him permission to vaccinate on an additional day in the week, say on a Friday, at 2 o'clock, for the next 6 weeks.—After some , conversation the matter was put to the vote, when 8 Guardians were declared by the Chairman to be in favour of acceding to the request, and 11 as opposed to doing so.—Mr. GILL disputed the correctnossof the counting ot hands, and asked that the names of those who voted be recorded.—The CLERK : Too late now.— Mr. GILL said that under the Act, if any Guardian dis- puted the Chairman's decision, he was entitled to have the names taken down.—The CLEns said that was not so, unless the Board considered the Chairman's decision was not correct.—Mr. RATCLIFFE: I have been in the Board for many years, and never heard the Chairman's decision disputed before.—Mr. DAVIES pointed out that his desire was not to oppose the doctor, but to facilitate him in his work, but it was not considered that the existing arrangements were sulcient.
FOREIGN COMPETITION

The CLERK read a letter from the llackuey Board Guardians suggesting that time for action it was in the matter of the supplanting of native labour by cheap foreign labour. The .tommunication stated that the unfortunate competition by foreigners made thestruggle for existence so keen that the native toiler often broke down mentally and physically under the strain, and retired beaten from the unequal strife, to spend the remainder of his life in the seclusion of an asylum. That this state of things was becoming more general was painfully attested by the fearful increase of lunacy among the struggling poor and trading classes.—The clerk also read a letter from the Bolton Guardians on the subject. In comment on the letters he said he did not think that Board were very much troubled in the matter of aliens. Far greater trouble sprang from the fact that their district was the first crossing place over the river Mersey ; and consequently they had a greater proportion of tramps and poor people coming that way than would otherwise come. That district was also on the high- way between London and Scotland, and that again brought an influx of people upon them. But he cer- tainly questioued whether they had many. foreign , people travelling that way.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said it was not for the Board to interfere as between labour. and , capital in the matter of employment. very foreigner had a right to sell his own labour in this country, the 1 same as Englishmen had in other countries.—The subject dropped without any resolution. THE VACCINATION INSPECTOR.

_— The CLERK read a notification from Mr. T. W. Thomp- son, of his intended visit ot inspection as to the vaccina- tion arrangements of the union ; and desiring certain information, with which the Clerk said he had supplied him.

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARIES.
div.p: INCREASE OF SALARIES.

On the motion of Mr. Ratcliffe, seconded by Mr. A. Jolley, the salary of Mi,s Curry, the porteress, was in- creased from £25 to £27 10s. per annum, as recom- mended by the House Committee —Mr. Houghton moved that as recommended by the Schools Committee, the salaries of Dr.Peacocke and Mr. Mines, school superin- tendent, be each increased £lo.—Mr. Shaw seconded. Mr. Davies said he was not going to raise any objec- tion, but he did not think that was the time for raising salaries. He asked if the committees were unanimous. It was replied that they were.—The motions for the increases were carried.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION.
div.p: AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION.

A crowded meeting of farmers residing in North Lan- cashire was held at Lancaster on Saturday afternoon, under the presidency of the Mayor (Mr. William Smith, M.P., for North Lonsdale), to consider the question of agricultural depression. Mr. H. Whittaker introduced the subject, declaring amongst other causes that tithes, exorbitant rents, rates—which should be paid by the landlord to the extent of one-half—and " lords' "rents (charges due to the lord of the manor) were responsible for the present depression. The income-tax should be as applying to farmers, and the false measure- ment of farms advertised to let were dwelt upon. Rail- way rates needed revision, and there should be a law ensuring to t‘nants the right of all improvements made in their holdings. The law of distress needed reform. and the law of entail was one of the worst in connection with land, and should be got rid of. His remedies were agitation, combination, federation, amalgamation, or better still, a land league for the repeal of all bad laws, the reform of others, and the passing of good ones. He advocated land courts (so as to enable farmers to get fair rents, and so encourage them to calculate their land properly), and fixity of tenure, and suggested that large farms should be split up into small ones. After a discussion, it was unanimously resolved that a farmers' club or association be formed in the district for the pro- tectiGn of their mutual interests. A goodly number of farmers gave in their names as members. The Liverpool and District ?annex.' Club met on Saturday, when reference was made to bad markets and ruined crops. It was stated that the lowest price ever known was obtained on Friday for foreign wheat,hence farmers of Lancashire were passing through a severe crisis. In the Ormskirk district farms had been given up by tenants owing to utter inability to make anything out of them, and many were living on the savings of their forefathers. Eventually,it was resolved to urgently appeal to landowners, including Lords Derby, Sefton, Lathorn, and Salisbury, to defer their rent audits till March next year. At the meeting of the Council of the Central and Associated Chambers of Agriculture held in London on Tuesday it was resclved to adopt the suggestion of the - Federation of the Lancashire Farmers urging the im- portance of a national conference to consider the depres- sion in agriculture. The first meeting of the conference was fixed for the 7th of next month in London, during • the Smithfield Show week.

THE Board of Guardians of Stock A "Religious pojust rtare now face to face with E DifficuittY." one of those crises which are gener- ally spoken of as "religious difficulties." In this instance, however, the " difficulty " is not a grave one, at least, the Stockport Board of Guar- dians do not seem disposed to take it too seriously, At the same time, they have to reckon with the Rev. P. H. MoonE, vicar of Romiley, and guar- dian of that township,Who has raised the difficulty, and who looks upon the issue involved as one of weight and importance. It appears that the Stockport Guardians have trained a choir of chil- dren, or their officers have done so with their sanction, and these children have been in the habit, and, in fact, were trained for the special purpose, of attending the services in the work- house conducted by both Church of England and Nonconformist ministers. The Rev. P. H. Moonz does not object to the training ,of the children to ,sing, nor yet does lie object to their singing but he does object to their singing at the Nonconformist services. We do not know of what political or religious complex ion the Stockport Board-of Guardians happens to be,but it seems to contain a fair proportion of sensible and levol- headed members. They could not be impressed witl the superfine scruples of their clerical colleague. Look at the thing as they might,th.ey could not per- suade themselves that there was anything heinous in the Workhouse children singing hymns at a Nonconformist service, even though the parents of these children might say that their particular denomination was that of the Church of England. But the Rev. P. H. MOORB had another card to play. Behind the Board of Guardians there is a greater power, that of the Local Government Board. He consequently appealed to the Local Government Board, and on Monday, Mr. Dam; the Poor-law Inspector for the district, visited Stockport to look inte the complaint. Mr. Mooßn now had his opportunity,and he made the best of of it. It is laid down by law that Workhouse children of one denomination shall not be required to attend the services of any other denomination, and upon an examination of the creed book of the Workhouse it was found that out of seventy children in the Workhouse no fewer than forty- ' two were . entered as helonging to the Church of England, all the rest being Roman Catholics. This, as Mr. DAnsEv said, was a rather extraordin- ary state of things. As we all know, there is, out- side of Workhouses, a very fair proportion of Non- conformists. In some places, they outnumber the adherents of the Church of England; and in no place, and certainly not in the Stockport Union, are they in the non-existent minority, of none to forty-two. It seems, howayer,,a.a though at the Stockport workhouse there waa fl !rogue a w method of dividing the children, :midi, hatever else might be said of it, had the meritof All children who are not Roman Catholics are designated as of the Church of England. As long as the minister of the Church of England and the Nonconformists worked amicably together, there was, perhaps, little to complain about, and cer- tainly the Nonconformists do not scorn to have displayed any dieposition to find fault with what,
in some respects, looked like a complete wenig—

of their particular denominations. Butnow that. the Rev. P. H. Moore is inclined to take full advantage of the letter of the law, probably the Nonconformists of Stockport will manifest a tittle more keenness in looking after their own ; and who knows that the present trivial interposition of the Vicar of Romiley will not result in the estab- lishment of a juvenile choir of Nonconformists where none existed before?
The THERE has been so much said Ship Canal. that is adverse to the Ship easel - -

and its prospects, that the address' which Mr. MARSHALL STEVENS has, thiiiveek,,gieen to shareholders in Manchester should answers WM` ful purpose. Mr. Sravirars is rather severe apon pro- phets, or at all events upon prophets of evil. gome of the London journals are in the habit of speak- ing disparagingly of the prospects of the Canal as a paying concern, but Mr. STEVENS points out that they were equally dolorous in their anticipations with regard to the Suez Canal. The" Daily News," for instance, on the day after the Sses Canal was opened was "sorry to depreciate that enterprise," but it was much concerned at the "small prospects of profit to the shareholders, to whose sacrifices the work was due." ,It further declared that " the Suez Canal -bae apparently not escaped the usual fatality of splendid and novel engineering works." Yet,as we now all know, the shareholders have had no cause to regret venturing their money in that "splendid and novel engineoring work." It seems from what Mr. STEVEN gays, that alreadr some former strong opponents of the Manchester , Ship Canal are beginning to manifest their con- version in a practical way, and that some of the obstacles that were at one time declared to be "insuperable "are now found to be no obstacles' at all. When the promoters of the Shin Canal Bill were before Parliament, one of their opponents' was Mr. ALFRED- HOLT, late chairman of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, but now, it said, Mr. HOLT has two vessels building at ' Greenock, to be used on the Canal, sand,,wbat is- more, he has made an application for a tradint berth at Manchester. A familiar objection to the . possibility of satisfactorily working the Canal was that of getting masted vessels underneath the , bridges over the C anal, but Mr. Hor.r seems. t°' have settled that ptoblem in his own min, for his new vessels are being provided with suitable. masts. There used, also, to be something. said about big vessels never entering the Canal, but we 11 are now informed by Mr. STEVENS that within a week the completed portions of the Canal will be I navigated by a vessel with a capacity of 4,700 tons of cargo. It was once,too,held out as a threat by the railway companies that, if the, , Canal we" completed, they would allow none of the "Canal traffic to get upon their rails. The railway coo- , palms, however, changed their minds,, and, to- , day the Lancashire and Yorkshire have powers to connect with the Canal at Salford; the London and North-Western at Mode Wheel, and the Mid" land, Great Northern, and Manchester,. Sheffield and Lincolnshire have arranged a means of access ' near Old Trafford. It is not our intention to recapitulate the figures given by Mr. Srxvslfs- They are those upon which the commercial case of the Ship Canal Company was put before Parlia— ment, and, he contended, they had not been affected.by adverse criticism. From these figures he calculates that, within a period of two years ,of the opening of the Canal, the earnings will het sufficient to pay a reasonable interest on a capita' of about £16,000,000, an amount which it is Ow' expected the Canal will cost; and that in seven years the income from the Canal will be equal t9' payingfive per cent on £30.000,000.

The Agritultural TUB British farmer is not It ' Depression, volatile individual. Indeed, tak- ing him in the gross, he niel' without injustice, be described as of the phlegma- tic temperament Ho is slow to move, elree sometimes when his own interests would be all the better served by a little alertness and some change of action. A.hove all things he often plays an unwillingness to" face a° landlord," or even the landlord's agent, with a demand for duction of rent. When he is hard hit by bmi seasons and low prices, he seems as though he would rather make an effort to economise ia direction, before making a request for an abate" ment to the gentleman who receives the rant. At the present time, however, the depression in agri- culture isof a character so severe that it is break- ing through all restraints, and farmers are exhilit7 ing an unwonted activity. At the same timeildg- ing from published accounts, it is to be feared that the effort has come too late to save many a farmer who was a few years. back in a fairly prusPel°lls condition, from financial ruin. The farmers of Lancashire, and of North Lancashire in particular? are showing especial activity, and on they held a crowded meeting at Lancaster, under the presidency of the ialayor, Mr. W. SMITH, 311•P'; for North Lonsda/e, to consider the question 01 agricultural depression. Farmers as a body ha" not been distinguished for their support of the Saturday party of progress in politico, yet it is reraarhaVe how, now in their hour of need, they turn for salvation to the reforms which have been aciv°- cated for many years, in saason and out a woo, tv Liberal politicians. They have nor thr0,7,1: aside as inadequate all such panaceas as "docking" of of labourers' wages, and the cry f°r, impossible protection. What is needed, and tr.,balr was advocated at the meeting referred to, ar° rents, fixity of tenure, the division of rates v7f tween owner and cccupier, reform of the laW distress, and, wonderful to relate, considering the proposal comes from farmers themselves, the splitting up of large farms into brealler holdings. These were the ends—or some of them, for there were many others spoken of—which thes: farmers displayed a desire to accomplish; be then what as to the means for accomplish- ing these ends As every one knows, the' mere passing of resolutions does little towards forcing measures of legislation through Farh mint, and it would certainly do little to brill about the reforms named, seeing that there woe' be arrayed against them the immense influence the landed interest. But a spirit of self-helP pervaded the meeting. Combined action was rightly spoken of as the only hope of success, and the formation of a Land LOSII.IO was hinted at. In the end a farmers' association was foaled, and, it is said, many farmers gave in their names as members. Whatever may be the outcome of this latest agitation amongst the hard-pressed agricul- turists, it may safely be said that the remedy is almost entirely in their own hands. Their grie- vances are largely the result of unjust laws; it would be futilcion their part to ,continne to sup- port politicians who are against reform, and to withhold their aid frora a party which has advo- cated, and still advocates,the abolition of unequal laws.

There was not a very numerous response to th'e invitation of the Chairman of the Board of Com- missioners to consider the establishment of a Life- boat Saturday, in toe town. But the meeting possessed one good feature. All present were earn- est in the work; there were no drones in the hive. and: there can be little doubt that with their co- operation as a Committee, Mr. Wiswall will be able to accomplish his desire. It was satisfactory to find that Runcorn had done something for the Lifeboat Institution in past years, chiefly through the exertions of Mr. Hamilton, the collector of cus- tom, but the object of the Lifeboat Saturday is not to deal with subscribers, but to give those who wish it an opportunity of contributing their mite to aid those in peril on the sea, be it ne'er so small, and it is to be sincerely hoped the object will be attained, and that through the, greater prominence given to the subject,-Mr. Hamilton's ‘subscription list will swell beyond his highest expectations.

The municipality of Widnes is now fairly launched on its onward way. The constitution 'or the Town Council was pracically decided on Tuesday, and flthough the ratepayers did not endorse the claims of several candidates who were entitled to con- sideration by reason of length of service and work accomplished for the public godd, yet the general result is far from unsatisfactory. The Councillors may be classified as six independent, five Nationalists, four Liberals, and three Conserv- atives, but the majority of the units that compose these four classes are likely to prove themselves townsmen first and party men afterwarls. '

It is noteworthy that of the 15 gentlemen who i formed the members of the Lleal Board, which will make its boW• on Monday, and become a thing of the past, only live find seats in the Council ChaMber. Certainly live of them did not seek elee- -1 tiOn;but it is "Plgnificanr that the rat'epayers re- , 1eet.41.• 'five in ia.vour of " new blood,' a phrase will& is underatood to mean, much, but,, which frequintly signifies nothing.:Let us hope for better hings here.

4 3 • • • TheiellOtien Was conducted in a remarkably quiet and ord¢tly..ilinanner, and considering the great itmountO, Interest taken in the event f as testified. by the hear poll, it is surprising that there was -bot more excitement visible. Then too the arrange- -pienfs for counting, to accept the testimony of these qualified to know, were admirably conceived and admirably carried out,a fact which reflects great credit not only upon the returning officer, Mr. Gossage. but upon his chief adviser, Mr. Oppen- beim. There is one direction in which a reform might be instituted. Some• provision might be "Made forthe members of the Press to obtain tha zesults in comfort, and with some degree of despatch. -The reporter. is sometimes compelled to, work under very adverse circumstances, which; cannot be ltfafttett-but in this case there was no, reason why :be should be- kept standing in a corridor ' for an rbour, whilst candidates and their agents could pass to and from the counting room dropping scraps of inforruatioh3o,their familiars outside. It certainly as very unpleasant and iva:§ the means of delay- ing the transmisiiion—Of fliirii'lkats not only to those ratepayers whom the candidates had been so assidu- ' ously moving during the day, but farther aield.

Now the election is decided, the chief interest is liillre—ilies on of who is t.to first Occupy the posi- tion of chie magistrate. ‘There is only one answer. Mr. F.X.Gqssage has presided over th-e delibera- tions of th Local Botird.:‘ fax an uninterrupted period of tei years ; his rule *Nip firm, has been judiciona and imparti4l, and enfoyed respect, cer- tainly andel the old ieginisaid it is believed with good reason will order thar new. It is therefore'confi- dently anticipated that when the Council meets on Wednesday tiext, Mr. Gossage Willte creatediAlder- man and first Mayor of the borough;by universal con- sent of his fellows. His late father,Mr.Wm. Gossage, was the first chairman of the Local Board, and the coincidence will be an unusual one in the. annals of a public governing body. div.p: WESTPN „C\RICKET CLUB.

, On Thursday evening the members of this club brought to a conclusion a most successful _season by a dinner at the Royal Oak Inn, Weston. Mrs. Green, the propriatress, placed a capital spread be... fore the numerous company present. After the cloth was cleared, the president took the chair, and proposed "Success to Weston Cricket Club." The club, he said, had made its marx in the neighbour- hood, and they had started one exSwe clubs • in the district. They had in the Village a great deal of cricket talent,and iL only wanted a little encourage- ment and a little practice to bring it to the fore.(Ap- plause.)—Mr. T. T. Sill seconded the toast, and said they must follow up their success of the past season by travelling farther afield and playing better clubs. He made an . appropriate and feeling allusion to the death of the late Captain, Mr. H. Dean, to whose exer- tions much of their prosperity was due. (Dear hear.) Mr. G. 0. Jones responded. The health of the president was proposed by Mr. S'll in complimentary terms.—Mr. J. Tudor senior seconded, and the toast was received with musical honours.—Mr. A. J. Williams gave The Vice presidents and patrons " coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Sill. Mr. Dodd also spoke,and the toast was honoured musically. Mr. Sill spoke in acknowledgment.—" The Committee" was proposed by Mr. G. 0. Jones seconded by Mr. D. Basnett, and responded to by dr. Frayer.—Mr. Sill gave" The offi- cers," coupled with the name of the Captain, Mr. J. Tudor senior, whose energy and ability were touched upon in complimentary terms, and the toast was enthu- shuxically drudk. Mr. Tudor suitably respondel. Before separating Mr. Bleakley was presented with a bat by Mr. Sill for his high average of runs, and a belt was handed to Mr. Tudor for his service with the ball. The proceedings were enlivened by songs given by Messrs. Tudor pinr., W. Hope, Maddock, G. 0. Jones, Lunt, C. Pendlebury, J. Ball, and A. J. Williams. Mr. Temporley provided the pianist,

POACHING PHEASANTS NEAR RUNCORN./

Before Major liazlehuret and Dr. Steele, at Run- .corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, a young man named Alexander Jackson, of Newtown, Frodsham, was charged with trespassing in pursuit of game on land in the occupation of John Davies, Aston- by-Sutton. The defendant was also charged with assaulting Jas, Tomlinson, sen., the keeper, and a cross-summons had been issued against the latter, charging him with assaulting Jackson.—Mr. 'A. Linaker prosecuted for Mr,:' Hervey Talbot, of , Aston Hall, the owner Of.the lend, and Mr. Pe cy Davies defended Jackson.--FrOm Mr. Linaker's opening statement, it appeared that about five o'clock on Tuesday afternoon on the 25th October, Tomlinson and his son were walking across land in the occupation ,lof Messrs. Percival, of Park Side,and when at the bottom' of the Old Moat Cover, they heard a gun shot. Young Tomlinson went into hiding, and the keeper went in the direction' whence ' the sound came. He then saw the defendant walking from the cover, on land in the occu- 1. nation of Jno. Davies, and get upon the towing path ot. the River Weaver Navigation. 'The keeper,followed.liim for about a mile, when young Tomlinson get in front,of him, endllie defendant filutine he Was between .two ;fires, stohped. He i'ppeenel very bulky, and Was esked what he had got under his coat, and' he replied "1 !think you are on the wrong track: I Mem got nothing." The keepers saw the end of a doubt barrelled' gun pro- trudine beneath his (Mat, and they were about to search him, when he resisted violently, and a long and deeper-. ate struggle ensued. Eventually he was overceme and put upon the ground, and from his coat pocket were taken the stock and barrels of a doubled gun, .a powder flask, and a shot hag, and a round stone. Hid- den in his trousers was a pheesa nt,which was warm and bleeding. The defendant asked the keepers to take the gun and pheasant and- let hirn ges, but thee tied his hands with thongs, which he broke asunder. The defendant then asked them if they could swim, as some- one would have to go into the river, but the keepers, however, succeeded in again securing his hands and took him to Aston, where P.S. Costello identified him. The defendant had previously given a wrong name.—Cor- roborative evidence was given by Tomlinson senior, who was put through a long cross-examination by Mr. Daniels. He said the defendant never struck him, but he hurt his thumb in the struggle. Defendant kicked, and fought with his hands. Witness denied that he used any unnecessary violence In securirg the defend- ant. Tomlinson the younger also gave evidence, and in cross-examination he said he and his tether tied the thongs on the man's wrists. Defend- ant never said he found the pheasant on the towing path.—For the defence Mr. Davies said the defendant was of previous good character, and was only 20 years of age. He had only been charged once for drunkenness. He was employed by Messrs. Heywood and Massey, Weaver Chemical Works, Freeishain, who gave him an excellent character. On the day in question he was walking to Northwich along the towpath, intending to have his gun repaired there. He admitted that he meant to have a shot if there was a chance, but he denied that he was ever off the footpath. He had not walked many yards when he saw the pheasant lying there, so he picked it up and put it inside his waistcoat. He alleged that the keepers treated him most brutally, , the elder' Tomlinson striking a violent blow on the side of the body, and the younger struck him on the head with a stick, and the tlungs they placed upon his wrists cut through the flesh as they dragged him to Aston Hall, through bracken, bramble, and wood.—Mr. Davies called Sergeant Costello, as to the defendant's character, remarking that not a word lied passed be- tween them on the matter.—The Sergeant said he knew the defendant very well. He had never been convicted for poaching, but lie was a very had character and the associate of poachers. He had been convicted of sheep stealing.—Mr. Davies (to defendant) : Is that true.— Defendant: Yes.—Mr. Davies:' Why did not you tell me? (Laughter.)—Mr. Davies (to Sergeant) : Is it not a fact that you expressed surprise to find the defendant at Mr. Talbot's.—Witness: No. The defendant said" Another bit of bad luck ?" and he (witness) replied "You are only having the luck you are looking after."—Mr. Davies : But was it not his brother who was convicted of sbeep stealing.—Witness: It was him and his brother, hie father and his mother. (Loud laughter,) They are about as had a family as there, is in Frocisham.—Mr. Davies i I don't think I will ask you any more. :(Loud laughter )—The Bench dismissed the summonses with regard to the assaults, and fined the defendant 40s. and costs for poaching.—The gun and pouches were for- eited.
• f RUN CORN BOARD OF G UARDIANS]

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Mr. J. Mclntyre (chairman), Colonel Fox, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, and Messrs. J. Brandreth, E. Aaron, J. 0. Williams, 11, F. Heywood. W. Pickering. J. Bawlley A. R. Norman, T. Lee, T. Baxter, C.C., J. W. Rawlley, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-INFECTIOUS DISEASES.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-INFECTIOUS DISEASES.

The Medical Officer reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 32. The 32 deaths showed an average death-rate of 19-2 of the estimated population. As to the recommendation of the Health Committee as to furnishing particulars of the cases of infectious diseases notified, the medical officer said the information could be more easily supplied by the secretary who kept the register.—At a later period when the minute came up for consideration, Mr. Bis- bsown moved and Mr. Lea seconded its adoption;After 'some discussion, Mr. T'ritchard moved, and Mr. Meadowcroft seconded an amendment that the minute to be referred back for further consideration, and this was carried by ten votes to four.

div.head: -THE GRANOLITHIC PAVEMENT.
div.p: -THE GRANOLITHIC PAVEMENT.

The Highways and Buildings Committee recommended that the footways at the following places be paved with granolithie:—High-st. (south side) from Isielson-st. to the boundary of the Salvation Army's property; Bridge- t. from Ellestnere-st. to near Gas-Bt. ; also aurciest. (north side), from lligh-st. to King-st. ; that the plan of the Primitive Methodist Connexion for the erection . of a Sunday school with class rooms in Green wav-road he approved.--rMX. Bisbrown moved,, and Mr. Speakman seconded, the adoption of the, minutes.—Mr. Meadow- croft, alluding to tile,paving of Higli-at. and liridge-st.`, with granolithic pavement, asked if this work Acid not been done.—Mr. Smith : Yes, just fi•dshing.—Mr. Meadowcroft objected to receiving reoltnalenclat ions, for work which had already been carried out.. He consi- dered it was,a great blunder to. pave the main streets with granolithic.—The Law Clerk said the work had been carriad out under a contract made on July VII, but he must sav the instructions to do the work in this case were rather late.—ln answer to Mr. Lea, the Chairman said the granolithic pavement was supposed to last 20 years. He had seen places where it had been in use for eight years and was as good as ever.—Mr. flankinson : They sharpen their picks upon It is Liverpool.—The minutes were passed.

HEALTH COMMITTER. , The Inspector had reported nuisAnces on property in St. John-street, Trinity-street, and Bridge-street, caused through structural detects, and it was recommended that in the event of non-compliance with the notices to abate the aforesaid nuisances, legal proceedings be taken against the owners :—That one month's notice be given to Mrs: E. A. Whitby to terminate her appointment is Nurse and Caretaker at the Hospital, and that the Com- mittee be empowered to advertise for a Nurse and Care- taker on terms te be decided upon. Mr. Smith moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Hankinson seconded. Mr. Dobson pointed out that a question he asked at the last meeting, with reference to the non-removal of a case of typhoid fever to the Hospital had not been answered. The Chairman said the Law Clerk had answered it. The Law Clerk stated that one reason why the patient was not removed was that the parents objected, and the medical man had not given the certificate required.—Mr. Dobson then demanded that the Inspector's report on the subject should be read, but the Chairman ruled him Out of order. No business unless it was mentioned in the minutes could be dealt with.—Mr. Dobson said he would take means for enforcing the information re- quired.—The minutes were pallSed. THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACRDi9 TRH MERSEY. The' Commissioners next consid 'red a proposal of the Mersey Bridge Committee to (tout in bine a sum of £30.000 towards the cost of constructing a vehicular bridge across the Mersey to connect Lancashire and Cheshire at Widnes and Runcorn. The conditions laid down were that there should be authority to levy tolls for the use of the bridge, which tolls were to be a first charge to secure repayment of ' the contributions, and that the Widnes Lecal Board or their successors should contribute a like amount. The contribution was to be made inn the understanding that the balan.:e of the Cost of the .bride would be provided by Vie County Councils of Lan- cashire and Cheshire.—Mr. F. Wiswall (chairman of the boards in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the contribution would not come upon the rates. The county council informed the committee when they had an interview that thr local authorities would be expected to contribute largely to the undertaking, and declared that they were not in favour of tolls. The local autho- rities could not see their way to contribute without exacting toll, but they proposed to have only a small toll, about half that now charged pedestrians for crossing the railway footbridge. The committee estimated that they would get an income of £5,000 a year from pedes- trians and vehicles. As they could borrow money for 80 years at 3i per cent., the contribution of £BO,OOO from Widnes and Runcorn would entail an annual payment of £2,285 for principal and interest, and with the income estimated, they could pay off the capital in 20 years, or in other words, they,could have a free bridge in that time, perhaps in considerably less time, pecliuse no one could calculate the advantages to be gained by such a bridge, and the great influx of traffic and trade it would bring into the district. A reduction of rates and charges would also be brought about. The only opposi- tion ths.y might.expect would be from the L. and N. W. By. Co.—Mr. Smith : As you are expecting the county councils to contribute the, greater, part of the money, won't they want the greater part of the tolls ? —The Chairman . No. The county council's were in favour of free bridges ;it was their duty to provide these bridges. For instance, Westminster Bridge it ;1 Chester was freed, and the ratepayers of the whole county had to bear the 'cost, so that they in Run- corn district were entitled to the same cons-deration, It was estimated that the bridge would cost £lBO.OOO, of which £140,000 was for construction and £40,000 for Parliamentary expensPs and for compensation for disturbance. It was their endeavour to get the two county councils to each contribute one-third of the cost and Runcorn and Whines the remaining one-third. The cemmittee of the comthissioners were pledged to Widnes Local Board to contribute 8..30,000. There was no doubt that the bridge would pay for itself, and be a great boon to boththe districts and the counties.—Mr.. Meadow- croft suggested that in a scheme of such immense importance the minutes should be fully considered in committee, and .after discussion it was decided to call' the Bo.trd together again, specially to deal with the subject.

div.head: FRER PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMITTER.
div.p: FRER PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMITTER.

This Committea submitted this resolution : That the Free Public Library Committee, recognising the need of books of a technical characterin the various branches of science, which would be invaluable i promoting the technical educathwof the youth of Runcorn, but which their limited. funds will not enable them to purchase without crippling the general work of tho Library, re- quest the Conimissioners to make a special grant for this purpose out Of the funds which they hold for tech- nical education or endeavour to obtain a grant of £5O from the County Council for that purpose.—On the sug- gestion of Mr. Speakman, the minute was referred to the. Technical Instruction Committee. Mr. Speakman' promised to do all he could to procure the grant . , required. .
INSANITARY rHoNturi.

Mr. Leach moved that it he an instruction •to the Health Committee to at once take steps to close the fol- lowing insanitary property :—All the houses in Zion Place or Dolph-hole, all the cellar-dwellings in Grindrod Square, all the sinall dwellings in Cholmondeley Place,as unfit for human habitation as condemned by Dr. Spear, Medical Inspector to the Local Government Dos rd.on his ! late visit to Runcorn and as recoMmended by him in I his recommendation, in his report. Mr. Leach said he found that some of these properties had been con- demned over and over again by various Local GoVeru- ment Board Inspectors, and Runcorn was in a fearful state. The death-rate of 22 per .1,000 was far beyond that Runcorn should have, considering its natural ad- vantages for draining and ventilation.—Mr. ScPith asked if there was any sickness in the places named.—Mr. Leach said he was not dealing with that.—Mr. Lea seconded the motion,because he thought it WAS a reason- able one, and he asked why was only Gilbert-st., closed when this Property was condemned at the same time.— The Chairman replied that the reason was because ' the Medical Officer condemned Gilbert- street, and not the other 'properties. Mr. Smith said Mv. Leach had not shown that there was a single case of sickness,and yet he wanted to push people out of their houses into the street, when he knew quite well there was-not a house to be got for love or money. —Mr. Coward said he, visited Grindrod-square on the previous'day, and found the houses very well ventilated and clean. There was an old couple who had lived there for forty years, and well they looked. He did not sae that anything ailed the cellar property there.—Mr. Meadowcroft asked if the Board were prepared to com- pensate the property owners,and said they could not act on a general statement like that Mr. Leach had made.— After further discassim, the motion was lost by five votes to three.--Mr. Leach said they would very likely soon have to pass a stronger resolution.—The Chairman t We don't want any threats.
RESIGNATION OF MR. WASS.

Mr. W. R. Wass wrote stating that in consequence of his whole time being occupied with his own business, he begged to tender his resignation as a memtor of the Board. lie thanked the Chairman for the courtesy he had shown to him.—The resignation was accepted, on the motion of Mr. Smith, seconded by Mr. Meadowcroft.

TECIINICAL INSTUCTION. Mr. Ward secretary of the County Technical Instauc- tion Committee, wrote informing the Beard that the contribution to Runcorn for the current year would be £222. ACOTATI-obt FOR POOR LAW REFORM.

The Clerk read a letter from Mr: A. Thomas, M.P. for _East Glamorgan, and chairmai, of, the Poor Law "Reform' Association. He stated that in 'October, ran, he addressed to the various board of Guardians a series i of questions, bearing on the administration and practi- cal °Oration of the po6r law, and from the replies and subsequent enquiries, he was persuaded 'that it was an imperative necessity that the whole, subject be again investigated, as in 1832-3, by Royal Commission. He therefore proposed on the re-assembling of Parliament, to move .the reappointment of a royal commission to enquire into the practical operation of the poor law, and the best means of adapting. the system to the cir- eunistances and requirements of the present day. He asked the Board, in case they were of opinion that the ' new order.of things which had arisen during the last WI years demanded such an enquiry, to embody the opinion in a resolution.—Mr. Heyward moved, and Mr. Norman cooded a motion, expressing an opinion that such an enquiry was desirable ; and the proposition was unani- mously adopted.
