div.head: ASSICSSUIINT COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION,.
div.p: ASSICSSUIINT COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION,.

The Assessment Committee submitted the following resolution, and asked for the Board's adoption of it : " That, in the opinion of this Board the average annual income reesived by the lords of copyhold manors from all fines on admissions of copyhold tenants in such manors, from'all fines or sums paid on enfranchisement of copyhold lands, and from all rights or interests re- served to the lords of manors on enfranchisement, ought to be rated for all parochial purposes, and that a copy of the resolution be sent to the Local Government Board, and also to the several members of Parliament, portions of whose constituencies are comprised in this union, and that they be asked to support such an amendment of the rating laws."—The resolution was adorned by the Board, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Aaron.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

Mr. Brandreth moved the adoption of this Committee's report, which stated that the balance in hand was £1,975 19s. sd.—Mr. Heywood seconded, and observed that the Runcorn relief was going up to the old average, hoping that the Runcorn Guardians would do their utmost to keep it down as much as possibls.—Mr. Bran- dreth said that the amount used to be £9O to £lOO for the tortnight.—Mr. Heywood said it was now £Bs.—The Committee's report was adopted.

div.head: VOTE BY BALLOT.
div.p: VOTE BY BALLOT.

Dr. Gastaldi said it had been thought advisable by that, Board not to have their elections on the old system but by ballot, and nothing further had been heard on the matter simse the Board had made that representa- tion to the authorities. He thought it desirable to bring the matter up again.—The Chairman ;I am afraid that would require an Act of Parliament.—Tlie Clerk reminded the Board that they had sent a resolution to to the Local Government Board on the subj-ct.—Mr. Heywood proposed that the members of Parliament connected with the Union be written to on the subject, and asked to bring it before the House of Commons.— Dr. Gastaldi seconded ,and the motion was unanimously agreed to.—This cone.uded the business.
SAD END TO A LONG CAREER AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday.before Major Hazlehurst and Dr. Steele, an elderly man, named John Peacock, of Oretnway-road, was charged with having .stolen half-a-ton weight of , _deal and pitch pine boards, value £2, the goods of the United Alkali Works.—John Gleeson, foreman, said the prisoner had been employed at the Run- corn Alkali Works as sawyer and foreman joiner for many years. He identified the boards in the police yard as the property of the company. They were safe in the yard at seven o'clock on Saturday morning, and he missed them about half-past eight.—Thomas Gregory, of the Halfway House,Halton- road, deposed that the prisoner was at his house about a fortnight ago, and he asked him if he could let him have some boards to roof a shed he had built. He understood the prisoner had the management of selling timber from the works. ,The prisoner promised to let him have, soMe, and the boar& were brought to, Bates Bridge on Satur- ' day morning in a boat.—By Superintendent Atherton : Ile built the shed of wood supplied by Mr. Peacock about six or seven weeks ago. He paid him 10s. on accouut, on the promise that he had some more, and arraiaged the price afterwards.—Vt'illiani Ashley, brick- layer, Halton, said on the 14th October ho went to the works and arranged with the prisoner for about 400 or SOS feet of timber. He did not get it, because the stuff he offered him would not snit the job he wanted it for. —By superintendent Atherton :He bought tire ber from the prisoner four or five years ago. He hada pigcote he erected from timber, supplied by the prisoner.—P.C. Worth_ deposed to findieg the stolen timber at Bates Bridge, and he apprehended the prisoner, who made no reply to the charge.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and said he had been at the works since 1888, and he had always had the power of selling timber. The money hed always gone through the office in the proper form. Gregory.recalled,said it would 'se live or six weeks since he paid the 10s. on account. —Major flazlehurst (to pd. I eimer). Do you say this money has been paid into the Office 2—The prisoner : It has not gone in because he told me he had not got enough.—Mr. CHeeson said Mr. Sowerby, the manager, and Mr. Poole, the clehier, said there was no arrangement for the prisoner selling tim- ber, and they gave him instructions to prosecute.—The prisoner reasserted that he always paid the money for timber to Mr. Peol.—ltlajor Hazlehurst said that would he easy of proof, and the case would be adjourned to enable Mr. Poole to be sent for and to produce the books. —Mr. Poole said the prisoner had no authority whatever to sell timber and he had not accounted to him for any money. Before timber could be sold, an order would bp inquired for from Mr. Sowerby or tram the office. Vie timber was bought for a special purpose in the works and was not (or sale.—The prisoner now said he had acted unthinkingly and added that it was very wrong. He pleaded for a lenient sentence because it would, be a stain on his character for life, and he would lose his emplorment—The Bench fined him £2 and costs £1 Bs, total £3 83.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Toa n Hall on Tuesday evening. Mr. Jas. Pritchard pre- sided, and there were present Rev. Canon Wood (vice chairman), Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. T. Handley, Dr. McDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, and Mr. G. Mobs (C 110 SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. _

The School Attendance Clmmittee. reported that 98 parents had been summoned to appear before them, of wham 84 attended, and proceedings had been taken against 28 parents. The average attendance during the past month had been 3,117, and the percentage 83.3, sgainst an average of 3,012 and a percentage of 83.9 for the corresponding,month last year.—Dr. Gastaldi in moving the adoption of the report, said he must again draw attention to the fact that it was nearly always the same parents who neglected to send their children to school, and he was sorry that the Board had not greater II Ipowers to punish them in a special manner—imprison- I [Anent perhaps, would be the only thing that might be I felt but they could not do this.—Mr. Handley seconded. —Carried.

div.head: SCHOOL HANAGEMRNT.
div.p: SCHOOL HANAGEMRNT.

The School Management Committee recommended that Eliza Ellisrm be appointed assistant mistress at Greenway-road Girls school, at a salary of MD per annum : that Miss Bertha Hill be appointed assistant mistress at Mill,Brow lniantls School at a salary of £4O per annum ; that the salary of Mr. H. H. Jarvis assistant master at Green way-road goys' School be increased to £8.5 per annum ; that the allowance made to Mr. Bury for extra services in connsetion with the evening school be ucreased to 43. per week.—Passed on the motion of Mr. Handley.
MORE SCHOOZ, ACCOMMODATION WANTED.

_ The Committee appointed to consider the want of accommodation for girls in the elementary schools of Runcorn had held a meeting at which the Clerk report- ed that there were 44 more girls in average attendance than the certified accommodation, and there were 26 girls who were unable to obtain admission, making in all7o for whom accommodation was required. The head teachers of the girls schools in town had furnished lists of girls whose fathers worked on the canal, showing a total of 151, about 90 of whom were known to the visitors as belonging to Runcorn families, who would probably remain in the town after the Ship Canal Works were finished. The Committee were of opinion that in view of the decrease in the numbers which would probably take place when the Ship Canal Works were completed, the necessitAes of

the case wosild be met by opening a termporary school in a roorn-to be rented for- the- -purpose, end the Clerk was instructed to write to the Education Department, I inquiring if under the circumstances, sanction would be ! given to such temporary provision. The clerk said he had written accordingly, and had not bad a repfy.---The report WAS adopted without comment. With regard to the over-crowding of Greenway Board School, the Education Department had written, stating that under the circumstances explained, my Lords would consider favourably of the claim of the Board, to annual grants for the current *atoll year, notwithstanding a slight excess in Lim average attendance, over the limit pre- scribed by ankle 85 (a) of the code.

div.head: LIFE-60AT SATURDAS FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: A LIFE-60AT SATURDAS FOR RUNCORN.

On Monday evening a public meeting, convened by Mr. F. Wiswall, the chairman of the Board of Improvement Commissioners, was held at the rdwe Hall for the purpose of considering the advisabil- ity of establishing a Lifeboat Saturday in the town for the. benefit of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. Mr. Wiswall presided, and there were present; the Rey. Dr. Gastalili, Captain Le Gbuteur, Messrs. W. Shaw (seamen's missionary), S. Taylor, D. BitbroWn, E. W. Humphreys; T. Lea, W. Cooper, :I:Hamilton (collector of custams),'J. W. Light burn. F. Jolley, F. A. Lake (Law Clerk, and E. Marshall (secretary). At the outset, Mr. Marshall read the appeal received , from the Mayor of Manchester. set ting forth the claims rof the Institution upon the generosity of the public. There was also forwarded a description of bow the Life- boat Saturday was organised in Manchester and Salford. The Chairman said he did not think the cause needed any advocacy : it spoke for itself_ The question was which was the best way of raising money in Runcorn for so important and laudable an object. It was not intended that this effort should interfere with the i,fforts which had already been made in behalf of the fund of the Institution and which last year, ended May 2nd, resalted in subscriptions amounting to £47 17s. 11d. Mr. Bisbrown expressed the opinion that if the scheme of a Lifeboat Saturday were started with any degree of unanimity it was hound to he a success. Captain Le Couteur, said it afforded him much pleasure that Mr. Wiswall during his first year of office as chairman of the Board of Comrnistionerw should have inaugurated this movement for helping so laudable an 'institution. They must all acknowledge that the prosperity of the town depended greatly upon its shippingcand conte- quently on its sailors, directly or indirectly. If inland towns could give such great support,he did not, see why a seaport should not do the same. There were nurnbers' of people in Runcorn who were monuments to the ser- vices of the Lifeboat Institution, one of whom was Mr. Shaw, and there were many more. Those at present subscribing to the funds of the institution would riot withdralw their donations if the " Lifeboat Saturday " was formed, and he sincerely hoped the Chairman would succeed .in forming one. The speaker also sug- gested that the ministers, of religion should have an an- nual collection •in their respective ph+ ees of worship.— Mr. Shaw said that had it not been for tire lilt-1107ft he should not have been aide to spend the last 18 years working amongst the sailors at Runcorn. Be moved that a Lifeboat Saturday be organised, and added that he was confident it would not affect the subscriptions, but would give hundreds of people an opportunity of , contributing their mite who otherwise would not do so. The Rev. Dr. Gaeta Idi seconded. He had great sympathy with the object in hand, and his expectation was that the scheme, like many others, would be carried on for } the welfare of those engaged on the sea. Under the circumstances, no man with common sense could but adopt the proposal which had been put ; and he hoped and trusted the people of Roncorn would heartily co- operate to make the matter a great success.—Mr. S. Taylor said they could not help a more worthy object than the one in hand. He loped ,that although the meeting was not largely representative they would persevere with the project, and be sa as satisfied that something good would come of it. He suggested a large committee including the principals of the different works, because to snake the movement a success a collection must be made in every place of employment.—Mr. Humphreys suggested that a Life- boat Sunday should also he formed, and that the help of , the ladies be invoked.—Mr. Shaw said if they started' the Lifeboat Saturday, the Lifeboat Sunday would fol- low, as had been the case in other places—The motion was unanimously carried.—On the proposition of Mr. Lea, seconded by Dr. Gastaldi, it was resolved that those present form themselves into a Committee with power to add to their number to carry out the previous proposal. —Mr. Humphreys proposed that the Chairman of the Commissioners 'be chairman of the Committee, Mr. Hamilton treasurer, and Mr. Marshall secretary, all pro tins. In the diseussioti that eusued great credit was accorded to Mr. Hamilton for the success of his efforts on behalf of the Institution.—Mr. Hamilten remarked that this year the subscribers would be almost double the total of last year.—The motion was carried, and the meeting having passed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, , went into Committee.
THE WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S OPEN AIR TOTAL ABSTINENCK MISSION.

On Sunday Z;:i Open air meetings were bold at the usual place, the end of Bewsey-et. Mr. R. Storey conducted the meeting in the afternoon, and Mr. John Drury also spoke. Mr. T. Rigby conducted the meeting ip the evening, Messrs. R. Grout, J. Drury, R. Storey. and H. Taylor, police court mis- sionary, delivering speeches. One person signed the temperalltepledge.

div.head: CAUCUS MEETING OF TIIE TOWN COUNCIL. •
div.p: CAUCUS MEETING OF TIIE TOWN COUNCIL. •

A caucus meeting of the Town Council was held on Thursday evening at the TOwn Hall. The Mayor presided, and there was a full attendance of mem- bers. The main business of the meeting was the selection of committees. la most cases no change was made •in • the membership. On the Street Improvement Com mitt cc, however Councillor Plumpton took the place of Alder- man - Francomb; on the 'School Attendance Committee Councillors end WilkinSon succeeded to Alderman Chandley and Chuncillor Greening, Councillor Wilkinson was 'also elected to the Ceme- tery Committee in plate ,of Councillot%Greening, and Councillor Dixon, replaced Mr. F. A. Roberts on the Gas Commit-tee. Councillor Fietning was appointed to the Rivers Committee, filling the vacancy caused by the retirement of Mr. F. A. Roberts. A Health Committee was formed in place of the old Sanitary Committee,and it was composed of the same members with the • exception of Coun- cillors Muir and Wilkinson who succeeded Council- lors Greening and flepherd. entirely new committee is the Sanitary Works Committee which is to have charge of the Longford and intercepting depots. It consists of Councillors Monks,. Green- ing, Bonnell, Beaman, Hepherd, Walker,Smethurst, Flood, Roberts, and Dixon.
ODDFELLOWS' JUBILEE CELEBRATION.

On Saturday there was celebrated the jubilee, or fiftieth year of the Loyal Prince of Wales Lodge, No. 3,306, Warrington District, 1.0.0. F., M.U. A large number ot the members sat down to an ex- cellent knife and fork tea, prepared by Bro. F. Massey, at the Roebuck Hotel. 1 At the present time, the total number of members is 260, and the financial worth is about £1,400. The average age of the members is 34 years, and this will bear comparison with most of the lodges of the unity. The capital invested by the Prince of Wales Lodge totals £1,375, and the interest from this is now dping a great deal towards relieving the sick and funeral fund. Dur- ing the past year 20 new member; have joined, and the average age of these is about 21 ytars. It will thus be s..!en that both numerically and financially the lodge is in a very favourable position. .

After the tables had been cleared, an en- tertaining programme and toast list were gone through, under the presidency of Bro. Flolford, N.G. of the lodge.—Bro. J. H. Norbury proposed "The Manchester Unity and Board of Directors." Be paid a great compliment to the Board of Directors, who,, he said, were gentlemen who gave up their time to the furthering of the interests of the order. He coupled with the toast the name of Bro. Samuel Turner, corresponding secretary of the Bury district,and a member of the Board. —Bro. S. Turner, in responding, said Lancashire could juatly claim to be the founder of the Unity, and in the Unity they had formed one of the most successful of the friendly societies in the United Kingdom. (Applause.)i He mentioned the name of the late Mr. Henry Ratcliffe,. referring in eulogistic terms to his great services, while he acted as corresponding secretary of the Manchester Unity. The adoption of the system of graduated tables of payment was a great step in their history. He referred to the superannuation and old age pensions, to the juvenile branch of the Order, the good work it was doing, and expressed a hope that although that was the first it would not be the last time he would be among • the members of the branches in the Warrington district. (Applause.) —Bro. Turner having to leave by an early train. Bro. J. Emson, corresponding secretary of the Warrington dis- trict, propored a hearty vote of thanks to bun for his instructive and lucid speech. The vote was carried with acclamatien.—Bro. Swindells:followed with a recitation, and Bro. J. Massey proposed the toast of the Warring- ton District, coupling with it the name of Bro. F. Webster, the G.M. of the district.—Bro. Webster res- ponded.—Bro. F. J. Whittle,N.G., of the Admiral Nelson Lodge, proposed the toast of the Prince of Wales Lodge, coupling with the toast the names of Bros. Miller, (senior trustee of the Prince of Wales Lodge,) and T. Wadsworth, the secretary, and they responded. The toast of "The visiting brethren" was given by Bro. Wilson. and was responded to by Bro. S. Wright, N.G. of the Olive Branch Lodge. The toast of the Host and Lostess " was responded to by Bro F. Massey, and after a hearty vote of thanks had been ateorded to the Chair- man, Mr. Barton, who kindly presided at the piano, the singers, and all those who had contributed to the even- ing's entertainment, the, meeting closed with the National Anthem. fekneisTryliOr.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL FOR WARRINGTON.
A COMMENDABLE SCHEME.

Agitation for a new Public Hall for Warrington, has existed in alternate ebbs and flows ever since the old Hall became ,the Royal Court Theatre. Schemes have been promulgated one day, but have cows to a sudden smash the next day, like the collapse of aerial castles. Always the Corporation have been connected with these schemes, but never in a definite manner. When the necessity for a Public Hall was brought before them by a deputa- tion of local gentlemen' they offered to consider the matter, and in the meantime many people, thinking the Corporation would act, proposed that they should not erect an entirely new building, but alter and renovate the present Market Hall. The matter was debated in Council, and the Corporation found that they could not spend the rates in carrying out the object without the aid of a special Act of Parliament. The question of procuring this special Act was also debated, hut soon the shadow of such an expenditure paled and eventually disap- peared under the bulky and substantial expense of repairing Bridge-street, and oC paving • for the new baths. The various members of the deputation parted, leaving the corpse of their agitation behind them. Time pasood on, and then an unexpected party came along in the shape of several' meinbers of the Musical Society, and other gentlemen who commenced to resucitate that agitation. And, they have already infused more vitality and life into it than it originally possessed. ' ' 'We knew" said one of the gentlemen associated I with the scheme, to our reporter" that some active step would have to be taken. Warrington cannot do withmt a Public Hall. We apply the position to no'- selves an wonder where we can bold our concerts. We ask politicians where they will hold their ma.os mee•iref,, but they know not, andlhere is no place in which there I timid be held a public meeting. I believe, that even at present an attempt to organize a series of public lectures I has been knocked on the head, in consequence of their I being no place large enough in town where they could beheld." Hearing that the society, in co-operation with Mr. Jeans,, solicitor, and other gentleman had got Wens for I the proposed new Hall, our reporter obtained a view of them. They have been drawn up by Mr. Percy Silcock, architect, of Egypt-street, and contain the dimensions- for a building which should be a veritable boon to the town. The largest portion of the building will be a con- cert hall 98 feet by 50 feet, with galleries round three aides, the whole being: somewhat larger than the present theatre, and providing accommodation for about 3030 persons. The main entrance, which will be situated at one end'of the building, is to contain ladies' and gentle- man'a cloak rooms on each side. This entrance also forms an approach to a commodious " crush " room. The specifications for thia are such that the room could be utilised as a splendid babquet hall on the occasion of a ball or any such event. From this room an easy access will be found to the stage. This presents another advantage, for on the occasion of a large concert or meeting, the chorus, or the speakers, could be ac- commodated here to the number of 50 or 80;whilst wait- ing to go on to the stage. At the south ehd of the build- ing a lecture room will be constructed. It will be 581 t. long by 301 t. in width, and will include a spaciOnS"plat- form. The approach to this will he from an open porch, which will also form an entrance to the back portion of the concert hall. Extra doors will be provided from the gallery to serve in times of emergency. It is estimated that the cost of the erectien of this buildine would amount to about £4,500. No site has been definitely agreed to yet. Of course, the reason of this is, that it has not yet been settled to erect the build- ing. The suggested site, however, consists of a plot of I ,ground opposite the Gymnasium, and bounded by Win- marleich-st., Springfield-road,. and Palmvra-square. The agent, Mr. John Whlta,has,wo understand, not vet been negotiatsd with, but that is one of the incidents of the agitation which cannot he dealt with until it is finally decided to erect a new Hall. " How do you propose to raise the money for the erectianr is the question which naturally is often put to the gentlemen concerned. The course which Mr. Jeans and others propose to adopt is this. A deputation, which they have formed shall first wait upon the Corporation, and endeavour to persuade them to take the matter up again. If they fail in this, an attempt will be made to form a private company to carry the scheme out. Before forming a company, however, it is most likely that a pqblic meeting will be held, at which representativet of

the public will to invited to attend and offer any sug- gestions which they might Walt necessary in the interests of the public. The one dtfficulty, however, which stands in the way of form:ng a company, is a reluctance which many of the moneyed men of the town appear to entertain in taking the matter up. But there is no doubt that if the Corporation decline to move i the matter, such energetic gentlemen as Mr. Jeans, wiat. are interested in the affair, will 80011 find a way of overcotning the difficulty of finding the money. It is possible that a deputation will wait upon the Cor- poration newt week.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGION.

I understand that the prevalence of smallpox. ie beginning to prove detrimental to Warrington front a commercial point of view. Many of the country people who used to do their marketing at Warring- ton are, in consequence of the disease, now doing. this business in Manchester,. aud Liverpool. This is the more to be deplored; as I know from experi— ence that when people once get into the habit of going to another district to do their marketing, it. is very difficult to bring them beak.

I fear, from all accounts, that there is no likeli- hood at the epidemic being got ander for some months to come, at least. I am afra,d we are likely to have our Uhriatmas saddened by the black cloud that is banging over us, and which as yet doee not appear ta have any silver lining. Since the out- break of the disease various gatherings have had to be suspended, including a concert this week, and I have been wondering whether the usual Christmas and New Year's treats will have to be postponed. too, as it seems almost . likely they will be, if there is no moderation in the present pestilence. It would be a pity if the poor aged people and. juveniles, .whose hearts are made glad by the generosity of the public at that seasonvshould be disappointed. But there is an alternative to feed- ing them publicly in toe customary manner. As a correspondent in the " Examiner " leaver, who condemned these public dinners as humilhating to the recipients, suggested, the money subscribed might be devoted to treating them, for once at least, in their own honnia, not necessarily al.l with meals, but some with °they. commodities,. each as coals, clothing, and the like, according as their necessities demanded This ought to be a matter for the consieeration of the committees who have the Christmas and New Year treats in hand.

Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, is a jolly solicitor, and mixed up comicality and pathos in a most happy manner in his defence of the accused publican, at the Borough Police Court, on Monday. He must haveluite charmed the Bench and Unrest of his audience into forgetfulness of the gloominess and stuffiness of the old,•building. But it was rather hard on Alderman Harrison that he should have saddled upon him that he had formerly quoted as his own definition of drunkenness a well-known verse once cited by Justice Lopes with approvaL This definition is explained in a verse which de- clares not to be drunk a man who can rise from the floor and cull for more drink, but a man who lies there unable to speak or rise. Now, it will be re- membered that Alderman Harrison did some months ago draw a very fine distinction between drunkenness and intoxication, which I took occa- sion to criticise, and 1 humorously commended to Alderman Harrison's attention the verse in ques- tion. Mr. Knowles or his client must have mis- read my remarks, and supposed that Alderman Har- rison had adopted this versical definition as his own, hence the mistake. Alderman Harrison, how- ever, did not seem very anxious to take great pains to disclaim the imputation, hence I do E 0 for him.

Since the case was heard. I have read of another standard, by which to determine whether a man be drunk or not. The other day, it seems, a Major Frank Fisher was found by a policeman lying asleep on a doorstep, at Putney, and taken by kim into custody as drunk. A Dr. Symthe was called in to pronounce whether he had passed the pro- blematical line that divides temperance from drunkenness. He asked the Major if he under- stood Latin, and on being informed that he did, called upon him to repeat the first line of Virgil. 'The Major had doubtless never. dreamt that he would have to renew in mature age, the experience of his school days, by repeating and correctly trans- lating Virgil, under fear of punishment in case of a slip, but he viumphantly passed the ordeal. The- Malor's case is a unique contribution to the metaphysics of that modern perplexing problem— When is a raan drunk ?

The education of the collier grows apace. His primitive tastes and ideas are advancing rapidly in a parallel to those of a more .refined community. At any rate this is so with the Burtonwood collier, and it was conclusively proved at the War- rington County Sessions on Wednesday. A number of colliers were summoned for refusing to quit a beerheuse, and during the case there came forth some facts, proving to what extent the colliers of , that neighbourhood are bravely trying to keep up to modern progress. He has caught the hang of the luxurious dissipations of gaming. Of course be is a little slow in this way yet,and cannot rise to the per- fect state of his brothers in town. No; while they madly plunge their"tanners" on billiards," nap,"solo- whist, andloke nothing for dinner and some more for tea, he is limited to "tip it," for pints. But "tip it " is slow,and very pristine. The average bil- liard-playing townsman coala nt endure it. It consists in one of the gamesters concealing a button in one hand, and closing both fisticular members, placing them on the table and inviting the others to tip the hand with the button in. When one man has "tipped it" 64 times he is entitled to tipple a pint. If the men bould console themselves to t,ake nothing but the drinks they win, there would be a , chance for the temperance cause around Burton- wood. But their wild restive natures ca'nt do that yet; so just while they educate themselves to the game they drink pints between their wins.

It seems that the case at the County Sessions arose chiefly out of one of the collier's keen sense of honour. They bad been playing " tip it' and drinking pints,and socially swearing at each other. But the plemant tenor of the evening is said to have been suddenly broken by the laticikr•d's son calling one of the men a " liar." With Quivering lip and gashing eye the collier arose. He grasped the table fiercely and with a voice trembling with rage and ,beer said, " Ize-a-hic-gent-hic-gentleman. I shall now-hic7 smash er head into squashed clam- hie.' He might have done it, had not P.C. Grundy 'moved him. Be might bare gone to bed that night and been restless under his sense of the .in4alt. or he might not. But at any rate the next day e went to the, public-house and:demanded sati,faction from the son. The on is said to be of I a saving disposition, and wouldn't 'give any satis- faction, Be chose to save his head.

-- What was the collier to do next to maintain Me attitude of a modern gentleman ? Be had asked for satisfaction and been refused.. He seemed to spend a few moments in thinking what his refined brothers in the town would do under the circumstances. His mind was soon made up. 146 snatched off his cap and banged the land- lord in the face with it. He then systematically overturned several forms, kicked someone, and ' smashed a quart bottle. After thia,. his wife and the lodger came and took him. But he still craved for satisfaction. It was when the magistrates heard of this, that they 'gave tho man what he wanted,satisfaction. They the satisfaction of paying over .£2 costs.

But there is another phase of modern life, which- the Burtonwood collie/ likes to inclu}ge in. That is the much enjoyed luxury of afflicting his fellows with a speech. Of Course his oratory is more con- spicuons for its sentiment than its eloquence, and from a little affair that occurred near Collins Green last week, the collier's speeches prove him to,have more heart, than ltnowledge of what 18 proper. A dinner was held in connection with a local institu- tion. The previous day one of the members had " shuffled off this mortal coil." When the toasts came the Chairman alluded to the sad event in pathetic tones, and then called upon another brother to speak. This gentleman arose. His large heart was full. Tears conned quickly along his rugged cheeks, and his eyes were Bud with a far nway gaze on the water bottle before him. He seemed to catch an idea presently, and. started off to apologise for his ordtorical defects, pulled up shaTp, sobbed, and wanted to sit down.: after remarking that he would, assist the poor widow to borrow money for thefuneral.

The gathering appreciated this show of feeling and clapped. A light of inspiration came into the brother's eyes. Ile jumped to his feet, and said, I" G'men, afore I sit, I beg to propose our missing i brother's health." Perhaps the gathering thought jhe meant the dead man's celestial health, for they drunk the toast. )4IERLIN.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE couRT.
SATURDAT.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), Mr. L. Voisey, and Mr. Jahn Geddes. - •

STRANGE ADVENTURES AND THE SEQUHL.—Joseph Smith, hailing from Bury, was charged with attempting to steal certain goeds between Buttermarket-st. and Bridge-st., on the previous evening.—P.O. Turner stated on the previous evening he was on duty in Butter- market-st., and observed the prisoner moving about in a suspicious manner. He watched him, and at length observed him make an attempt to steal a pair of boots from Mr. Booth's shop. He tried to pull them off a hook, but when he saw witness he went away. Witness watched him go up the street, and turn into Bridge-st. He then told a young man to follow him and take observation of his movements. Subsequently witness found that the prisoner had been in Mr. Richard- son's warehouse, and he took him into custody.— Fred Harrington, assistant to Mr. Richardson, stated that when he went to look for the prisoner he could not find him at first, but ultimately he discovered him in the warehouse concealed among some soft soap casks. He declined to come out of the stores, and witness ejected him. Prisoner then put himself in a fighting attitude, and when ke got outside he struck witness. He retaliated, and P.C. Turner came up and took the prisoner into custody. The prisoner was sober. The prisoner denied that he tried to steal anything.—Mr. Voisey (to prisoner) : You seem to treat it as a smiling matter.—Prisoner : I did not expect to be charged with stealing boots. I expected to be charged with being drunk.—ln reply to the chairman, the prisoner said he came from Bury on Tuesday.—The Bench committed him to gaol for 14 days' hard labour. DRUNIEBNNE9B.—WiIIiam Griffin, farm labourer, ss. and costs.
Mom:Pvt.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) in the chair, Aldermen Sutton, Harrison and Francomb, and Messrs. F. Monks and E. J. Guest.

ASSAULTING ERR EIUSBAND.—Mary Ellen Welfe, wife of Joseph, 3, Bankat., was charged under a warrant with assaulting her husband on the 28th of October.— The complainant said that on that date his wife accused him of having taken 6d, from her and threw? a bandful of salt in his face. She found the 6d. in her pockeE, and he struck her on the head with a quart bottle inflicting a serious wound. He did not want her to go to jail,but wanted a separation. (Laughter.)—Alderman Harrison: It is the other way about.—ln reply to the Bench the defendant said she was not sorry for what she had done. —She was bound over to keep the peace for six months. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Mary Coyne, In Fennell-st., on Saturday night, was lined ss.—Margaret Keogh, in Buttermarket-at., on Saturday night, was dismissed on promising to take the pledge.—Thos. Williams was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick- road, at a quarter to one on Sunday morning, and also with a.ssaulting P.C. Leathwood on the same occasion. The officer said he struck him twice on the way to the police station and commenced kicking at the doors.—He was fined 10s.—John Kilgariff, in Winwick- st., on Saturday night, 55.-5 b inifred Mason in Bank- st., on the 22nd ult., 6s.—James Hopkins, in Scotland- 'road, on the 26th Oct., 55. VAGRANCY.—Wm. Coyne, aged 16, was charged with sleeping at Bewsey Forge that morning.—The watchman said he was sleeping where the red hot slag ran out,and if it had run out it would have burnt him to death.—P.C. Lawrence corroborated.—The case was dismissed on Coyne promisiaa to go to a home in Liverpool, to which Mr. Taylor undertook to send him. WIFB ASSAULT.—Thomas Dagnall, forge labourer, 4, Gandy's Terrace, was charged with assaulting Margaret Dagnall, his wife, about a quarter to 12 on Saturday night.—P.C. Cooper 20, said he saw the defendant and his wife fighting in his house, and they rolled out across the footpath up and down ; then into the itarden. The defendant there had her down, and witness pulled him off her.—lt appeared that the ground on which the footpath was was private, and the case was dismissed. FIGHTING.—MichaeI Preston and Peter Garrity for fighting in Buttermarket-street, on the 22nd October, were bound over for each odier to keep the peace six months, and had to pay 7.4. 6d. costs each. UNSEEMLY LANGUAGE.—Thos. Browne, forge labourer, , Wright-street, Sankey Bridges, was charged with using unseemly language in Church-street, on Saturday night. P.C. Phillips proved the case, and said the ladies at the training college must have heard every word he said. He was fined 10s. A DOG CASE.—Joseph Brierley, 289, Kent-road, was charged with allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled, and without a collar with his name engraved legibly thereon. The cases were dismissed.
TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair) and
W. Owen.

DRUNICENNESS.—WiIIiam Owen and Thomas William Dickenson were both fined for drunkenness. " Two-o-Rum AND A STouv."—Thomas Walsh, labourer, son of a Warrington recruiting sergeant, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-at. on the previous evening, and with assaulting two women, Mary Ellen Wolfe and Mary Preston.—P.S. Cheney stated that on the evening in question the two women came to him and complained that they had been as- saulted by prisoner in the Pelican Inn. Witness pro- ceeded to the Pelican and walked into the snug. The prisoner was there reclining in a corner in a drunken condition with a quart pot before him. He asked the landlady if she knew the man was in the hoase. She said she did not, and thereupon ordered the man out. He then became disorderly, and had to be locked up,—The two women said that when they were in the Pelican someone sang a song, after which prisoner arose and went" round with his cap." When he got to them they refused to subscribe, so he struck both of them, and threw them out of the room, and as they were going through the doorway he kicked them severely.—" What were you doing in the public-house ? " , asked Mr. Garnett "Oh, oi was alter 'aving some stout," said Mrs. Preston, "and Mary Ellen was 'eying two-o- rum."—Mr. Garnett remarked that as both were married women they would do better to look to their homes than go frequenting public-houses. The charge of assault was dismissed, and prisoner was fined 10s. for drunkenness. TEE LAST CALLING HOUSlL—Martin Maguire, aII EX- cavator on the Ship Canal, pleaded guilty to hating been drunk and disorderly in Bridge- st., on the previous night, and assaulting Elizabeth Monks, landlady of the Packet House Inn, Bridee-st. Mr. Monks said prisoner and several other men, one or two whom were under the influence of drink, went to the Packet House. The prisoner acted as "spokesman of the party." The land- lady, seeing he was drunk, refused to serve him, where- upon he became very violent and used bad language, and while being ejected he assaulted not only Mrs. Monks, but her husband.—ln answer to the Chief Con- stable, Mr. Monks said he had occasionally to put out men who called at his house, and who had already had enough to drink. It was regarded by some of them as "the last calling house."—For being drunk defendant was fined ss. and cost 4 while fur the assault he was committed to prison for a month with hard labour.— The Chairman: Those publicaLs who endeavour to con- duct their houses in a respectable manner must be pro- tected. We cannot allow a man to go into a public. house and do as he likes. The publicans are bound to have the protection of the law. CONSIDERED His PREVIOUS GOOD CIIARACTEIL—Joba Jones, a horse trainer, was charged with being drunk and

disorderly the previous night, and breaking a window at the Royal Exchange Inn, and further with assaulting the landlord, Win. Bolton. Mr. Bolton stated that the prisoner came into the house the worse for drink, and raised a disturbance., in the course of which he struck witness in the face and broke one of the windows. He was thus compelled to send for police protection. P.C.'s Dean and Meacock spoke to finding the prisoner in a very disorderly condition.—:ln consideration of the prisoner's good character, he was only fined 103. including costs for drunkenness. TRIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman T. Sutton (in the chair), Captain Ridgway, and Mr. J. Fairclough. A NOISY DEVENVANT.—Feter Howson, 10, Jones' Buildings, Winwick-road, was charged with ccining from land where he had been in search of game ; he was further charged with being in posses- sion of nets. 'Defendant came into court in a drunken condition. :He lounged about the prisoner's box, and grinned blankly at the Bench, and waved his cap about. Mr.4Jenkins, solicitdr, appeared to defend h!..m, but at first :said he should withdraw from the case in consequence ,of defendant's condition. After loudly demanding %Lad the policemen should adhere to the truth, during Which time the court officials were calling " Be quietTeter," the defendant consented to be tame, and Mr..Fenkins went on with the defence.— P.C. Cooper said the he found the defendant in company with another man -proceeding down Longford-street at eight o'clock at night. The other man ran away, and witness searched defendant and found upon him two nets and stakes and two rabbits. He charged him with coming from land where he had been in search of game. —Mr. Jenkin's defence consisted of the contention that no game was found in the possession of the defendant, and that no evidence had been or could be given to prove that Rowson was coming from any land where he had been in search of game.—P.C. Cooper was called to speak of the condition in which he found the nets. Prisoner turned round to him and said " Th' are a joskin, thou art, and that's telling thee straight." Then turning to the Bench and banging his fist on the box he said "my character's as good as any in this room, there's nothin' again it whatsome- ever." After this defendant made many speeches and invited the Bench to use the stakes for walking sticks. He was fined 20s. including costs.—Wm. Rowson, last defendant's son, was charged with using threats to P.C. Cooper on the same occasion. The evidenoe showed that defendant came up the road as his father was being searched. He came up and abused the constable and threatened to break his head. Defendant pleaded guilty. The Bench said the offence was not a serious one, and inflicted a fine of 55. TRAVELLINIII WITYOUT A TICICIAT.—James Woods, Stockport,was charged with travelling from Liverpool to Warrington on the London and North-Western Railway, by the 11-15 train on Wednesday night. Prisoner pleaded guilty to travelling without a ticket. He said he went from Stockport to Liverpool that morning to see some friends off to America. He took a return ticket. In Liverpool he enjoyed himself, spent his money and lost his ticket.—A railway official said they had made in- quiries but could not ascertain any truth in the pri- soner's statement.—Fined ss. and ordered to pay the cost of the ticket.
FRIDAY. —l3•fore Alderman Harrison (in the chair), Alderman Wright and Dr. Homan. , . .

, A FOOTBALLER ROBBED.—James Taylor, labourer, Latchford, was charged with stealing from the licensed premises of the Old Crow Inn on the afternoon of Saturday 22nd October, one leather handbag, a pair of trousers, and a pair of boots, value El, the property of James Hamblett, 128 Knutsford-road.—Mr. Hunt, chief constable, said that the complainant was a member of a Warrington football club, which met at the Old Crow Inn, to dress. He, together with his compan- ions, dressed in their football clothes and went out to play. When they came back complairont missed the articles mentioned and gave information to the police. Detective Monaghan during some inquiries visited the shop of Mrs. Leslie, second-hand clothes dealer, Mersey-st., she spoke Pf the prisoner having been there on Saturday, endeavouring to steal clothes. On Thursday evening, however, prisoner came to the police office and surrendered himself on the charge, The com- plainant, however, was unable to be at the court that day, and he wished to ask for a remand until Monday. —The Bench therefore remanded the prisoner until Monday. ROBBING HIS FRIEND.—John Barrow, 2, Oliver-st.,was charged with stealing from the pers3u of Alice Stubbs, of St. Helens, at the Shannon Inn, Winwick-road, the sum of 83. 4d. The complainant stated that on Thurs- day she came from St. Helens to Warrington on business. IShe missed her last train back at night and went to the house of the prisoner, whose wife was a friend of hers. IMrs. Barrows invited her to spend the night there, and she consented. After a while she went in company with the prisoner and his wife to the Shannon public-house. They were having a lark at the time. She had donned the prisoner's hat and coat and he was wearing her hat and cloak. When in the public- house complainant paid for three "beers," and out of the coin she tendered she received 8s 4d change. Pre- sently a woman named Mrs. Glee came in. The com- plainant invited her to drink, but when she put her hand in her pocket for the money she found her purse had gone. While she was searching for it, prisoner drank up his beer at one gulp and went out.—Frederick Hampton. son of the landlord of the public-house, said he saw the prisoner put his hand in complainant's p,,cket and take out the purse.—Sergeant Taylor said that in consequence of a complaint he received, he went ' to prisoner's house at two o'clock in the morn-1 ing. They examined prisoner and found es 9d upon him. Complainant was present, and prisoner ' offered to give her 7s. 6d. if she would not press the matter, as it would ruin him. He then commenced cry- ing. Previous to making the offer he said he had no money about him.—The Bench took into consideiation prisoner's previous good character, and fined him 10s. and costs.

CHEAP OYSTFRS AND DRINIC.—James Meadows,a black- smith of Winwick-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous night,and also with stealing a quantity of oysters from the shop of Thomas Shuffle- ton, Town's-end.—Prisoner entered Shuffieton's shop and ordered four pennyworth of oysters. He swallowed them and walked out. Mr. Shuffiston's son followed him and informed a constable of the affair. Prisoner was then drunk and behaving in a disorderly manner. He was taken into custody.—Fined 10s. and costs.

INFRINGEMENT OF THE I`ACTORY ACT.—A fine of 40s.and costs was inflicted upon Mr. William Hodgkinson, draper, Bridge-st., for causing two of his apprentices, Annie Reed and Jane Brough to work one hour longer than sanctioned by the Factory Acts, on Saturday, Oct. Ist. The girls were engaged upon a "mourning order," and worked until five p.m. instead of four p.m.
WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDLT.—Before_Mr. J,Ryla nds (in the chair) and
Mr. G. CoMber.

THREW THE POL.-ICEMAN- INTO -THE ROAD.—Daniell Edwards, and Edward Bastard, labourers, Croft, were charged with being drunk and disorderly, at Craft, on the 16th October. P.C. Ballagban stated that just as the people were leaving church on the evening in quee• tiou the defendants with another man were creating a disturbance in the highway. When he trent to them they lifted him from the gronnd by the legs, and threw him into the middle of the road.—Both defend- ants denied the offence, but were fined 2s. 6d. and costs each.

PLAYING "Tip IT" AND REFUSING YO QUlT.—Thomas Fariyrnan and John Kelly. were charged ith being drunk and refusing to quit the Chapel Inn, the licensed premises of William Houghton, Burtonwood, on the 16th October.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for Ferryman.— P.C. Grundy said that about ten to eleven o'clock on the night of the 16th of last month he was called to Mr. Houghton's premises and requested by the landlord to put the two defendants out. They were both then acting in a disorderly manner. He had to put both men out by force. He understood there lied been a row in the house previously.—William Houghton said the row commenced in this way. Ferryman came to him and swore at him. He ordered hint out. Ferryman would not go, and a man named King remonstrated with Ferryman. The result was a row, caused by the two defendants.—Witness ordered all the men in the room out, and they all went with the exception of Ferryman, ' who said he had got a glass of beer which he intended to drink. Witness then brought his two sons out of bed to assist him, and Farryman threatened them all round.—Cross-examined by Mr. Davies: The quarrel did not arise tkrough a dispute amongst the party who were playing ". tip it." He admitted colliers camo there and played "tip it " for beer.—Mrs. Houghton in her evidence said the defen- dants were playing "tip it."—Mr. P. Davies in his de- fence, said that his client had merely endeavoured to quiet a disturbance, and after being ordered out with the other five men, he rightfully returned to drink his beer, and refused to leave again until he had had what 1 he was entitled to.—Farryman was fined 2s. 6d. and Kelly ss.—Farryman was next charged by the Licensed Victuallers' Association,on behalf of Mr. Houghton, with refusing to quit the Chapel Inn on the following day.— Mr. Houghton said that defendant came in the worse for drink, threatened to punch witness's head, then struck bins on the bead with his cap. Ultimately lie threw his cap down and ordered witness to pick the cap up ; , and when he refused defendant threw the contents of a glass of beer at him. A general disturbance ensued. He ordered defendant Out; but he refused to go, and had ultimately to be removed by his friends.—Mr. Percy Davies who ap- peared for the defence contended that his client unfortu- nately went into the Chapel Inn to ask the landlord's son for an explanation for calling him a scamp the previous night. But he contended that he did not act disorderly, and although at first he refused to quit when asked, he ultimately left quietly. Prisoner had a previous good character and had only broken the pledge the night before.—Defendant was ordered to pay £2 9s. costs and bound over to keep the peace for three months.—Joseph Lawton, collier, was also charged with refusing to quit the same premises on the 15th October. He was one of the six men referred to in the same case.—Defendant was ordered to pay £1 13s. 6d. costs and bound over to keep the peace for three months. A CRUEL SEQUENCE TO A TROTTING MATCH.—Thomas Wood, a butcher, of St. Helens, was charged with ill- treating a pony, at Sankey, on the 15th of October.—

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1892

Inspector Wall, R.S.P.C.A., appeared to prosecute, and said the facts of the case were these. Defendant had been hired by a horse dealer named Thomas Sumner to ride a bay mare which he was trotting against a horse owned by Antoney Shields, of St. Helens. The stakes were £5 aside, and the course was from the Sankey second mile stone to the fourth mile stone. The race was run and Saunders' horse lost. The latter was going home in a trap later on, and the defendant was following riding the mare. Another horseman suddenly came up and defendant at once entered a race with him. During the race defendant was seen to belabour the horse in a cruel manner with a whip stock, and by the force of his blows felled the animal. The result of the fall was that a wound nine inches in length was inflicted on the animal's leg, and several bruises about the body. The defendant took no heed of this but pulled the horse up and continued the race. The animal was in such a con- dition when it reached the Butcher's Arms, Bold, that it had to be killed a few hours afterwards.—Thomas Saunders and other witnesses gave evidence coroborat- ing this, and defendant was fined £l, and £3 ss. costs.

From some cross-kicking Plumpton got possession from a kick by Tomlinson, and easily eluding Piercy ran in a clever try, which Fair. Turner failed to turn to account. The visitors tried hard now to gain a footing in the War- rington quarters, which they ultimately gained by the aid of Craven and Sawyer. Minors were their only re- ward. The Warringtonians again returned to the attack just before the close, but the score was not augmented, and when time was called Warrington had advanced a couple of points in the competition, the final score read- ing—Warrington, 0-3-3 ; Broughton, 0-0-2. Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, full back ; F. Plurnpton, F. Heesom, and H. Webster, three-quarters ; James T. Bate and J. W. Evans, half-backs ; Fair. Turner, H. Ashton, G. Hampson, J. Jalley, T. Donohue, W. Berry, W. Bandies, J. Holmes, and H. Teare, for- wards. Broughton: A. C. Tomlinson, full back ; G. H. Piercy, Sawyer, and C. E. Craven, three-quarters ; D. Roberts, and W. Whiteley, half-backs ; E. W. Broad- bent, H. Hadwin, H. Hamilton, G. Ibbotson, J. Shep- herd, G. Skidmore, J. A. Squires, R. Tomlinson, and G. Tomlinson (captain), forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
SATIIRDAT.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley.
THEFT. —Mary Murphy, a woman of loose character, was sentenced to fourteen days' hard labour for stealing a shirt belonging to Samuel Catterall.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Before Major Hazlehurst, Dr. Steele, and Mr. James Handley (chairman). DRUNNENNESS.—For this offence the following were fined : Samuel Brian Richard Smith, Emma Smith, Geo. Thompson, and William Smith, and Thomas Bishop. Prionua LANCE:TAGIL—James Finegan was fined ss. and costs 15s. 4d. for using obscene and profane lan- guage. TRANSFER OF LICENSES.—The Harwell Vaults, Ben- tinck-st.. from Samuel Spann to John Hilton ; and the Albion inn, Nelson-st., from George Johnson to Henry Hill junr. MAINTENANCE OF Partawrs.—An order was made upon James Oultram, of Frodsham, to pay is. per week towards the maintenance of his mother, Martha Oultratn of Kingsley, who is receiving 35., per week from the Union.—An order was made upon James Bate, engineer on the river steamer Gower to pay 23. to wards the sup- port of his mother Catherine Bate, who was in receipt of 33. per week from the Union.—Mr. Frodsham, the collector, proved the case. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO HORSEB.—VVIIL Miller, assistant stableman at the Duke's Stables, Top Locks, was sum- moned for cruelty to a horse by causing it to be worked in an unfit state.—P.C. Proctor stated that on the 21st. ult. he saw a boy named Owen driving two horses past , the Highfield Tannery. They were drawing a large flat. One of the horses was lame, and he examined it, and found two large raw wounds on one shoulder, and one on the other shoulder. The boy said he had been ordered Ito work the 6A-seg.—Mr. James Tickle, from the Ship Canal Office, said the horse had not arrived at the Run- corn stables from Preston Brook and the defendant had no oversight over the horses. His duty was to clean and whitewash the stables.—The case was dismissed, and Superintendent Atherton said they would endeavour to find the right person.--John Owen was then charged with working the horse. He said he drew the attention of Thomas Routledge, at Preston Brook stables, to the state of the horse, and he told him he must take the animal.—The Bench adjourned the case for a week. Smoot, BOARD CASEN.—Fifteen parents were summon- ed by the School Board for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fee of ss. was imposed in each case.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDlT.—Before Messrs. J. Brock and H. Wade Deacon.

FINED FOR DRUNICENNESS.—John Wright, Dock-st. ; John Howard, Peel-street; Thomas Burns, Marsh. street ; Hugh Tulley, Farrant-street ; John Roch ford, no fixed abode ; Sam Webster, no fixed abode; Johanna Sinclair, no fixed abode; Roger Buckley, Birchfield- road ; John Logan, Midwood-street ; Isaac Oakes, Rain- hill; and Matthew Burns, Fisher-street.
Tuarr OF BOOTS.—Fred Wheeler was charged with stealing a pair of boots from 29, Victoria-road, valued at 45., the property of J. W. Lee. He was sent to gaol for 14 days,

TIM KICKING CASE.—Richard Taylor, Bold-street, was charged on remand with doing grievous bodily harm to Eli Steinardt, by breaking his left leg, on the 16th Sept.— Dr. McCambridge stated that Mr. Steinardt was still unable to appear, but would most likely be able to do so next Monday.—Defendant was accordingly remanded another week.

div.head: OSI4IAN DIGAIA STILL LIVES.
div.p: OSI4IAN DIGAIA STILL LIVES.

A telegram from Suakim says that Osman Digma is endeavouring to muster various tribes for an attack on the Egyptians. He occupied Sinkat on the 23rd ult., and Erkowit on the following day, and on the 27th his horsemen made a raid close to Suakim.

div.head: DREADFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN
div.p: DREADFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN
YORKSHIRE. TEN LIVES LOST AND MANY INJURED.

An appalling railway disaster occurred on Wednesday morning on the North-Eastern line at Thirsk. A train forming the second portion of the East Coast express from Edinburgh to York and London (the train having been divided into two portions owing to the large num- ber of passengers) whiJli left the northern capital at 10 40, came into collision with a goods train and was totally wrecked. Ne fewer than ten people, including the guard of the goods train were killed, and there is a long list of injured. To add to the horror, the wrecked carriages took fire, and there is reason to apprehend that some passengers were burned to death. There was a dense fog when the accident took place._ . _ . .
The falowing is a list of the killed and Injured : KILLED.

J. H. Boyle, 85, Newgate-st., London. Captain Duncan M'Leod. 42nd Highlanders, Hugh Brodie, Railway Villa, Leytonstone' Essex. H. Lee, Camera-st., Spitalfields Market, London. James J. Anderson, 8, Panmure-st., Dundee.
.1. Beswell Hill, Great George-st., Edinburgh. George Petch. goods guard, Middlesborough. Miss M'Culloch, 2, Gilmore-st.,Alexandria, Dunbarton- shire.
Miss Lottie Hamilton, neice of above, of same address. Mrs. Mackenzie, Leven-t., Edinburgh.
INJURED. Lady Stewart, 73, Harrington Gardens, London. George Rhodes, Headingley, Leeds. David Reid Petrie, Edinburgh.
David M'Culloch .(head .injured), Alexandria, Dun -
bartonshii

[re. Provost Sutherland, Bathgate. Mrs. Dadd, of Aderdeen. Sarah Robinson, Montrose. Rose White, of the Boosey Theatrical Company. Alexander Mackenzie, Leven-st., Edinburgh. J. H. Buchanan, Glasgow. Most of these were only slightly injured. The driver, Ewart. of the express, has a broken thigh, and is in Thirsk Hospital. At nine o'clock the line was cleared. During the day traffic had been worked round by Melmerby, and trains south and north were greatly delayed. The coroner's inquest will be opened to-morrow afternoon.
STATEMENT BY THE MARQUIS OF TWEEDDALE.

Amongst those who were in the wrecked train and who came to London by the special on Wednesday after- noon was the Marquis of Tweeddale, chairman of the North British Railway Company, with whom a repre- sentative of the Press Association at once had an inter- view. His lordship said :—" At the time of the acci- dent the express, in which I was a passenger, was travelliag at the rate of nearly sixty miles an hour. The , goods train into which the expzess ran was loaded chiefly with iron, and had it been stationary at the , time the consequences, in view of its enormous weight and power of resistance, must have been much more , serious. But fortunately the goods train had at that time commenced to move onward, and this, of course, somewhat lessened the violence of the shock. Yet the collision was very severe and most serious in its I consequences. At the time of the accident I was asleep in the Pullman car. Amongst the other passengers in the same saloon were the Marquis of Huntly, General Lambton and Mr. Kynoch, one of the directors of the Highland Railway. None of us were injured, al- though we all got a great fright and a severe shaking. The accident occurred about fcur miles beyond Thirsk. I believe that eight persons were killed. These included the driver of the goods train and the stoker of the express train. The engineman of the express had his thigh broken. The engine and tender of the express were smashed, also the carriage next to them, but the body of the Pullman carriage stood the shock, although its forward end was knocked off. I believe the Pullman first-class passengers were all asleep at the time of the crash, and it is a marvel that we all escaped so well, considering the terrible character of the wreck in which we so suddenly found ourselves. The engine and tender were doubled back from the shsck upon whatever was between them and the Pullman car, forming one heap, which took fire; but, so far as I saw, the fire did not spread to the rest of the train. The carriage behind the. Pullman was injured. I saw two gentlemen get out of it.

No further deaths are reported among the injured passengers by the express which was wrecked at Thirsk on Wednesday morning, but one or two persons remain in a critical condition. The coroner's inquest was opened on Thursday, and after evidence of identification had been given with regard to the persons killed it was ad- journed for a fortnight.
CADBURY'S Cocoa is &Whiny pure.—The Public Ana lysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests and the result has always proved its great value as a sustain ing and nourishing boverage.--AdvE.
