div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

DALLAM BREWERY V. LATCHFORD (IST TEAMS).—This match was played on the Latchford ground in fine weather, the Brewery team having the best of the game throughout. Final score :—Brewery, 2 tries and 7 minors ; Latchford, nil. BREWERY 2ND V. W BATE'S TEAN.—TiIiS match was played on the brewery ground in fine weather, the ground being in splendid condition. The forwards on the winning side played a very good game throughout, J. Spencer and S. Kelly being the pick. Final score : Brewery, 2 tries to nil. RUNCORN RECREATION V. Booma.—The Bootle Rugby team journeyed to Runcorn on Saturday, to play the Recreation club. The home team ran up a score of two goals (one dropped), two tries, and five minors to nil. The scoring was opened by A. Abel dropping a fine goal after some splendid passing, in which nearly all the home team had the ball through their hands. Shortly after this W. Bowden scored a try near the corner, Carr landing a good goal. J. Pendlebury and Jos. Nickson also scored tries.

BIRICRNHBAD PARK V. RUNCORN ("A" Teams).— Played at Birkenhead Park, on Saturday, before a moderate number of spectators. The visitors soon com- menced to press, and had exceedingly bard lines. From a line-ant at the Park 25 Hayes secured and ran in, the goal kick failing. Half-time—Runcorn, one try; Park, nil. Resuming, the visitors again pressed, the Park having very little of the play. From some scrimmages on the home line Green scored a try, the attempt to con- vert being a failure. Final—Runcorn.two tries, Birken- head Park, nil.

WARRINGTON 2ND V. B !tenet-MN 2ND—Played at IBroughton. Broughton kicked off, and Boldsworth re- turning, Warrington pressed, Lawless scoring in first few minutes, no goal resulting. From the drop out the visitors again attacked, a rush headed by Monks and Lomas ending in Forster scoring. Up to half time War- i rington maintained the attack, and owing to faulty pass- ing some splendid chances were thrown away. In the second half Warrington pressed throughout; in fact the home team were never once dangerous. Nice passing by the Warrington backs ended in Hinchcliffe scoring under the posts, Speakman converting. The same player fol- lowed with a try a minute later, Lomas kicking a grand goal, but to the surprise of all the referee decided against them. Nothing of any importance occurred afterwards. A one-sided game ended in a victory for the visitors by 1-3-4 to nil. WARRINGTON " A " v. BROUGHTON "A,"—When these antagonists faced each other on the Broughton ground. rain was descending heavily, and only two 25's were arranged to be played. Although Warrington had to face a stiffish breeze and the rain, a clever dribble by Barnes, Glover, and Edwards, and a capital run by Gib- son, gave their side a foothold inside the home quarters, the attack only being frustrated in the nick of time by Hood. A penalty kick for offside against Broughton al- most ended in their discomfiture, as Potts and Lally, in quick succession, were only pulled up on the line. This sort of thing did not suit the Broughtonians, and pulling themselves together, they made their presence felt, by rushing to midfield, where Potts saved. In this break away they were materially assisted by their half-backs, Roberts and Smith, who totally ignored the offside rule, and were allowed to adopt this style of play throughout the match. However, the Warrington forwards were showing splendid combined play, and by manipulating the sarew in the scrimmage, dashed away, Higham, Bailey and Edin dribbling into Broughton lines. Smith and Roberts averted disaster to centre, where Smith (Warrington) got beautifully away, but delaying to pass at the right moment the chance was lost. The over-zealousness of the home team was here penalized, and Hood was forced to kick dead. After Gibson had repulsed an attack, some grand forward play by the visitors continually harassed the home defence, but the daring saves effected by the busy defenders kept their lines intact. The wind and rain had ceased when the re-start was made, but for some time pack succeeded pack through the instrument- ality of the home halves. At length Smith got the leather away to Lally, who threw to Potts the latter dashing finely away, and repassing to Lally, the ball was taken close to the posts, and subsequently forced , over the line, Broughton escaping with a minor. The drop-out enabled the homesters to reach half-way, but Lally and Potts ran the oval back, and Bradbury, 'Barrett, and Molyneaux headed a rush to the line. IWhile the pressure on the citadel Was proceeding, the homesters, es usual, in their attempts to foil the attack got off-side and were penalized. From the ensuing loose play, Barnes picked up and almost dropped a goal, a minor resulting. 'nen Bailey dribbled single- handed from the kick out, but Auty and Vichoff by some fast work were the means ef their side gaining a footing for the first time in Warrington 25. In the last few minutes the home team were subjected to a heavy pressure, and Warrington claimed a try,but the decision was against them, and the game ended in a draw, War- rington 3 minors to nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.

The fact that Broughton were the visitors to Wilders- pool on Saturday was sufficient inducement for a large crowd to assemble, but when it is considered that the first meeting this season was in connection with the above-named competition, there was no wonder that the " gate " reached above ordinary dimensions. The day favoured an open game, and both sides had their best available teams, James (" Smack ") Bate again taking his place at half back. Jolley, too, figured on the War- rington side, this player having been summoned to Man- chester to take part in the county match, only to find at the last moment that his services were not required. A stiffish breeze blew towards the railway goal, and Ashton winning the toss defended the pavilion end. Skidmore kicked off, and soon the homesters reached the Broughton quarters, Webster and Jolley bringing about this state of affairs. From the effort by the last- named, a penalty kick was granted against Hampson, but Evans speedily punted the oval back, and Sawyer saved splendidly. Whiteley got away from a pack, but failed to travel far, Bate pulling him up, whilst the next minute saw the Warrington crack passing finely to Heesom, and the pair, with give-and-take transfers, landed the oval once more on the visitors' line. Not to be denied,the Broughton forwards obtained the mastery, and it is due to their energies that the attempts of War- rington were staved off for so lengthened a period. R. and (1. Tomlinson dribbled effectively, and reached half way only to see Jolley and Holmes come away from the ruck, and the game was at the Broughton 2.5 again. Sawyer was floored by Fair. Turner in a long throw-out, and Jolley made away again, the finishing touch being faulty. Skidmore now shone for the visi- tors, and looked like clearing the opposition, until Evans nipped the oval from his feet, and a judicious kick placed the homesters on the aggressive. A tricky bit of work by Bate almost landed a score, whilst some erratic pass- ing by the backs gave Broughton a rare chance for relief. This they readily took, and Sawyer got away along touch, being ultimately pulled up by Heasom. Bosc.ow was next called upon for the first time, and his kick landed the game in the mouth of the Manchester goal. Plumpton was the recipient of a wild pass, and as a consequence Craven relieved. Heesom, Bate, and Webster next passed well, the latter kicking well in close quvrters. The visitor's forwards packed splen- didly, and once more asserted themselves, and half-way being reached Ashton now came to the front with a rush and Turner assisting with a short run, a pass forward spoiled a fine opening. A mark to Plumpton was taken by Ashton, and a good shot registered a minor. This point did not satisfy Warrington; for on the drop-out we saw them combining better, and pretty play by Jolley, Evans, and Donohue. was negatived by Whiteley, R. Tomlinson dribbled out of danger, but Warrington persisted in their attack, and Tears, Holmes, and Hampson reached the line, A. C. Tomlinson saying. Bosoow was once more reached, and S. Tomlinson and Roberts brought about a better state of affairs for Broughton, when a long dribble landed them aggressors for the first time during the match. A spell of stiff scrimmaging ensued, and eventually Bate, Heesom, and Fair. Turner got the oval away, and half- way was reached. Hampson got finely away from a line-out, passing to Jolley, the latter being brought down before he travelled far. The movement led up to War- rington maintaining a permanent position, for the next item of interest was a spirited display between Evans, Bate, and Webster, the latter scoring near the corner, Ashton failing with the difficult place. After another minor had been credited to Warrington a long spell of passing awl fumbling saw Heesom scoring at the popular corner flag, and Turner's shot at goal being short, the interval arrived with Warrington leading by two tries and two minors. Directly on resuming the homesters, aspite the fact that the elements were against them, attacked in earnest. Awakened to the fact that they had not established a sufficient lead during the initial half, when the elements were in their favour, the for- wards abandoned the sluggish style, and settled down to their work in business-like manner. Whiteley passed • across to Piercy, who ran and kicked to BGsoow, giving early promise that he was a dangerous candidate. Boa- cow met the kick in his usual cool style and punted back, a dose he repeated a moment later, in response to one from Tomlinson. By degrees the oval reached the Warrington quarters, but Evans, dodging round a pock, made a grand run, landing his side in the Brough- ton quarters. Twice Bate passed to Webster, but the lengthy three-quarter found the opposition safe in their tackling. Bate tried himself to force a way through with like success, and then a minor fell to Warrington from a drop at goal by Webster. Piercy and Roberts but in good work, but failed to clear, and from a pass by Bate, Plumptoia (who was far from well), ran well, and neutralised an effort by Skidmore ,and Ibbotson.

div.head: RUNCORN v. BIRKENHEAD PARK.
div.p: RUNCORN v. BIRKENHEAD PARK.

These old rivals met for the first time this season on Irwell-lane ground on Saturday afternoon, before 2,000 spectators. Derbyshire and Lee played in place of Rogers and Williams for Runcorn. The only alteration in Birkenhead Park team was that Baxter took the place of Phillips in the forwards. Clauss set the ball in motion against a strong wind fifteen minutes late, and the ball was allowed to roll over the goal line. From the drop out Pendlebury put his team on the attacz by a series of lines-out. The three-quarter flag was reached by the home team, but Clauss and Anderson defended finely, play settling in midfield. The Park was awarded a free kick, which Crompton attended to in his usual style, and Clauss was loudly applauded for breaking up an ominous rush by the home forwards. The Scotchman was instrumental in placing his team on attack, and directly afterwards Crompton robbed Clause grandly, and raced away, but was pulled up by Stratt. The home forwards, however, were not to be denied, and some really fine combined play ended in Riley scoring a try at the corner flag. Faulkner made a good attempt at goal from a difficult place, but the wind carried the ball to the side of the goal posts. The home forwards held the advantage in the scrimmage,and Whistle pulled up Abrams when he had a good opening. Numerous scrimmages enabled Runcorn to visit the Park lines again, and Langley put the finishing touch to a fine piece of play by the Runcornians by placing the ball over the line underneath the post. Crompton placed an easy goal. The visitors were hard pressed for same time, and a free kick to them brought no relief until the forwards compelled Houghton to show some of his defensive powers, the Runcorn back being equal to all emer- gencies, and Strath conceded a touch down from one of his huge punts. A grand passing movement among the home forwards enabled Abrams to score a third try under the posts, Crompton missing an easy goal. The homes- ters now asserted their superiority, but good play by Spence and Anderson put Houghton on his mettle, and he eventually transferred play. Crompton had to leave the field owing to an injury to his ankle, but resumed a few minutes afterwards. The Park team showed very poor combination when they had some favourable opportunities, and Houghton had little difficulty in breaking up their rushes. Play afterwards became rather monotonous owing to scrimmages on the centre. Half-time score—Runcorn 1 goal 2 tries, Birkenhead Park nil.

Riley restarted, and after a lot of desultory play in midfield Runcorn were awarded a free kick, but Faulk- ner's attempt at goal was unsuccessful. The homesters were soon on the attack again, and Langley scored their fourth try, and Hughes landed a goal. The game was interrupted owing to injury to a Park player, the Birkenhead club being left with fourteen men. Just on the call of time Nicholson eluded the home backs and scored .a capital try. - _ .
Final resillt.-11'uneorn 2 goals 2:tries 2 minors (14 points), Birkenhead Park 1 try 1 minor (2 points.)
ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON CRICKET A.F.C. v. ST. ELPIIIN'S.—Thess clubs met on the cricket field on Saturday. A strcng wind was blowing diagonally across the field, and St. Elphin's winning the toss took advantage of this. When the whistle blew, the score was St. Elphin's,4 ; Cricket Club, 3. Cricket Club team: Goal, Forrest ; full l.acks, Chidlaw and Francomb ; half backs, F. Williamson (captain), W. Hannah, and W. D. Jeans; forwards, Reed, J. C. Barlow, A. R. Hoare, G. Williamson, and H. Wright. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION v. LITHERLAND.—These teams met at Arpley on Saturday, to play their return engagement. Forbes kicked off for Warrington, Heaton scoring for the visitors shortly afterwards. The play continued even up to half time, no further score being made. During the second half Warrington played ten men, but nevertheless had the best of matters, but were unable to score, the final result being—Litherland, one goal; Warrington nil. The home team were minus the services of Davies and J. Mather.

RUNCORN V. CASTLE TRUE BLUES.—Played on Runcorn I ground on Saturday. The start was late owing to the inconvenience of the Northwich trains, it being 4.15 when Whiteman kicked off for the home side. A rush was made for the visitors' goal, which was promptly attended to by their backs, and the ball was quickly back in midfield when play was very even, both cus- todians being equally called upon to defend their charges. Then a grand rush was made by the home forwards, [ which resulted in the True Blues' goalkeeper being "sat upon "by Limb and Garvie, but what appeared to the [ spectators to be a palpable goal the referee held other- wise, which caused great disappointment to players and ' spectators alike. After this neither side could claim an advantage, and half time arrived with no score for either team. On restarting the same oven play was seen, and it seemed as if no point would be scored by either side, when from a good pass from their outside right the visitors' centre forward headed through. It was now growing dark, and accurate play was impos- sible. Soon after this Castle centre forward passed to the right inside, who shot the ball through the posts. Offside was at once claimed, but the referee allowed the goal. It was now too dark to see the ball, and the game was stopped, the Blues being lucky winners by two goals to none.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED.

Mr. Fowler was on Thursday waited upon at the Local Government Board by a deputation from the laboUr members of the Lon ion County Council, who desired that local authorities should be urged to under- take works which would give employment to the unem- ployed. The right hon. gentleman pointed out that in the present state of the law this matter rested entirely with the local authorities, but said he would give very careful consideration to the proposals laid before him.

div.head: WHOLESALE MURDERS BY A MAD POLICE AN.
div.p: WHOLESALE MURDERS BY A MAD POLICE AN.

On Tuesday morning a fearful crime was discovered at the Ballynadrumny police barrack, near Enfield, county Kildare. On the pravious night Constable Pil- kington went mad, and murdered Sergeant Rogan, his wife, and three children. The maniac attacked four other childen, and beat one of them 5) savagely with his baton that the little one's recovery is doubtful. Only three constables and the sergeant were stationed at the barracks, and when the tragedy was committed two of the constables were out on patrol. The murderer, who made several desperate efforts to set fire to the barrack, ultimately committed suicide.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

The municipal elections took place on Tuesday in the various boroughs of England and Wales. One of the most determined of the contests was at Liverpool,where the Liberals gained three seats, and will thus be able, for the first time for fifty years, to elect the Mayor on the 9th and to fill the aldermanic vacancies. The Liberals also gained four seats each at Bath and Exeter, and three each at Hereford, Bolton, Crewe, and Ply- mouth. The Conservatives gained four seats each at Newcastle-under Lyme and Macclesfield, and three each at Leeds, Shrewsbury, Portsmouth, Mossley, and Staf- ford. On the whole the balance of gains is in favour of the Liberal party. Owing to the Liberal victories at the municipal elec. tions in niverpool the Conservative members of the City Council have decidrd that" it is undesirable to offer any opposition to the election of Mayor or aldermen by the Radical party."

THE CURE OF SMALLPDX. Sir,—Will you kindly f. ive the following space for the benefit of the public at large. A writer in the " Liverpool Mercury some time ago asserted that the worst case of smallpox could be cured in three days by the use of cream-of-tartar, an ounce dissolved in a pint of water to be drunk at intervals, when cold. This is pronounced to be "a never failing remedy." It is certainly simple and probably harmless. —Yours truly, 48, Horsemarket-st.
WILLIAM BESWICK.
LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.

Sin—Will you allow me, quite unofficially, yet very earnestly, to urge upon the readers of your paper the claims of Lifeboat Saturday. There can hardly be any nobler object on which to bestow both our sympathy and money than the National Lifeboat Institution, Its splendid work is too widely known to need either praise or description, but, to carry our that work on an adequate scale, it needs a much larger income. Hence has arisen, and not without reason, the Lifeboat Saturday movement in which we are now asked to take our part. It is replied that trade is bad, and this, alas, cannot be denied, but the duty remains to give what we can, and wish, at least, that it might have been more. It is also objected that Warrington should be free fr6m , claim because it it is an inland town, but so too is ' Manchester, where the movement originated, and so too are Stockport, Bolton, and Bury, which have followed its successful example. Let not Warrington be behind, even though the procession is abandoned. As the Lifeboat Institution is national in name, let it be truly national as well in the range of those voluntary contributions by which alone it is supported.—Yours faithfully,

div.head: FRANK K. FREEStON.
div.p: FRANK K. FREEStON.
THE BIRCH FOR "A LEARNER." " Full of sound and fury signifying nothing."

Sir,—Your correspondent is great on the emotions. He can even detect in me the non-existent feeling of fury, in the attempt to demonstrate which he makes manifest the fact that another emotion dominates his little soul—spite. This female feline feeling has been aroused within him by my having been on his track,and his corns, on a former occasion, when he brayed under another disguise. He has changed his skin, but the bray is still there, and by that, like" Bottom,' he stands " translated." As" a learner," and a backward one, we must feed his mind with fables. Let him learn the fable of the fly and the chariot wheel, wherein the fly, riding on the knave of the wheel, exclaimed " What a dust we are raising !" Risibility, and not fury, is the emotion I experience, when I find this conceited insect pluming himself upon having raised such a dust! . .

If" A Learner's" conceit is laughable, so is he when in the agonies of argumentalon. Take a few sweet examples. "For if man" says this profound first- form philosopher, " if man along with the lower animals shares the same invaluable and irreplacable possession how can he be justified in taking away life at all I' Man has no right in consequence to kill even the vermin which infest his garden or his nightcap." Now, first let me ask who said man had the right to kill ? I hare asked—Where does man get this right ? But I have never conceded it. But I freely concede to" A Learner" the right to exterminate the intruders into his garden or his nightcap By the very fact of that intrusion they have forfeited their lives to man in his own self-defence. . . _ _

But the gem of our novice's logic is to be found em- bedded in his concluding paragraph and is, when dis- interred, a jewel of first water ! In a former letter I 1 have said that some savages assume the prerogative of Inature and take upon themselves to decide who, among ' the sick and weak, shall survive. Then mark, if you can for laughing, the conclusion this budding Aristotle draws from these premises ! Hear him—" But the study of !nature is the special province of science. Accordingly Mr. Peers would exclude from snch study the cultured naan of the 19th century and fling the study of nature into the hands of the savage." It is almost inconceivable' that a person who pretends to discuss these questions ' should flounder as hopelessly over such simple proposi- tions! One would have thought that even a first form learner would have been able to distinguish between "the assumption of the prerogative of nature " and "the study of nature." I am net quite decided whether I attribute this bemuddletnent to dishonest disengenuity or to his native incapacity, the one to blame tho other to 1 I pity. le'charity, let us pity him ! The idea that be- cause a says a kills his old father as a useless incum- brance, the, (fore" the cultured man of the 19th cen- tury is excluded from the study of nature " is surely a triumph of reasoning. Shades of Watts. Mills, and Whatley. what are we coming to P What we have come to is to see " A Learner" afflicted with the caeoethea scribencji, floundering in a logical slough of his own making. The conclusion from this is that we have a super-abundance of writers but are rath.!x short of thitzkers. To write specious commonplaces is easy ; but this facility is clearly bought at the price it entails —of the loss of the faculty of right judgment. But there is no fear of the world being_ stricken with a sad- ness by too much logical lucidity so long as we have " Learners " to laugh at.—Yours, Esc. JOHN PEERS. Penketh. Oct. 30th, 1892.

WARRINGTON SANITARIAS. Sir,—A stranger walking through the streets of War- rington, and observing their disorder and want of eleanliness would naturally enough conclude t hat we had no sanitarians in this quarter, and this view would be strongly emphasised by the abominable odours that would assail him at every turn. But a little further acquaintance with the venerable borough would dis- sipate such a hasty and unfavourable conclusion. Scanning the columns of the " Examiner," he would discover, to his astonishment, that we are blessed with a real, living Sanitary Committee guided by a head of superior wisdom and experience, and ably supported by a competent tail. His information would excite a desire for a sight and hearing of these wise and able men, and seizing the opportunity presented by a family washing day at the town Half, our stranger would repair thither to have his curiosity gratified. And truly the spectacle there presented would compel his hair to stand on end with admiration. The splendid grammar and elocution of the speakers, their wonderful grasp of the subject in hand, and the cleverness with which they manipulated their dirty linen, as becometh sanitarians of a high order, would make a powerful impression upon his mind. Sur- veying the heated partisans through his eyeglass, and carried away by their peculiar rhetoric, the conviction would seize upon his soul that here in Warrington, at least, we have a Bumbledom whose members are skilled adepts in sanitary and other washings and whitewash- ings. After anexperience of this kind our visitor would, sf course, be anxious to see the practical outcome of the screaming and gesticulating at the Town Hall. Follow- ing in the wake of a procession of sanitary locomotives, with his pocket handkerchief applied to his mouth and nose, he would have a convincing demonstration of the provisions made by the Sanitarians for sweetening our streets, and preserving health and decency. And this demonstration would be clenched by the sights of the Intercepting Depot, to which the "Dolly Vardens " would lead him. Surveying the barn-like structure and its unsavoury- and repulsive sur- roundings lie would cry out, what a thing of beauty and grace is this amongst the homes of the poor, yea at their very doors. It must be a veritable art teacher to their simple souls. True, the noise and stench emitted from it might stagger his faith a little ; but then he would remember that the Sanitarians were of opinion that the noses of the poor were not made to distinguish r, would no doubt form a beotwnetehnepu whole,re oaund rs tsrtai nn gk e. high opinion of the completeness and efficacy of our sanitary arrangements, and conclude that they must entail a heavy charge upon the ratepayers. Let me assure the vod man, on the authority of the Borough Treasurer, that our expenditure for sanitary purposes is a mere flea bite when compared

( rcr(rf r .f • t THE EXAINIINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5 1892 with the solid and lasting benefits which i THE BOROUGH OF WIDNES. it confers on the community. For the paltry sum of nine thousand, two hundred pounds sterling per all AUDI, we have an unlimited supply of the vilest and most deleterious gases carted about the town at all hours of the day,and then concentrated in centres whose abomin- able and deadly influence is more or less felt in every Quarter. Yes, at a cost equivalent to a yearly rate of three shillings and nine pence upon every man, woman, and child in the borough. We have all these blessings liberally showered upon us by a set of men who never tire of blowing their own trumpets; and posing as sani- tary reformers of the first water. The Hope Hospital is another specimen of the incom- petence of our sanitarians. When smallpox first broke out, it surely was the bounden duty of the Guardians of public health to make immediate and comfortable pro vision for the unfortunate victims of this infectious disease. But what have they done ? Extemporised an old and deserted iron works in a thickly-populated dis- trict into a hospital for its treatment. The selection of such a site for such a purpose reveals a thoughtless- ness and an ignorance of, or disregard for, the require- ments of the case that are truly lamentable. Every- body knows that quietness and sleep are two most iin- portant factors in dealing with disease. But these con- ditions are absolutely impossible in Dallam-lane, which is this dirtiest and noisiest quarter in the town. OBSERVER.

Since the Charter of Incorporation was granted by Her Majesty's Privy Council in June, Widnes has been a borough, but the system of Government remained unaltered, and the inhabitants scarcely realised the change, until Tuesday, when the first municipal election took place. The dignity has not been conferred upon the place because of its antiquity, for Widnes is of very modern growth, l.ut rather because of its importance in the indus- trial world and the wealth of its possessions. Fifty years ago Widnes was a rural spot, with rich orchards and smiling meadows, and the Mersey's banks were wooded slopes where the angler and fisheruaan most did congregate. It woe especially noted for its eels, or snigs, and Mersey-road is even now commonly designated " Snig-lane " and that barren spot where the docks are situate is mis- named by ancient and modern watermen on the river as " Woodend " as though in memory of the plantations that once graced the spot. It was in 1846 that the first step was taken towards fame as a centre of inaustry and to the dignity of a muni- cipal corporation. In that year Mr. Wm. Gossage, Mr. John Hutchinson, and Mr. M'Clellan recognised the advantages the Once offered for trade, and con- structed alkali works there, and from this small beginning has sprung up a town which has become world-wide known as the Chemical Metropolis There are now fourteen alkali works, three copper works, three founderies, one large soap works, and numerous other small works and trades are carried on. The borough has an area of 3089 acres, of which 1490 acres are occupied by houses, works, and streets, 1489 acres of agricultural land, and 160 acres of railways, docks, and canals, and included within its borders are the ancient village of Palm- worth, and the village of Appleton. There are no fewer than six passenger railway stations,five goods stations,and two docks,and the facilities afforded for trade by railway and water, are such as few muni- cipalities ot a similar size can boast. The Local Board was constituted in 1865, with nine members, afterwards increased to 15, Mr. Wm. Gossage, one of the pioneers of the town, was the first chairman, and his son, Mr. F. H. Gossage is by common consent fixed upon as the first Mayor of the borough. The history of the Board is not one of uninterrupted pros- perity, but the bright side eclipses altogether the black, which n:ay be lost sight of altogether. In 1867 the Board purchased the Gas works at a cost of £8,927, and up to last year there: had been expended upon them £67,566. In the same year the Board also took over the water supply from a private company, and up to the present time the expenditure on capital account on this undertaking has been about £171,000. These figures give some idea 'of how these works have been extended and developed, and this farsighted policy of the first rulers of the town is seen in the fact that the inhabit- ants reap the advantage in the supply of gas and water at far cheaper rates than can be obtained in neighbour- ing towns, and there is also a handsome profit each year. Besides acquiring these important undertakings the Board have provided other public works. The market buildings and :land adjoining, cost £9,800; the Town Hall, yet unfinished, and Free Library, £9,200 ; the Infectious Diseases Hospital. £4,400 ; the Accident Hospital; £2,797 (of which £1,797 was raised by private subscriptions) ; and stables and stores £2,000, and re- cently fire engine and station and firenaen's cottages. Altogether the Local Board during its 27 year's existence expended £300,000 upon permanent public works. The mileage of public sewers is about 13 and there are 34 miles of streets and 10f miles of back passages in the to wn. There is a School Board of 11 members, which has had an existence since 1874, and this body has erected at a cost of £3B,sBs:three schools providing accommodation for 8,992 children. There are also five denominational schools, which accommodate 3,381 children, and Farn- worth Grammar School, which has an endowment ot £7O per annum and provides six free scholarships of £8 for three years. There is also a Science and Art School, which has done admirable work in the past, but which will be superseded by a fechnical Institute on a much larger and grander scale in the near future. Amongst other public places there are tour churches of the Establishment, three Roman Catholic churches, 15 other places of worship, three political clubs, a theatre and a drill hall.

In regard to population, Widnes has increased by leaps and bounds. In 1851 the population was 3,217, and in the next decade it more than doubled, being returned at 6,893. In 1871 the number of inhabitants was 14,359, in 1881, 24,918 and in 1890, 29,971, and is now reckoned at 30,612. The rateable value of the town has also enormously increased. The gross value of the township in 1867 was £37,625, the rateable value £31,846 and the assessable value for the purposes of the general district rate, £26,755. Last year the gross value of the town was £184,405, the rateable value £139,339 and the assessable value £114,448. The expenditure on general district rate account was £2,102 in 1871, £10,372 in 1881, and £13,079 last year. In estimating the importance of the town it should not be omitted that Widnes is the centre of a Parliamentary division having a population of 64,507 at the last census, and returns one member, Mr. J. S. Gilliat being the pre- sent representative. The town also sends two represen- tatives to the Lancashire County Council. It will thus be seen that all the necessaly qualifica- tions for a Corporate borough are not wanting, and the hope may fittingly he expressed that under thl rule and guidance of aldermen and councillors there will be con- tinued prosperity in trade, increased comfort for the people, and more extended means for the social and in- tellectual advancement for those whose lot is cast in what is often called in allusion to its trade, the black spot on the Mersey.
TUE FIRST MUNICIPAL ELECTION.

' The first outward manifestation of the end of the old administration, and the commencement of a new regime took place on Tuesday, when the burgesses were called upon to elect 18 gentlemen to the position of town councillors. It was at one time thought that the elec- tion would have been a straightforward honest fight be- tween the two political parties. Circumstances transpired which altered the complexion of affairs considerably. In the first place the Conservative party lost no fewer than 500 vntes in the Revision Court, through the objection of Mr. Shores the Liberai agent, and they did not feel inclined to measure swords. Then the action of the " Liberal Club Caucus " did net give satisfaction. Some old and well tried servants of the public in the Local Board were thrown over for younger, and inex- perienced men and the selection of candidates was far from being approved. The introduction of politics was condemned by a number of Liberals, and the consequence was a lack of that coheion so essential in a political battle. Nomination day shewed that there were 32 candidates for the 18 seats, and they consisted of five Liberals, three Tories. seven Nationalists, and seventeen Independents, the names of whom are all set out in the results. An eleventh hour surprise was sprung upon the electors by the issue of a placard by Mr. Joshua Midwood, one of the Liberal candidates for Simms Cross, who stated that he had withdrawn for reasons he would divulge later. It quickly transpired that Mr. Midwood had been accused by Mr. Sadler, one of his colleagues, of causing his canvassers to solicit plumper. from Mr. Midwood's tenants. The allegation was indignantly denied, and the names of the informants demanded, but Mr.Sadler did not feel at liberty to divulge them. It is un- derstood that Mr. Midwood will take legal proceedings to compel Mr.Sadler to withdraw t 111 a Bev d mpulations,and also to publish an apology. Another disturbing influence was an attempt made to induce the Catholics to vote only for Catholic candidates, which would have been a serious matter for Major Wareing and Mr. Shores, but the Irish National League stood firmly by their Liberal allies. The polling arangements were on the most complete and satisfactory scale. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., pro- visional mayor, acted as returning officer, and the ar- rangements were carried out on his behalf by Mr. 11. S. Oppenheim, acting Town Clerk, who was assisted by his deputy, Mr. T. Craik. Throughout the day' the town was enveloped in fog, and the oppressive atmosphere apparently had an effect upon the electors, for there was a complete lack of excitement. The polling, however. was of a steady and continuous character, the greatest crush occurring between six and eight o'clock in the evening. An effort had been made to get the United Alkali Co. to close their works, but it did not succeed. A large number of tradesmen, however, closed their shops in the afternoon. At eight o'clock precisely, the polling booths were closed and the ballot boxes conveyed to the Town Hall with all despatch. The counting of the votes was carried out by the presiding officers and their clerks, under the supervision of Mr. Goseage. Nearly the whole of the candidates were present, but they were also represented as follows :—Mr. W. Patten for Messrs. Btrlow, Lengton, and Shuttleworth ; Mr. Valentine for Messrs. Bullough and Christie; Mr. Rowe for Messrs. Fitzpatrick and O'Donnell ; Mr. Stuart Deacon for Major Wareing ;. Mr. G. Outram for Mr. G. I. Neil ; Mr. F. Lawrinson for Mr. S. Owens ; Mr. G. Davies for Mr. Sadler ; Mr. Atherton for Mr. Gerrard ; Mr. Hough for Mr. F. Neil ; Mr. Faulkner for Mr. Quinn ; Mr. Delaney for Mr. Singleton ; Mr. Carroll for Mr.Tilley ; Mr.Treacy for Mr. Brookes ; Mr. Flynn for Mr. Carney ; Mr. Eaves for Mr. Hemingway ; Mr. D. Lewis for Mr. Shores; Mr. Harper for Mr. Williamson •, Mr. Emery for Mr. Brown ; Mr. Hargreaves for Mr. Hodgkiwon ; Mr.Shuffiebotham for Mr. Smith ; and Mr. S. Jackson for Mr. Timmis. Not- withstanding a cold raw wind and a dense fog, some hundreds of people awaited the results in front of the Town Hall, and a cheer arose when Mr. Gossage stepped oe to the balcony at 1015, and made the declarations for the several wards. The first three in each instance are elected.

Workers and convey- ances were very plentiful, but Mr. Wright appeared to have had a small share. Voting proceeded without excitement. Result.

FRAUDS ON AN AUSTRALIAN BANK.
HEAVY SENTENCES.

SYSNEY, Thursday.—The second trial of the late directors and manager of the Australian Banking Com- pany for defrauding the shareholders has been proceed- ing for several days past. On Thursday the jury, after deliberating for three hours, brought in a verdict of guilty against F. Abigail, one of the directors, and formally Minister of Mines. They also convicted Roderick M'Namara, late manager. The rest of the defendants were acquitted. The judge sentenced Abigail to five years imprisonmext, and M‘Natnata to seven years.

div.head: FAREWELL VISIT.
div.p: FAREWELL VISIT.

Last evening week, the Ilindoo preacher, Gnana- mutthu J. Israel, paid a farewell visit to Penketh. He is about to return to his missionary work in India. Mr. Israel had with him a large variety of Indian wares and curiosit!es. These were on sale in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The silk shawls, fans, &c., presented a very gay and attractiv- appearance. The proceeds are in aid of his work among the poor children of Madras. A very inte- resting feature was the display of dolls, in different costumes, given by Penketh friends as prizes in Onanamutthu's school. There was no charge for admittance anci there was a good attendance, the aales being very fair. Mr. Israel also gave a abort address, in which he thanked his friends at Pen- keth. Mrs. R. Garnett, Mrs. C. E. Parker and the Misses Garnett presided at the stalls.

div.head: FRODSHAIf PAROCHIAL CODIMITTRE.
div.p: FRODSHAIf PAROCHIAL CODIMITTRE.

The minutes of this Committee, October 26th, reported that it had been resolved that application be made to the Local Government Board under section 176 of the Public Health Act, 1875, to declare the provisions of this Act in force in urban districts, to be in force in the contributory place of Frodsham, and to invest the Guardians of Runcorn Union as the Sanitary Authority for the rural sanitary district of the Union with all the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabilities, and obli- gations of the urban authority, under the said Act with in the contributory place of Frodsham. On the motion of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. Williams, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.
div.p: INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

The Chairman said two meetings of the committee had been called but no quorum had been present. It was very essential that the question of the proposed hospital should lee dealt with by a strong committee.— Mr. Heywood suggested that the Committee remain as it was.and that a special whip be sent to the members. —The Chairman proposed that Messrs. Heywood, Williams, Brand reth, Pickering, and Baguley. be added to the Committee, and, that the members who did not attend be communicated with by the Clerk.— Mr. Heywood thought the committee already appointed should have the responsibility of the matter. It was too bad, he remarked, that the willing horse should always be urged. He moved that the committee remain as it was.—Mr. Williams seconded.—Mr. Rrandreth seconded the Chairman's motion, and urged that the matter should be proceeded with with promptitude. He mentioned that a boy was suffering from typhoid fever at Rock Savage who was sleeping with his mother and sister.—The Medical Officer reported that this was cor- rect, the child being 7 years of age. He had only just received the report, and had not had time to make enquines.—Mr. Brandreth moved an amendment that the Clerk make the best arrangement he could with the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for the reception of any cases of infectious disease within the Union. The amendment was seconded, and four voted for it and four for the original proposition, which was carried by the Chairman's casting vote. There was no other business of importance.

div.head: ANOTHER TERRIBLE CRIME AT OLDHAM.
div.p: ANOTHER TERRIBLE CRIME AT OLDHAM.

Another terrible crime was committed at Oldham on Wednesday, a man known as James Jackson, who had formerly been in the army, murdering his sister and afterwards attemptisg to commit suicide. The man and his victim both lived with their mother. and it is said that Jackson's peculiar temper caused frequent quarrels in the house. In consequence of one of the man's outbursts the mother declined to stay in the house with him, and went to take the place of her daughter at the mill where the latter worked. Early in the after- noon Jackson killed his sister by cutting her throat, and afterwards inflicted injuries upon himself which will possibly prove fatal,

div.head: BASTARDLY RAILWAY OUTRAGE. PLACING STONES ON THE UAILWAY NEAR
div.p: BASTARDLY RAILWAY OUTRAGE. PLACING STONES ON THE UAILWAY NEAR
LEEDS.

The Leeds police are investigating the circumstances of a series of attempts to vTreck the trains on the North- Eastern Railway near Leeds. On Friday night a train from Leeds to 'Hull crashed into several large stones which had been placed upon the metals, and the shock greatly alarmed the passengers. When the train was examined at Gascoigne Wood Junction, between Leeds and Selby, a large piece of stone was found wedged be- tween the brake rods and one of the front carriages, thus preventing the brake from working. The police incline to the belief that the attempts are in the nature of mischief rather than malice, though they are, of course, none the less dangerous on that account. •

div.head: COTTON TRADE CRISIS.
div.p: THE COTTON TRADE CRISIS.

The Executive Committees of the operatives' trade unions in the different branches of the cotton trade met in Manchester on Saturday. Matters of importance to the trade generally were dealt with. The Legislative Committee of the United Textila Workers drafted an Eight Hours Bill for cotton operatives. This Bill will be submitted to members of Parliament, and "efforts are to be made" to obtain support for the measure when it is brought before the House of Commons. With regard to the proposals for outside arbitration in the threatened lock-out in the spinning trade which were suggested from Liverpool, the secretary of the Amalgamated Asso- ciation of Operative Spinners, Mr. Mawdsley was in- structed to thank "the Mayors of Liverpool and Manchester for their well-meant offer to meddle" in the dispute and to decline their proposal. The Textile Workers' Committee will also endeavour to obtain the amendn-.ent of the" particulars" clause in the amended Factory and Workshops Act, 1891, as difficulties arise in the giving of particulars to workpeople by the em. plovers. The cardroom workers also held a meeting, and resolved to resist the five per cent. reduction.

div.head: INTERESTING LICENSING APPEAL.
div.p: INTERESTING LICENSING APPEAL.

In the Queen's Bench on Thursday an interesting licensing appeal was heard. The appellant, Mary Cowap, of the Horse Inn, Little Leigh, Cheshire, had been fined for selling drink during prohibited hours. It was alleged that Altred Halsey, a railway porter, had ebtained beer 1 at the inn at nine o'clock on Sunday morning; but the appellant, in seeking to get the conviction quashed, urged that the man was a bona-fide traveller, and that he was entitled to refreshment. The police contention was that the man, who had been (.1a duty at Acton Bridge station, had not travelled beyond the three-mile limit; but, on the other hand, it was stated on behalf of the appellant that Halsey had breakfasted before six o'clock and tra- velled nearly seven miles. Mr. Justice Hawkins did not see why a man should be deprived of refreshment because he could not get home, and said he desired to be gener- ous in favour of men of this class and to give a liberal interpretati-.n to the Act. Mr. Wood, for the respond- ents, said the man should have supplied himself with refreshment. Mr. Justice Hawkins asked the learned counsel if he thought the Legislatuie intended that working-men should have stale beer; and Mr. Wood, amid laughter, replied, " Most obviously, my Lord." Baron Pollock held that Halsey was a traveller for the whole of the journey, from his home to the station, and from the station to the inn, and that he was perfectly entitled to obtain refreshment. The conviction was therefore quashed.

div.head: THIRSK RAILWAY DISASTER.
div.p: THE THIRSK RAILWAY DISASTER.
THE QUEEN'S SYMPATHY.

The injured persons in Thirsk Hospital are making fairly satisfactory progress, but Ewart, the driver of the ill-fated express, is still in a dangerous condition. A Royal message of sympathy, received in Thirsk yester- day morning, has been commhnicated to the sufferers, to whom it has afforded considerable gratification. Major Marindin has inspected the scene of the calamity prior to opening the inquiry.

div.head: TOTAL. WRECK OF AN ENGLISH ' -BATTLESHIP. LOSS OF H.M.S. HOWE.
div.p: TOTAL. WRECK OF AN ENGLISH ' -BATTLESHIP. LOSS OF H.M.S. HOWE.

Madrid, Thursday. Contrary to the announcement made yesterday at the Ministry of Marine that the British ironclad Howe had been refloated, and was expected to be able to put into dock and repair in a few days, a private telegram from Corunna, dated 3 p.rn.,yesterday,affirms that the loss of the Howe is inevitable, the vessel having grounded on the sunken rocks on Perero Bank, at the entrance to the harbour, opposite the Castello de Palm a, and strained herself seriously in consequence.. Signals of distress were made, in consequence of which the Spanish gunboat Prosperidad and boats from the Arsenal of Ferrol proceeded to the Howe to render assistance in lightening her. The officers and crew and their effects have been transferred from the Howe to the flagship. All are safe. The Howe entered the harbour sailing in the wake of the flagship.

div.head: INSULTING MR. T. M. HEALY.
div.p: INSULTING MR. T. M. HEALY.
A SCENE AT THE DUBLIN FOUR COURTS.

Yesterday, in the Queen's Bench Court, Dublin, just as the election petition judges, who had an application in the matter of the East Clare election before them, were about to rise, Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P., who was one of the council in the case, immediately returned into court and said he had to call their lordships' attention to a personal matter which had occurred as he was leaving the court. This person (pointing to a middle aged men, who had been brought into court in charge of a constable), had, he said, insuited him in the grossest manner both as to a private matter and as to the way be had conducted the cise.—Mr. Justice O'Brien: Do know who tbeprisoner is 2—Mr. HealE : No, my but be his -done it before.—The alleged off, nder said Mr. Healy MU mistaken.—Mr. Healy : lam net mistaken. It is not the first time this man has insulted ine.—Mr. Justice O'Brien : This is a very unpleasant matter. You complain that when having the court this man insulted you—Mr.- Healey : lie usol most insulting observations, sun of so foul a diaracter that I don't care to repeat them. 'These observations not only affected myself but my wife.—Ultitnately, the man was released from custody for the present. Mr. Healy saying he did not press for severe punishment.

div.head: SHIP CANIU.
div.p: THE SHIP CANIU.
THE PROSPECTS OF A DIVIDEND.

A meeting of Ship Canal shareholders was held on Tuesday night. in Manchester, to hear an address from Mr. Marshall Stevens on the revenue prospects of the canal once it is completed. Mr. Stevens submitted a number of tables to show that in seven years after the opening of the canal itwonld be earning a net revenue of at least £1,500,000, a sum sufficient to pay 5 per cent upon an expenditure of thirty millions, He estimated that in two years after the opf,ning of the canal there would be revenue enough, counting in what would come from the Bridgewater and other sources, to pay all working expenses and provide interest on a capis al of Biteen
LECTURE AT RUNCORN.

" •On Wednesday evening, under the auspices of the Runcorn Brunswick Improvement Society, an interesting lecture on the Ship Canal, was delivered by Mr. C. A. Timmins, in the Brunswick School. There was a large and appreciative attendance,and the chair was occupied 'by Mr. Simister.—The Lecturer, in speaking of the Manchester Ship Canal, referred to its being the largest work of its kind ever-undertaken in this country. Be alluded to the Parliamentary inquiry regarding the Bill lasting 175 days, and the expenditure thereon being ' £150,000. The length of the canal was 351 miles, 21 of which were tidal, and the remainder a canalized river. The minimum depth was 281 t., and the lock sills were 2311. below water level ; the width at water level being 12011. He illustrated the work that had been ac- complished from E4stham to Salford locks by means of 120 slides from photographs taken by himself. A cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Timmins on the motion of Mr. J. D. Jones, seconded by Mr. Rawlinson. Mr. Crosby wail also thanked for manipulating the lantern.

THE SHIP CANAL LOAN. PROPOSALS BY THE CHAIRMAN OF THE COM- PANY. _ _ _

Lord Egerton, the chalin-l-a-n- of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, has addressed a letter to the Mayor of Manchester with reference to the prorosed further loan •of two millions necessary to complete the canal. On behalf of the shareholders he makes the following pro- male :—First, that the Humber of directors should be Increased from 15 to 21; second, that the lenders of the £5,000,000 of new debentures (£3,000,000 of which have already been issued to the Corporation of Manchester) should have eleven representatives on the Board—that I is, a majority of one over the representatives of the shareholders ; and third, that an arrangement should be made by whlch the representatives of the share- ' holders shall from the date of the opening of the canal for traffic to Manchester have control over the revenue administration of the canal, including the fixing of the tolls and rates to be levied. The Board. his Lordship adds, ha‘ e been informed that the shareholders are not inclined to I,ok with favour on the condition that the lenders shall have voting power at the shareholders' meetings. As the Corporation have decided to promote a separate bill in Parliament, the Board are obliged to introduce a bill of their own. SHOCKING ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL. _

INQUEST. On Saturday morning, Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Ship Canal Hospital, Latchford, on the body of Edmund Tunstall, of 8, Vienna-street, Everton, Liverpool, a quarryman employed at Weston Point, who met with an accident on Tuesday, and who died at the Hospital the following day. Thomas Blease Tunstall, Benmore-street, Liverpool, son of the deeeased, said his father had been engaged as a quarryman on the canal about four years. Witness last saw him alive about three weeks before the accident occurred. His father was dead when he arrived at the Hospital. Alfred Owen Weston said that on Tuesday morning he was engaged a orking with the deceased on an Bft. bench in Weston Quarry lowering stones. Thee bad the same morning lowered two large stones into I ne quarry successfully. The next stone they tried to h,osen with a bar, but did not succeed. They raised t stone with a wedge, and put the chain round it, and afterwards fastened it to the crane chain. Hearing one of the other workmen shout, witness ran Out of the way of the stone. Then he saw the deceased at the bottom of the quarry, which was 17ft. deep from the bench. He went at once to the bottom, and found the deceased conscious, but severely injured. He was conveyed to the Latchford hospital. Witness considered the weight of the crane chain caused the one to fall. The jib of the crane was 30ft. from the

benching, and was slightly lower.—Wm. Hughes, Weston, said that he was employed in the quarry on Tuesday. When the crane chain was fastened to the one around the stone he shouted to the workmen be- cause he saw the stone move slightly. The deceased at- tempted to get away, but the edge of the stone caught him in the ribs, knocked him down on the bench, and rolled over his body. The stone continued its course down to the bottom of the quarry, and the deceased fell headlcng after it. It was his opinion that the • 1 weight of the crane chain (mused the stone to over- balance.—The hospital doctor deposed that the deceased ; was received into the hospital at ten o'clock on Tuesday t morning. He was suffering from a crush of the right I leg, a broken thigh, and a broken arm. Amputation . was performed in the presence of two other doctors,. but the deceased died on Wednesday from loss of blood t and shock to the system.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned by the jury.

D UNOORN UNION.—SCHOOL MISTItESS WANTED.— The Guardians of the above Union desire tg receive applications for the office of Schoolmistress, for the Girls' School at the Workhouse, Dutton (average attendance 27). The salary will be £2O per annum, with board, washing, and lodging in the Workhouse, and am allowance of £4 per annum in lieu of beer, together with such further sum, as may be awarded by the Certificate of the Local overnment Board. WAGES IN BELFAST. • A FIVE PER CENT. REDUCTION. A rednction in wages, averaging 5 per cent, all round, took effect yesterday, in all the shipbuilding and en- gineering works in Belfast. The reduction affects about 12,000 operatives. SUBSIDENCE OF A " SLAG " HEAT. TWO MEN KILLED. A shocking accident happened ay L_eli.ds Steel Works yesterday, whereby two labarkis,lgst their lives.. A number of men were engaged" removing a huge pile of " slag " when it suddenly subsided. Two men were killed an the spot, and • four others were entombed by the falling mass, but were afterwards rescued. THE AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION IN ULSTER. MEETING, OF TENANT FARMERS. The tenant farmers on the estates of the Marquis of Dufferin and several other Ulster landlords held a meet- ing on Thursday night, at Sillyleagh, near Belfast, and unanimously adopted a series of resolutions declaring that in consequence of the agricultural depression any- thing short of a reduction of 50 per cent. in rents would be totally inadequate.
